creation-light: The Bible begins with the most important sentence ever written.
In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
Before there was a sun, a sky, or even time, there was God.
Everything else has a beginning. He doesn't.
This was written for a people who were surrounded by neighbors telling very different stories.
In those stories the world came out of a fight between gods, and people were made as slaves to do the gods' work.
Genesis says something completely different.
One God, with no rival, spoke, and everything came to be.
At first the earth was empty and dark and covered with water.
Then God said, let there be light, and there was light.
He separated the light from the darkness.
He called the light day and the darkness night. That was the first day.
On the next days God made the sky, then the dry land and the seas, and he filled the land with plants and trees.
He made the sun, the moon, and the stars to mark days and seasons.
He filled the water with fish and the sky with birds.
Then he made every animal on the land.
After each step the Bible says, God saw that it was good.
Creation was not an accident or a mistake.
God made it and he loved it.
On the sixth day he did something different.
He said, let us make mankind in our image.
Men and women are the only part of creation described this way.
Every human being, of every age and race, carries something of God.
He blessed them and told them to take care of the earth.
On the seventh day God rested.
He blessed that day and made it holy.
This is where the Sabbath comes from. God was not tired.
He was showing us that life is not only work.
It also has rest and worship in it.
Why does this matter?
Because it tells us who we are and who God is.
The world was made on purpose, by a good God, and so were you.
John's gospel begins with the same words, in the beginning, and says that Jesus was there too.
All things were made through him.
What happened after?
The very next chapter shows a man and a woman in a garden, and then it shows how they lost it.
But the world God made was never thrown away.
The Bible ends with God making all things new, and the light comes back for good.
What does this mean for us today?
It means you are not an accident.
You were made by someone who looked at what he had made and called it good.
That includes you, even on the days you don't feel good.
It also means that darkness is not the end of the story.
God's first act was to speak light into the dark. He still does that.
When life feels empty, shapeless, and dark, the same God is able to say a word and begin again.
That is why this story is so important.
It is the foundation of everything else in the Bible.
If God made everything, then everything belongs to him, including your life, your worries, and your future.
You can start every day knowing that you were made on purpose, and that the one who made you is still speaking.
creation-eve: After God made the sky, the land, the sea, and every animal, he made the first man.
The Bible says God formed him from the dust of the ground and breathed life into his nose.
His name was Adam, which is close to the Hebrew word for ground.
He was alive because God breathed into him.
God planted a garden in a place called Eden and put Adam there to take care of it.
It had rivers, trees full of fruit, and everything he needed.
God was close, and walked with them in the garden.
It was the way the world was meant to be.
God said that Adam could eat from every tree in the garden except one, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. That was the only rule.
Adam also got his first job.
God brought every animal to him, and Adam named each one.
Then comes a surprising line.
For the first time in the story, God says something is not good.
It is not good for the man to be alone.
Adam had a perfect garden, a perfect job, and God himself nearby, and still the Bible says he needed another person.
We were made for each other.
Among all the animals, no partner was found for him.
So God made Adam fall into a deep sleep.
He took part of the man's side, and from it he made a woman.
The word for side is the same word used for the side of the ark and the side of the tabernacle.
Many readers have noticed that she was not taken from his head to rule over him or from his feet to be walked on, but from his side, to stand beside him.
God brought her to Adam, and Adam was so happy that the first poem in the Bible came out of his mouth.
At last, he said, this is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. He called her woman.
Later he would name her Eve, which means life.
Then the writer adds a sentence about us.
This is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh.
Jesus quoted this verse himself when people asked him about marriage.
He said it goes back to the beginning, and what God has joined, no one should separate.
The Bible says the man and woman were naked and felt no shame.
They had nothing to hide from each other or from God.
That is how close they were.
Why does this matter?
It shows that marriage and family came from God.
Before there were kings, cities, or temples, there was a man and a woman and a promise that they belonged to each other.
It also shows that men and women are equal.
They are made of the same stuff and both carry God's image.
What happened after?
Right after this scene comes the garden's greatest test.
They would soon throw all this away, and we will see how in the next scene.
Even so, God did not give up on marriage or on people.
The Bible ends with a wedding feast.
What does this mean for us today?
If you are lonely, this story says that is not a flaw in you.
God made people to need people.
Wanting love and friendship is part of how he built you.
It also says that relationships are a gift to treasure, not something to take for granted.
The first good thing in human life was not a skill or a job.
It was another person who would stand beside you.
That is why this story is so important.
It tells us where love, marriage, and family come from, and who they belong to.
Whether you are married, single, or hoping, the God who looked at Adam and said it is not good to be alone still pays attention to who is beside you.
eden: In the garden, God had given Adam and Eve everything.
They could eat from any tree except one.
God told them that if they ate from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, they would die.
It was a rule given by someone who loved them and wanted to keep them safe.
Then a serpent showed up.
The Bible says it was the most clever of all the wild animals.
Later writers in the Bible say that behind the serpent was Satan, God's enemy.
He didn't start with a lie that was easy to spot.
He started with a question.
Did God really say, you must not eat from any tree in the garden?
That question twisted what God had said.
God had said they could eat from all the trees but one.
The serpent made it sound as if God was holding something back.
Eve corrected him a little, but she added to the rule.
Then the serpent said it straight. You will not die.
God knows that when you eat it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God.
Eve looked at the fruit.
It looked good to eat and good to look at, and it seemed like a way to be wise.
The Bible doesn't say it was an apple. It just says fruit.
She took some, ate it, and gave some to her husband, who was with her. He ate it too.
Right away, the promise of the serpent turned out to be false.
Their eyes were opened, but what they saw was that they were naked. Shame was new to them.
They sewed fig leaves together to cover themselves.
And when they heard God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, they hid.
God called out, where are you? He knew where they were.
He was asking them to come out. Adam said he was afraid.
God asked if he had eaten from the tree.
Adam blamed Eve, and he even hinted at blaming God, the woman you put here with me. Eve blamed the serpent. Nobody said, I did it.
God spoke to the serpent first.
He said that one of Eve's descendants would one day crush the serpent's head, even though the serpent would strike his heel.
Christians have read this as the first promise of Jesus, who defeated evil by dying and rising.
God spoke about the future even in his anger.
Then God told Adam and Eve what sin would cost them.
Life would now include pain, hard work, and death.
He sent them out of the garden.
The Bible says God made clothes of animal skin for them before they left.
Even in judgment he took care of them.
He placed angels and a flaming sword at the entrance to guard the way to the tree of life.
Why does this matter?
This is the story of how everything broke.
It explains why there is pain, work that is hard, and death.
It also shows that the first sin was not about fruit.
It was about not trusting that God is good, and about wanting to decide for ourselves what is right.
What happened after?
The very next chapter has their son killing his brother.
Sin spread from there to everyone.
But God's promise to send a rescuer kept the story moving.
The whole Bible is the story of that promise coming true.
At the end, in Revelation, the tree of life comes back and the way is open again.
What does this mean for us today?
We still live east of Eden.
We still hide when we do something wrong.
We still blame someone else.
It helps to see that this goes all the way back, and that God's first question is not a threat. It is where are you?
He is still looking for us.
It also shows how temptation works.
It usually starts by making us doubt that God is good, and that he really wants the best for us.
When you notice that doubt, remember that the serpent's first move was a question.
That is why this story is so important.
It tells us the truth about ourselves, and it also tells us the truth about God.
Even when his children broke the one rule, he came looking for them, covered them, and promised a rescue. That promise was kept.
cain-abel: Adam and Eve had left the garden, and life was now hard. They had two sons.
The first was Cain, and he worked the soil.
The second was Abel, who took care of sheep.
Eve was so thankful at Cain's birth that she said, with the help of the Lord I have brought forth a man.
One day both brothers brought an offering to God.
Cain brought some of the crops he had grown.
Abel brought the first and best of his flock.
The Bible says God looked with favor on Abel and his offering, but not on Cain and his.
It doesn't say exactly why.
The New Testament says Abel brought his offering by faith.
It seems Abel gave his best with a trusting heart, and Cain gave something and expected it to be enough.
Cain was furious, and his face fell.
God spoke to him directly.
He asked why he was angry.
Then he gave him a warning that is one of the most important lines in Genesis.
Sin is crouching at your door.
It wants to have you, but you must rule over it.
God was not rejecting Cain.
He was telling him there was still a way to do what is right.
Cain didn't listen.
He said to his brother, let's go out to the field.
When they were there, he attacked Abel and killed him.
It was the first death of a human being recorded in the Bible, and it was a murder.
It happened within one generation of the garden.
God asked Cain, where is your brother Abel? Cain lied. I don't know.
Am I my brother's keeper?
He was trying to cover it up, just as his parents hid in the garden.
But God said, what have you done? Listen.
Your brother's blood cries out to me from the ground.
The ground itself would no longer give crops for Cain.
He would become a wanderer.
Cain cried out that the punishment was more than he could bear.
Anyone who found him might kill him.
And then God did something unexpected.
He put a mark on Cain so no one would kill him.
Even a murderer was still under God's care.
Cain went away from the presence of the Lord and settled east of Eden.
He had a wife, and he built a city.
Adam and Eve had another son named Seth, and the Bible says it was in his family that people began to call on the name of the Lord.
Why does this matter?
It shows how quickly sin grows.
One bite in the garden led to one murder in the field.
It also shows the way sin works.
God warned Cain, and the anger was a choice before it was an action.
The New Testament says Cain belonged to the evil one, and that anyone who hates a brother is like him.
What happened after? Abel's name lives on.
Hebrews says that by faith he still speaks, even though he is dead.
Jesus called him righteous.
The blood that cried from the ground is contrasted in Hebrews with the blood of Jesus, which speaks of forgiveness instead of revenge.
What does this mean for us today?
Most of us will never kill anyone.
But we know what it feels like when someone gets what we wanted, and our face falls.
God's words to Cain are for us too.
Anger is not a sin by itself, but it can crouch at the door.
You can rule over it, with God's help.
The story also asks the question every one of us has to answer.
Am I my brother's keeper?
The Bible's answer is yes.
Jesus said the second great commandment is to love your neighbor as yourself.
We are responsible for the people around us.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows the first family after Eden, broken by envy, and it shows that God still speaks to people before they do wrong, and still protects them after.
He gave Cain a warning and a way out. He gives us the same.
flood: By the time of Noah, the world had gotten very bad.
The Bible says the earth was full of violence, and that every thought of the human heart was only evil all the time. God was grieved.
This wasn't a sudden fit of anger.
It broke his heart to see what people had done to each other and to the world he had made.
But there was one man who stood out.
Noah was a righteous man, and he walked with God.
Noah was also the descendant of Seth, the family that had begun to call on the Lord.
God decided to start over, and he chose Noah to make that possible.
God told Noah to build an ark, a huge wooden boat.
The Bible gives the size as 300 cubits long, 50 wide, and 30 tall.
That is about 450 feet long, longer than a football field and a half.
He was to cover it with pitch inside and out.
Noah would have to build it on dry land, far from any sea, while his neighbors watched.
The Bible says that Noah did everything God commanded.
Peter's second letter calls him a preacher of righteousness.
It seems that for the years he was building, he was also warning people. No one listened.
We aren't told exactly how long it took.
Many have said, going back to old Jewish and Christian writers, that it took a hundred years or more, but the Bible doesn't say exactly.
When the ark was done, God told Noah to bring his wife, his three sons and their wives, and pairs of every kind of animal. Eight people in all. The animals came to him.
Then the Lord himself shut the door.
Then the rain began.
The springs of the great deep burst open and the windows of heaven were opened.
It rained for forty days and forty nights.
The water rose until it covered even the highest mountains.
Everything that had the breath of life on dry land died.
Only Noah and those with him in the ark were left.
The water stayed on the earth for 150 days.
This part of the Bible is hard to read.
But the story keeps repeating one thing. God remembered Noah.
When everything seems lost, the next scene begins with those words.
God remembered Noah and all the animals that were with him.
He sent a wind over the earth, and the water began to go down.
Why does this matter?
It shows that God takes evil seriously, and also that he saves.
Peter says the flood is a picture of baptism, where the water saves by raising the people in the ark above judgment.
Jesus said that the days before his return would be like the days of Noah, with people carrying on as normal and not paying attention.
What happened after?
The ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.
Noah stepped out into a washed world.
In the next scene we will see him send out a dove.
After the flood, God made a promise to Noah and to everything living.
He would never again destroy the earth with water.
He set his bow in the clouds as the sign.
What does this mean for us today?
It means that God sees what is going on.
He is not blind to cruelty.
He is patient, and gave Noah a hundred years or so to build and warn, but he is also just.
It also means there is a way of rescue. The ark had one door.
Jesus said, I am the door.
Noah's family didn't save themselves.
They did the one thing God asked, they went in, and God shut the door behind them.
That is why this story is so important.
It is not about a boat and animals.
It is about a God who is grieved by evil, who judges it, and who still keeps a faithful few safe.
When you feel like the only person trying to do right, remember that God noticed Noah.
dove: After forty days of rain, the water covered the whole earth.
Noah, his family, and all the animals had been shut inside the ark for months.
The Bible says that God remembered Noah.
That is the turning point of the whole story.
God sent a wind across the earth, and the water began to go down.
The ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat, in the seventh month.
But the water still covered the land, and Noah could not see anything from the window.
Another two months passed before the tops of the mountains were seen.
Then Noah did something careful.
He opened the window and sent out a raven.
It flew back and forth until the water dried up.
Then he sent out a dove to see if the water had gone down from the ground.
But the dove found no place to rest, and she came back to the ark.
Noah put out his hand and took her in.
He waited seven more days and sent the dove out again.
This time, in the evening, she came back with a fresh olive leaf in her beak.
Noah knew that the water had gone down enough for trees to be growing again.
The olive leaf is where we get the picture of a dove with an olive branch as a sign of peace.
He waited another seven days and sent the dove out a third time.
This time she did not come back.
The earth was dry enough for her to live on.
Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked out. The ground was dry.
But he still did not leave.
He waited until God told him.
Finally God said, come out of the ark, you and your wife, your sons and their wives.
Bring out every living thing.
After more than a year inside, they stepped out onto dry land.
The first thing Noah did was to build an altar and offer a sacrifice to the Lord.
He had gone through the greatest disaster the world has ever known, and the first thing he did was to give thanks.
God smelled the pleasing aroma and said in his heart that he would never again curse the ground because of people, even though their hearts are evil from childhood.
Then God made a promise.
He said he would never again destroy all life with a flood.
He set his rainbow in the clouds as the sign of that promise.
Whenever it appears, he said, I will see it and remember.
Why does this matter?
The dove came back with something small and green.
It was a sign of new life, and God's way of showing that the judgment was over.
Noah learned to wait for God in both directions, waiting to leave the ark as well as waiting to be rescued.
The dove shows up again at another important moment.
When Jesus was baptized, the Spirit of God came down on him like a dove.
Both times it was a sign that something new was beginning.
What happened after?
Noah planted a vineyard, and not long after, his story gets complicated.
Even a family saved by God could still sin.
The world was washed clean, but human hearts were not.
That is why the story could not end here.
It still needed a Savior.
What does this mean for us today?
When you are in a long season of waiting, this story is for you.
Noah spent more than a year in the ark.
He didn't know exactly when it would be over.
He sent out a bird and waited, and he sent out another one, and he waited some more.
It also teaches us to look for small signs.
An olive leaf is not much.
But it was enough for Noah to see that God was bringing back life.
God often shows his help in small green things before we can see the whole picture.
That is why this story is so important.
It tells us that God remembers us, even in the long silence.
The same God who remembered Noah remembers you, and the rainbow and the dove are still there, to show us that his promises hold.
babel: After the flood, Noah's family grew into a large number of people.
God had told them to fill the earth.
But the people had a different idea.
They all spoke one language, and they came to a plain in the land of Shinar, which is in what we now call Iraq, and they settled there.
They said to each other, come, let's make bricks and bake them thoroughly.
They used brick for stone and tar for mortar.
These were new tools, and they were proud of them.
Then they said, let us build ourselves a city, with a tower that reaches to the heavens, so that we may make a name for ourselves.
Otherwise we will be scattered over the face of the whole earth.
Look at what they were doing.
They weren't just building a tall building.
They wanted to make a name for themselves, and they wanted to stay together instead of spreading out the way God had told them to.
They were building to get their security and their fame from themselves.
Archaeologists have found the ruins of huge stepped towers called ziggurats all over the ancient Middle East.
They were temples built of mud brick, tall pyramids with steps up the side, and they were meant to give the gods a way to come down.
The Bible doesn't say this was one of them.
But the scene fits that world very well.
God came down to see the city and the tower.
The Bible is almost funny here.
The people built a tower that reached for the heavens, and God had to come down to see it.
He said, if as one people speaking the same language they have begun to do this, then nothing they plan to do will be impossible for them.
He wasn't afraid of them.
He was stopping the damage before it grew.
So God confused their language.
They suddenly couldn't understand each other.
They stopped building the city, and they were scattered over the whole earth.
The city was named Babel, which sounds like the Hebrew word for confused.
Why does this matter?
It explains why the world is divided into so many peoples and languages.
But it also shows what pride does.
When people try to reach God by their own power, they end up confused, divided, and scattered.
The more you try to make a name for yourself, the less you can understand the people next to you.
What happened after?
Just after this story, the Bible shows God doing it the other way.
He called a man named Abram and said, I will make your name great.
Instead of people making a name for themselves, God gave a name as a gift.
All the peoples on earth would be blessed through Abram.
Babel is also answered at Pentecost.
After Jesus rose, his followers received the Holy Spirit in Jerusalem, and people from many nations each heard them in their own language.
At Babel, language split people apart.
At Pentecost, God used language to bring them together.
What does this mean for us today? We still build towers.
We build careers, followings, and reputations, and we want to be known.
There is nothing wrong with building.
But the question is whose name we are building for.
The story is also hopeful.
God did not leave the world confused.
His plan from the start was to gather people from every nation and language back together.
Revelation shows a crowd from every tribe and tongue worshiping together before his throne.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that we can't build our own way to God, so God came down to us.
That is the whole Christmas story.
In Jesus, God did what the tower could never do. He came down.
three-angels: Abraham was an old man when this story takes place.
God had called him many years before to leave his home and go to a land he did not know.
He had promised that Abraham would become a great nation and that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him.
But Abraham and his wife Sarah were still waiting for a child.
He was about ninety-nine years old and Sarah was ninety.
One hot afternoon, Abraham was sitting at the entrance of his tent near the great trees of Mamre.
He looked up and saw three men standing nearby.
In that world, a stranger in the desert might die without shelter, so welcoming visitors was a serious duty.
Abraham ran to meet them and bowed to the ground.
He begged them to stay for a meal.
He didn't just bring a snack.
He told Sarah to hurry and bake bread from fine flour.
He ran to the herd, chose a tender calf, and had it prepared.
He brought curds and milk and the cooked meat, and he stood next to them under a tree while they ate.
It was a lavish meal for a few strangers.
As the story goes on, we find out who the visitors really were.
The Bible says that the Lord appeared to Abraham.
One of the three is called the Lord himself, and the other two are called angels.
Christians have long seen in this scene a picture of God coming to eat at a man's table.
They asked, where is your wife Sarah?
Abraham said she was in the tent.
Then the Lord said, I will surely return to you about this time next year, and Sarah your wife will have a son.
Sarah was listening at the tent entrance. She laughed to herself.
She was far past the age for having children.
The Lord asked Abraham why Sarah laughed.
Is anything too hard for the Lord?
Sarah was afraid and said she hadn't laughed. He said, yes you did.
A year later she did have a son.
They named him Isaac, which means he laughs.
Her laugh of doubt became a laugh of joy.
Before the visitors left, the Lord said something else.
He told Abraham about Sodom, a nearby city so evil that its cry had reached heaven.
Abraham, who had learned to trust God, did something brave.
He stood before the Lord and prayed for the city.
If there are fifty righteous people there, will you spare it?
He kept going down, to forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, and finally ten. Each time God agreed.
Why does this matter?
It shows that God keeps promises even when they seem impossible.
It also shows what a friend of God looks like.
Abraham welcomed strangers, and he argued with God for the sake of other people.
The New Testament says, do not forget to show hospitality to strangers, because some people have shown hospitality to angels without knowing it.
What happened after?
Sarah gave birth to Isaac just as promised.
Through Isaac came Jacob, and through Jacob the twelve tribes of Israel, and through them came King David, and finally Jesus.
All the families of the earth were blessed through Abraham, as God said.
What does this mean for us today?
Maybe you have been waiting for something for a very long time, and it seems too late.
Sarah was ninety and she laughed.
God did not scold her for being human.
He just asked a question that is still true.
Is anything too hard for the Lord?
It also means we should open our doors.
Abraham ran, he gave his best, and he stood with his guests while they ate.
You never know what a simple act of welcome might become.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that the God of the Bible comes close, eats at our table, and turns our laughing doubt into laughing joy.
He keeps his word, on his schedule, and it is worth the wait.
sodom: Abraham's nephew Lot had moved to the city of Sodom.
When the herdsmen of the two men started fighting, Abraham let Lot choose any land he wanted.
Lot looked out over the well-watered valley of the Jordan and picked it.
He pitched his tents near Sodom, and over time he moved into the city.
The Bible says the men of Sodom were wicked and were sinning greatly against the Lord.
When Abraham heard that God was about to judge the city, he prayed for it.
He asked God not to destroy the righteous with the wicked.
God agreed that even for ten righteous people he would spare the city.
Abraham knew Lot was in there, and he was trying to save him.
That evening two angels came to Sodom.
Lot was sitting at the city gate.
He got up, bowed down, and urged them to come to his house, to wash their feet and stay the night.
They said they would stay in the square.
He insisted, and they came. He made them a meal.
Before they went to bed, the men of the city surrounded the house.
Both young and old, from every part of the city.
They demanded that Lot bring the visitors out so they could abuse them.
The Bible says they meant to do violence to the guests.
Lot went out and shut the door behind him.
He begged them not to do this wicked thing.
They threatened him, and they came close to breaking down the door.
Then the angels pulled Lot inside and struck the men outside with blindness.
The angels told Lot, get out of here.
Bring your wife, your sons, and your daughters.
The Lord has sent us to destroy this place.
Lot went and spoke to his sons-in-law, but they thought he was joking.
At dawn, the angels urged him to hurry.
Even then, the Bible says, Lot hesitated.
So the angels grabbed his hand and his wife's and his two daughters' hands and led them out of the city, because the Lord was merciful to them.
One of them said, flee for your lives.
Don't look back, and don't stop anywhere in the valley.
Flee to the mountains or you will be swept away.
Lot begged for a small town nearby, called Zoar, and God allowed it.
Then the Lord rained burning sulfur on Sodom and Gomorrah.
He destroyed those cities and everything in the valley.
But Lot's wife looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.
Jesus told his followers to remember Lot's wife.
Her heart was still in Sodom.
Abraham got up early the next morning and went to the place where he had stood before the Lord.
He looked down toward Sodom and saw dense smoke rising from the land like smoke from a furnace.
The Bible says that God remembered Abraham, and so he brought Lot out of the catastrophe.
Why does this matter?
It shows that God is just, and that his patience is real but not endless. It also shows his mercy.
The angels pulled Lot out by the hand.
He was a flawed man who had made a poor choice, and still God saved him.
Peter calls Lot a righteous man who was tormented by the lawless deeds he saw every day.
What happened after?
Lot's life after this was sad.
He ended up living in a cave with his daughters.
Even so, his family line continued, and from it came Ruth the Moabite, who became an ancestor of King David and of Jesus.
God's mercy reached farther than Lot's failures.
What does this mean for us today?
Be careful what you move toward.
Lot moved a little at a time, from looking at Sodom to pitching his tent near it to living in it.
We are also shaped by the places we move toward.
And when God says to get out, don't hesitate, and don't look back.
The angels had to take Lot by the hand.
Some things we are tempted to go back to were never good for us.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows God's holiness and his mercy together.
He judges evil, and he rescues people who are barely hanging on.
If you feel like Lot, standing there hesitating, remember that God took his hand.
hagar: Hagar was an Egyptian servant in Abraham's household.
She belonged to Sarah, and she had no say in her own life.
When Sarah went years without a child, she did what people did in those days.
She gave Hagar to Abraham so he could have a child through her.
Hagar became pregnant, and almost at once there was trouble in the house.
Sarah was jealous and treated Hagar harshly, and Hagar ran away into the desert.
Out there by a spring on the road to Shur, the angel of the Lord found her.
He called her by name and asked, Hagar, servant of Sarah, where have you come from and where are you going?
It was the first time anyone in the Bible stories asked her a question.
He told her to go back and gave her a promise.
I will increase your descendants so much that they will be too numerous to count.
You will have a son, and you shall name him Ishmael, which means God hears.
Hagar did something that no one else in the Bible does. She gave God a name.
You are the God who sees me, she said, for she had seen the one who looked after her.
The well was called Beer Lahai Roi, which means the well of the Living One who sees me.
Years later, Sarah had her own son, Isaac, at last.
At the feast when Isaac was weaned, Sarah saw Ishmael, who was then a teenager, making fun of him.
She told Abraham to get rid of Hagar and her son.
Abraham was very upset, because Ishmael was his son.
But God told him not to be troubled.
Listen to Sarah, he said.
I will make the son of the servant into a nation also, because he is your offspring.
Early the next morning, Abraham gave Hagar some bread and a skin of water.
He put them on her shoulder and sent her away with the boy.
She wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.
When the water ran out, she put the boy under a bush.
Then she went and sat down about a bowshot away.
She said, I cannot watch the boy die. And she began to sob.
God heard the boy crying.
The angel of God called to Hagar from heaven.
What is the matter, Hagar? Do not be afraid.
God has heard the boy crying as he lies there.
Lift him up and take him by the hand, for I will make him into a great nation.
Then God opened her eyes and she saw a well of water.
She filled the skin and gave the boy a drink.
God was with the boy as he grew up.
He lived in the desert and became an archer.
His mother got him a wife from Egypt.
The Bible says that twelve princes came from Ishmael.
Many people in the Middle East trace their family to him.
Why does this matter?
Hagar was not a hero in anyone's eyes.
She was a foreign slave, used and thrown out.
Yet the God of the Bible stopped for her, twice.
He is the only one in Genesis who talks to her as a person.
It shows that God sees the people everyone else overlooks.
What happened after?
Ishmael became the ancestor of the Arab peoples, according to long tradition.
The Bible doesn't say exactly, but tradition has said that this is where their story begins.
Paul also uses Hagar in a letter as a picture of a different kind of relationship with God, but her own story stands on its own.
What does this mean for us today?
If you feel unseen, like nobody knows what you are going through, this story is for you.
God's name for himself here is the God who sees me.
He saw Hagar when she was a runaway and again when she was an outcast.
Notice too that he opened her eyes to a well that was already there.
Sometimes the help is close, and we just can't see it through our tears.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that God hears the cry of the powerless, and that no one is too small for him to notice.
When everything has run dry, he is the one who says, do not be afraid, I have heard.
jacob-dream: Jacob was the younger of Isaac and Rebekah's twin sons.
His brother Esau was born first, which meant Esau should have gotten the family blessing.
But Jacob, whose name means he grabs the heel, or he cheats, got both the birthright and the blessing by trickery.
He bought the birthright for a bowl of stew.
Then, with his mother's help, he dressed up as Esau to fool his blind father into giving him the blessing.
Esau was furious and planned to kill him.
Rebekah heard about it and sent Jacob away to her brother Laban, far to the north in Haran.
Jacob was running for his life.
He was leaving the only home he'd ever known, with no one to go with him.
He was alone, and he had done wrong.
At sundown, he reached a certain place and stopped for the night.
He took one of the stones there and put it under his head and lay down.
He was in the middle of nowhere, at one of the lowest points of his life.
Then he had a dream.
He saw a stairway resting on the earth, with its top reaching to heaven, and the angels of God were going up and down on it.
At the top stood the Lord.
He said, I am the Lord, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac.
I will give you and your descendants the land on which you are lying.
All peoples on earth will be blessed through you and your offspring.
Then came the line that matters most.
I am with you and will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land.
I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.
Think about what that meant.
Jacob had cheated his brother and lied to his father.
God didn't say, you have to fix your life first. He said, I am with you.
He kept the promise he had made to Jacob's grandfather, and he put it into the hands of a man who did not deserve it.
Jacob woke up and said, surely the Lord is in this place, and I was not aware of it. He was afraid.
How awesome is this place!
This is none other than the house of God.
This is the gate of heaven.
Early in the morning he took the stone he had used as a pillow, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil on top of it.
He named the place Bethel, which means house of God.
Then he made a vow.
If God would be with him and look after him and give him food and clothes, then the Lord would be his God.
It was a halting, bargaining prayer, but it was a start.
Why does this matter?
This is the first time Jacob meets God for himself.
Until now he had only heard about the God of Abraham and Isaac.
Now he knew God was his God too.
And it shows that God meets us in the worst places, often when we least expect it.
Jesus made a reference to this dream.
When he met Nathanael, he told him, you will see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.
Jesus was saying that he is the stairway.
He is where heaven and earth meet.
What happened after? Jacob went on to Haran.
There he worked for his uncle for twenty years, and the man who had been a trickster was tricked himself.
He married Leah and Rachel and had twelve sons, who became the twelve tribes of Israel.
And God did bring him home, as he said.
What does this mean for us today?
You do not have to be a good person to have God come to you.
Jacob was running away, with a guilty conscience and a rock for a pillow. And God showed up. That is grace.
It also means that places we think of as empty may be holy ground.
Jacob said, the Lord is in this place and I did not know it.
Maybe God is in the hospital waiting room, the hard season, or the strange town where you ended up.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows a God who does not wait for us to clean up before he comes close.
He said to Jacob, I am with you, and he says it to us too.
jacob-wrestles: Twenty years had passed since Jacob ran away from home.
He had worked for his uncle Laban in Haran, married two wives, had eleven sons and a daughter, and built up a large herd.
Now God told him to go home.
But going home meant facing his brother Esau, whom he had cheated and who had once threatened to kill him.
Jacob sent messengers ahead to Esau.
They came back with bad news.
Esau is coming to meet you, and he has four hundred men with him. Jacob was terrified.
He divided his people and flocks into two groups so that if one was attacked, the other might escape. Then he prayed.
It is one of the most honest prayers in the Bible.
He reminded God of his promises.
I am unworthy of all the kindness you have shown me.
Save me, I pray, from the hand of my brother Esau.
For I am afraid he will come and attack me, and the mothers with their children.
He then picked out a large gift for Esau, hundreds of goats, sheep, camels, cattle, and donkeys, and sent them ahead in droves, each with a servant.
He hoped to soften his brother before he saw him.
That night he sent his family across the Jabbok River with all he had.
And Jacob was left alone.
Then a man wrestled with him until daybreak.
The Bible doesn't explain at first who this was.
Jacob was strong, and the man could not overpower him.
So the man touched the socket of Jacob's hip, and it was wrenched as they wrestled.
Then he said, let me go, for it is daybreak.
But Jacob said, I will not let you go unless you bless me.
The man asked, what is your name? Jacob.
And the man said, your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with humans and have overcome.
Israel means he struggles with God.
Jacob asked for his name, but the man would only bless him there.
Jacob named the place Peniel, which means face of God.
It is because I saw God face to face, and yet my life was spared.
The sun rose as he passed Peniel, and he was limping because of his hip.
To this day, the Bible says, the Israelites do not eat the tendon attached to the socket of the hip.
Why does this matter? Look at what Jacob did.
He had been running and scheming and bargaining his whole life.
In this one night, he stopped.
He held on to God and refused to let go until God blessed him.
He came out of it with a new name and a limp.
God didn't take away his struggle. He changed him in it.
The limp is the key.
From then on, Jacob couldn't run away or fight in his own strength.
He walked with a limp for the rest of his life, and that was a sign that he now leaned on God.
The man who had always depended on himself was now broken in the right place.
What happened after?
The next morning Esau came running to meet him.
And, as we will see, Jacob got a very different welcome than he had been afraid of.
The nation God made from him took Israel as its name.
What does this mean for us today?
Some of us are afraid of something coming at us tomorrow, and are awake with it tonight.
Jacob prayed, and then he wrestled.
Staying up with God over the thing we're afraid of is not a lack of faith. It is faith.
It also shows that it is okay to hold on to God and say, bless me.
God doesn't push us away for being persistent.
Jesus told stories about people who kept knocking.
That is why this story is so important.
It tells us that real change comes from being alone with God, and that God sometimes marks the people he blesses.
If you have a limp from a hard season, it may be the very sign that God was there.
jacob-esau: Jacob had spent the night wrestling with God.
Now the sun was coming up and he limped toward the ford of the Jabbok.
He looked up and saw Esau coming with four hundred men.
This was the moment he had feared for twenty years.
Jacob arranged his family in order.
He put the maids and their children first, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph last, because they were the most precious to him.
Then he walked out in front of them all, and bowed down to the ground seven times as he approached his brother.
This was the way a servant would greet a king.
He was the one who had been given the family blessing, and he bowed to the brother he had cheated.
But Esau ran to meet him.
He threw his arms around him, hugged him, and kissed him. And they both wept.
Twenty years of fear and anger were gone in a moment.
The brother who had once vowed to kill Jacob was now holding him.
Esau looked up and saw the women and children. Who are these with you?
Jacob said, they are the children God has graciously given your servant.
One by one, the families came and bowed down to Esau.
Esau asked about the animals he'd met along the way.
What did you mean by all these droves I met?
Jacob said, to find favor in your eyes, my lord.
Esau said, I already have plenty, my brother.
Keep what you have for yourself. But Jacob insisted.
Please, if I have found favor in your eyes, accept this gift from me.
For to see your face is like seeing the face of God, now that you have received me favorably.
He pressed him, and Esau took it.
Think of how Jacob had spent that long night.
He had seen the face of God and lived.
Now he saw his brother's face and said it was like seeing God's face.
God's forgiveness had come first, and now it was showing up in Esau.
Esau offered to travel with him.
Jacob politely said the children were tender and the flocks needed to go slowly.
Let my lord go on ahead of his servant.
Esau went back to Seir, to his home in the south.
And Jacob went to Succoth and then settled near the city of Shechem.
Why does this matter?
Forgiveness is possible even for the worst betrayals.
Esau had every right to be angry. Instead, he ran.
Jesus told a story about a father running to welcome his son.
It sounds a lot like this one.
It also shows that Jacob had really changed.
The man who once took his brother's blessing now gave a blessing back.
The Hebrew word Jacob used for his gift is blessing, the same word as the one he had stolen.
What happened after?
The two brothers met again once, years later, at their father Isaac's burial.
They buried him together.
Both of them became the fathers of nations.
Esau's family became Edom, and Jacob's became Israel.
The two nations would later have a hard history, but at this moment the two brothers were at peace.
What does this mean for us today?
Is there someone you've wronged, or who has wronged you, and you've been dreading seeing them?
Jacob dreaded it for twenty years.
And what he found was that God had gone ahead of him and softened his brother's heart.
It also means that you can go first.
Jacob bowed, gave his gift, and said, I'm sorry, in everything but the words.
Reconciliation often needs one person to humble themselves.
That is why this story is so important.
It is a picture of what the whole Bible is about.
We were far from God, and we had earned his anger.
But when we turn, he runs to us.
He doesn't just tolerate us.
He throws his arms around us and weeps for joy.
joseph-sold: Jacob had twelve sons by four women, and he loved one of them more than the others.
Joseph was the first son of his beloved wife Rachel, born late in Jacob's life.
Jacob made him a special robe.
Most of us picture it as a coat of many colors, though some translations call it a long robe with sleeves.
Either way, it was a sign that Joseph was the favorite.
His brothers hated him and could not speak a kind word to him.
Joseph didn't help.
He was seventeen, and he told his brothers about two dreams he'd had.
In the first one, they were tying up bundles of grain in the field, and his bundle stood up while theirs gathered around and bowed to it.
In the second, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to him.
His brothers hated him even more.
Even his father scolded him, though the Bible says Jacob kept the matter in mind.
One day, the older brothers took the flocks to a pasture near Shechem, far from home.
Jacob sent Joseph to see how they were doing.
A man found him wandering in the fields and told him they had moved on to Dothan. So Joseph went there.
The brothers saw him coming from far off.
Here comes that dreamer, they said.
Come, let's kill him and throw him into one of these cisterns.
Then we'll say a ferocious animal devoured him.
Then we'll see what comes of his dreams.
Reuben, the oldest, tried to save him.
He said, let's not take his life.
Throw him into this cistern.
His plan was to rescue him later and take him back to his father.
When Joseph reached them, they stripped him of his robe and threw him into an empty cistern.
Then they sat down to eat.
A caravan of Ishmaelites was coming from Gilead on its way to Egypt, with camels loaded with spices.
Judah said, what will we gain if we kill our brother?
Let's sell him to the Ishmaelites.
After all, he is our brother, our own flesh and blood.
They sold him for twenty shekels of silver.
They took Joseph's robe, killed a goat, and dipped it in the blood.
They brought it to their father and said, we found this.
Examine it to see whether it is your son's robe.
Jacob recognized it and said, a ferocious animal has devoured him.
He tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourned for many days.
All his children came to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted.
In his grief he said he would go down to the grave mourning for his son.
Meanwhile, the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, one of Pharaoh's officials, the captain of the guard.
Why does this matter?
It begins one of the greatest stories in the Bible, about how God can bring good out of evil.
At this moment, nothing looks good.
Joseph is a slave, his family is broken, and his father is in despair.
But the Bible is already moving things into place.
The dreams will come true, though not in the way anyone expected.
It also shows that jealousy can destroy a family.
The brothers didn't plan this overnight.
It grew out of years of resentment.
And Jacob's own favoritism had planted it.
What happened after?
Joseph went from being a slave to a prisoner, and then, many years later, to the second most powerful man in Egypt.
The brothers would eventually bow before him, just like the dream said.
What does this mean for us today?
If you've been betrayed by people close to you, this story says that betrayal is not the final word.
God was with Joseph in the cistern, on the road, and in the house of Potiphar.
He is with you in the pit too.
And if you are the one who has been envious, notice where it led.
A few minutes of hatred changed a family for twenty years.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that nothing is wasted in God's hands.
Joseph's worst day became the first step to saving his whole family.
Later he said, you intended to harm me, but God intended it for good.
joseph-reveals: Twenty-two years had passed since the brothers sold Joseph.
In that time, Joseph had gone from being a slave in Potiphar's house to a prisoner, falsely accused.
In prison he interpreted dreams, and when Pharaoh had a dream no one could explain, Joseph was called.
He told Pharaoh that seven years of plenty were coming and then seven years of famine.
He suggested that Pharaoh find a wise man to store grain.
Pharaoh put Joseph himself in charge.
He was thirty years old, and second in command over all of Egypt.
The famine hit not just Egypt but the whole region.
Back in Canaan, Jacob and his family were starving.
Jacob sent ten of his sons to Egypt to buy grain.
Benjamin, the youngest and the only other son of Rachel, stayed home.
They came before the governor of the land, and bowed with their faces to the ground, just like in Joseph's dream.
They didn't recognize him.
He looked Egyptian, he spoke through an interpreter, and they thought he was dead.
But Joseph knew them right away.
He tested them.
He accused them of being spies, threw them in prison for three days, and kept Simeon as a hostage.
He told them to bring their youngest brother back, or they'd never see him again.
On the second trip, he had a silver cup planted in Benjamin's sack, and then said that the one with the cup would become his slave.
The brothers were terrified.
This was the real test.
Years before, they had sold one favored son and walked away.
Now they had the chance to do it again.
Judah, who had suggested selling Joseph, stepped forward.
He begged the governor to take him as a slave instead.
He said that if the boy didn't come home, their father would die of grief.
Please let your servant remain as your slave in place of the boy.
The man who had sold his brother was now ready to give up his own life for his brother.
Then Joseph could not control himself any longer.
He sent all the Egyptians out of the room, and he wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard him.
He said to his brothers, I am Joseph!
Is my father still living?
But his brothers couldn't answer him, because they were terrified.
Joseph said, come close to me.
When they did, he said, I am your brother Joseph, the one you sold into Egypt.
And now, do not be distressed and do not be angry with yourselves for selling me here, because it was to save lives that God sent me ahead of you.
For two years now there has been famine in the land, and for the next five years there will be no plowing and reaping.
God sent me ahead of you to preserve for you a remnant on earth.
So then, it was not you who sent me here, but God.
He threw his arms around his brother Benjamin and wept, and then he kissed all his brothers and wept over them.
After that, his brothers talked with him.
Pharaoh was pleased, and he told Joseph to bring his whole family to live in the best part of Egypt, the land of Goshen.
Joseph sent them back with wagons.
When Jacob heard that Joseph was alive, he was stunned. He said, I'm convinced.
My son Joseph is still alive.
I will go and see him before I die.
Why does this matter?
This is one of the greatest forgiveness scenes in the Bible.
Joseph had every right to take revenge.
He had the power to do anything he wanted.
Instead, he wept, and he said that God had been working through all the pain.
The story also moves the family of Israel to Egypt, which sets up the next big event in the Bible.
Jacob's family came as seventy people and, over the next four hundred years, became a nation.
That is why Moses and the Exodus come next.
What happened after?
Jacob came to Egypt and saw Joseph again.
He lived there seventeen more years.
When Jacob died, the brothers worried that Joseph would finally pay them back.
He wept again and said, don't be afraid.
You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good, to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives.
What does this mean for us today?
We almost all have something in our past that was done to us, or something we did to someone else.
This story shows what real forgiveness looks like.
Joseph didn't pretend it didn't hurt. He had cried for years.
But he chose to see God's hand in it, and he chose not to take revenge.
It also shows that forgiveness changes the person who gives it.
And the brothers changed too.
Judah, who once traded a brother for silver, now offered himself for one.
That is why this story is so important.
It points forward to Jesus, a rejected son who was handed over by his own people, and who then used the evil done to him to save them.
He said from the cross, Father, forgive them.
Joseph's story is a picture of how God works.
He takes what people mean for evil and turns it into rescue.
moses-nile: After Joseph died, the family of Israel stayed in Egypt for about four hundred years.
They grew from seventy people into a great nation.
Then a new king came to power who did not know Joseph.
He looked at the Israelites and was afraid.
They are too many, he said.
If war breaks out they might join our enemies. So he made them slaves.
They built his storage cities of Pithom and Rameses with brick and mortar.
The Bible says the Egyptians worked them ruthlessly.
But the harder the Egyptians pushed, the more the Israelites grew.
So Pharaoh gave an order that was even worse.
Every Hebrew baby boy was to be thrown into the Nile.
This was a plan to wipe out a whole people.
In the middle of that, a baby was born.
His mother was from the tribe of Levi.
The Bible says she saw that he was a fine child, and she hid him for three months.
We know her name from later in the Bible as Jochebed.
His father was Amram, and he had an older sister named Miriam and a brother named Aaron.
When she could no longer hide him, she did something very clever.
She got a papyrus basket and coated it with tar and pitch.
She put the child in it and set it among the reeds along the bank of the Nile.
The Hebrew word for the basket is the same word used for Noah's ark.
She had built a tiny ark for her son.
She couldn't save him from the water, but she could put him in a boat on it.
Then she left.
His sister Miriam stood at a distance to see what would happen to him.
Imagine what it took for a mother to walk away.
Her faith was not that she knew how it would turn out.
It was that she did what she could and left the rest to God.
The book of Hebrews says that by faith Moses' parents hid him for three months, and they were not afraid of the king's edict.
Why does this matter?
We often think of the Exodus as starting with the plagues.
But it began with a mother and a daughter and a basket.
God's rescue of a whole nation started with ordinary people refusing to give in to fear.
They didn't have the power to stop Pharaoh.
They did what was in their hands.
It also matters because of who the baby was.
His name was Moses, though that name came a little later.
He would become the one who led Israel out of slavery, delivered the law at Sinai, and wrote the first five books of the Bible.
Jesus himself is often called a new Moses.
And like Moses, Jesus escaped a king who killed baby boys, when Herod did the same thing in Bethlehem.
What happened after?
The basket did not go far.
As we'll see in the next scene, it floated right to the place where Pharaoh's own daughter came to bathe.
The very man who tried to destroy Israel would end up raising its deliverer in his own house.
What does this mean for us today?
Maybe you are in a situation that feels out of your control.
A child, a family member, or a future you can't protect.
Jochebed shows what you can do.
You do the next faithful thing, and you put the one you love in God's hands.
She didn't have a plan for what happened after the basket. She just trusted.
This story also shows that God works through small acts, and that nothing done in faith is wasted.
A basket of reeds, a sister watching, a river. That's all God needed.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that the God who hears the cries of slaves was already at work before anyone saw it. The rescue had started.
It was just hidden in the reeds.
moses-found: Moses' mother had put him in a basket in the Nile, and his sister Miriam was watching from a distance.
Soon someone came to the river.
It was Pharaoh's daughter, with her attendants walking along the bank, and she was coming down to bathe.
She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her maid to get it.
When she opened it, she saw a baby crying.
The Bible says she felt sorry for him.
This is one of the Bible's wonderful twists.
The daughter of the man who ordered baby boys to be thrown in the river was moved by the cry of one of them.
She said, this is one of the Hebrew babies.
Then Miriam stepped out of the reeds.
She asked, shall I go and get one of the Hebrew women to nurse the baby for you?
Pharaoh's daughter said, yes, go.
So the girl went and got the baby's own mother.
Pharaoh's daughter said to her, take this baby and nurse him for me, and I will pay you.
So Jochebed took her son home and nursed him, and was paid to do it.
When the child grew older, she took him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses.
The Bible says, she drew him out of the water.
That is what the name sounds like in Hebrew.
He grew up in the palace.
Stephen, in the book of Acts, says he was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was powerful in speech and action.
Think about what that meant.
Moses was raised with a mother who knew who he was, and also with the best education of the greatest empire in the world.
He knew he was a Hebrew, and he grew up in Pharaoh's court.
God was preparing him for both worlds.
When he was grown, Moses went out to see his own people and saw their hard labor.
He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew.
He looked around, and when he saw no one, he killed the Egyptian and hid his body in the sand.
The next day he tried to stop two Hebrews from fighting, and one of them said, who made you ruler and judge over us?
Are you thinking of killing me as you killed the Egyptian? Moses was afraid.
Then Pharaoh heard about it and tried to kill Moses.
Moses fled to Midian, in the desert far from Egypt. He sat down by a well.
There the seven daughters of a priest named Jethro came to water their flock, and some shepherds drove them away.
Moses stood up and rescued them and watered their flock.
Jethro gave Moses one of his daughters, Zipporah, as a wife.
They had a son named Gershom, which sounds like the word for foreigner.
I have become a foreigner in a foreign land, he said.
Moses stayed in the desert for forty years, tending sheep.
Stephen says he was forty years old when he fled, and the Bible says he was eighty when God spoke to him at the burning bush.
So he spent forty years as a prince and forty years as a shepherd before God began to use him.
Why does this matter?
It shows that God's timing is slow and careful.
Moses had tried to rescue his people in his own strength, and it failed.
He needed forty years in the desert to learn that it would be God's strength, not his own.
The man who thought he was a somebody in Egypt had to become a nobody before God could use him.
What happened after?
One day, Moses saw a bush on fire that did not burn up.
God called to him by name.
He sent Moses back to the very place he had run from, to free his people.
And the man who had been drawn out of the water would lead them through it.
What does this mean for us today?
If you feel like you've wasted years, or if you are in a season that looks like a desert, this story says God is not done.
Moses' first forty years were spent in a palace, and the next forty tending sheep, and the last forty leading a nation.
Not one of those years was wasted.
It also shows that God can work through the very people who oppose him.
Pharaoh's own daughter ended up protecting and educating Israel's deliverer.
That is why this story is so important.
It tells us that God is already working long before we see it.
Rescue was moving toward Israel the whole time.
It looked like a basket on a river, and it was God's plan.
let-my-people-go: Moses was eighty years old and herding sheep when God called him from a burning bush.
God said he had seen the misery of his people in Egypt, and had heard their cry, and was concerned about their suffering.
Then he said, so now, go.
I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring my people the Israelites out of Egypt. Moses protested. Who am I?
He said he wasn't a good speaker.
God told him that his brother Aaron would speak for him, and gave him a name for himself that Moses could take back to Israel. I AM WHO I AM.
Tell them, I AM has sent me to you.
Moses and Aaron went to Egypt and gathered the elders of Israel.
The people believed them, and when they heard that the Lord was concerned about them and had seen their misery, they bowed down and worshiped.
Then Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh.
They said, this is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says.
Let my people go, so that they may hold a festival to me in the wilderness.
Pharaoh said, who is the Lord, that I should obey him and let Israel go?
I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go. He didn't just say no. He made things worse.
That same day he told the slave drivers to stop giving the people straw for making bricks.
They would have to gather their own straw, and still make the same number of bricks.
The Israelites scattered all over Egypt looking for stubble.
They were beaten when they couldn't keep up.
The Israelite foremen came to Pharaoh and complained, and he told them they were lazy.
Then they turned on Moses and Aaron.
May the Lord look on you and judge you!
You have made us a stench to Pharaoh and his officials. Moses was crushed.
He went back to the Lord and said, Lord, why have you brought trouble on this people? Is this why you sent me?
Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has brought trouble on this people, and you have not rescued your people at all.
This is the part of the story that is easy to skip.
God's rescue began with things getting worse. It's what often happens.
The pressure on the people was greater than before, and Moses honestly told God he was disappointed.
God did not scold him.
He said, now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh.
Because of my mighty hand he will let them go.
And then God repeated seven promises. I will bring you out. I will free you. I will redeem you.
I will take you as my people. I will be your God.
I will bring you to the land. I will give it to you.
But when Moses told this to the Israelites, they would not listen to him because of their discouragement and harsh labor.
Why does this matter?
It shows that the road to freedom started with a hard no.
Pharaoh was not just a stubborn man.
In the world of the Bible, he was seen as a god, so this was a contest between the God of Israel and the gods of Egypt.
Every plague that follows is aimed at one of them.
The Nile, the sun, the cattle, all were things Egypt worshiped.
What happened after?
Ten plagues came, one after another.
The Nile turned to blood.
Frogs, gnats, flies, dead livestock, boils, hail, locusts, darkness, and the death of the firstborn.
Each time, Pharaoh would give in a little and then harden his heart.
Finally, after the last plague, he let them go.
What does this mean for us today?
If you have ever done what God asked and things got worse, you are in good company.
Moses did exactly what God said and the result was more pain.
Obedience does not always make the road easier, at first.
It also teaches us to be honest with God.
Moses told him exactly how he felt, and God didn't reject him.
He answered with promises.
That is why this story is so important.
It is the beginning of the greatest rescue in the Old Testament.
It says that God hears the cries of the oppressed, that no power on earth is too strong for him, and that when things look the worst, he may be just getting started.
His words to Pharaoh are still words to every power that holds people down. Let my people go.
darkness: Nine plagues had struck Egypt.
The Nile had turned to blood.
Frogs, gnats, flies, and a sickness on the livestock had followed, then boils, hail, and locusts.
Each time Pharaoh had bargained, promised to let the people go, and then changed his mind.
The Bible says that Pharaoh hardened his heart, and at other times it says that God hardened it. The story says both.
Pharaoh made his own choice again and again, and in the end God let him have what he wanted.
Now came the ninth plague, the darkness.
God told Moses, stretch out your hand toward the sky so that darkness will spread over Egypt, darkness that can be felt.
Moses stretched out his hand, and total darkness covered all Egypt for three days.
No one could see anyone else or leave their place for three days.
Yet all the Israelites had light in the places where they lived.
Think about what this meant.
The sun was one of the chief gods of Egypt.
Their god Ra was believed to be the one who carried the sun across the sky every day.
And now the Lord of Israel had made the sun disappear over the whole country.
Their greatest god was powerless against him.
The darkness was an attack on everything Egypt trusted, not just an inconvenience.
It was also a picture of what Pharaoh was like on the inside.
He wouldn't see the truth.
He was in the dark even when the light was shining.
The Bible later uses this kind of darkness as a picture of life without God, and of judgment.
Pharaoh summoned Moses.
Go, worship the Lord, he said.
Even your women and children may go with you.
Only leave your flocks and herds behind. Moses said, no.
Our livestock too must go with us.
Not a hoof is to be left behind.
We have to use some of them in worshiping the Lord, and until we get there we will not know what we are to use. Pharaoh was furious. Get out of my sight!
Make sure you do not appear before me again.
The day you see my face you will die.
Moses answered, just as you say.
I will never appear before you again.
But first, he said, one more plague was coming.
About midnight, every firstborn son in Egypt would die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh to the firstborn of the slave girl.
But among the Israelites, not even a dog would bark at anyone.
Then you will know that the Lord makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.
And Moses left Pharaoh, burning with anger.
Why does this matter?
It shows that nothing is hidden from God, and that he can use even the sun, which seems so solid and sure, as a tool.
It also shows how real the choice was.
Three days of darkness was a huge warning, and Pharaoh would not listen.
The darkness is also a picture of Good Friday.
When Jesus died, darkness covered the whole land from noon until three in the afternoon.
The same God who had judged evil in Egypt allowed it to fall on his own Son, so that we would not face it ourselves.
What happened after?
The tenth and final plague came.
On the night of the Passover, the firstborn of Egypt died, and Pharaoh finally sent Israel away.
The people left with silver and gold and clothing that the Egyptians gave them.
What does this mean for us today?
In the middle of the darkest night, the people of Israel had light where they lived.
God can give light to his people even in the worst place.
You may be in a dark time, but you are not alone in it. He knows where you live.
It also warns us that ignoring God doesn't make him go away.
The more Pharaoh closed his eyes, the thicker the darkness grew.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that God is over every power we are afraid of, even the sun.
And it points ahead to the one who said, I am the light of the world.
Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness.
passover: Nine plagues had hit Egypt, and Pharaoh still would not let Israel go.
Now God was about to send the last one.
Before it came, he gave Moses and Aaron detailed instructions for the people of Israel.
This month would be the first month of their year. It was a new beginning.
On the tenth day, each family was to choose a lamb, a year-old male without any defect.
They were to keep it until the fourteenth day.
For four days it lived in the house with the family.
Then at twilight the whole community of Israel was to slaughter their lambs.
They were to take some of the blood and put it on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they ate.
That night they were to roast the meat and eat it with bitter herbs and bread made without yeast.
They were to eat it in a hurry, with cloaks tucked into their belts, sandals on their feet, and staffs in their hands.
It is the Lord's Passover.
God said, on that same night I will pass through Egypt and strike down every firstborn, both people and animals, and I will bring judgment on all the gods of Egypt. I am the Lord.
The blood will be a sign for you on the houses where you are, and when I see the blood, I will pass over you.
No destructive plague will touch you.
Notice what the blood was for.
It wasn't a sign for the people. It was a sign for God.
The Israelites weren't spared because they were better than the Egyptians.
They were spared because a lamb had died in their place and its blood was on the door.

At midnight, the Lord struck down all the firstborn in Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on the throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon, and the firstborn of all the livestock.
Pharaoh and all his officials got up during the night, and there was loud wailing in Egypt, for there was not a house without someone dead.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron during the night. Up!
Leave my people, you and the Israelites!
Go, worship the Lord as you have requested.
Take your flocks and herds, and go. And also bless me.
The Egyptians urged the people to hurry and leave.
The Israelites asked them for silver, gold, and clothing, and the Egyptians gave them what they asked for.
About 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children, left Egypt that day.
A mixed crowd went up with them too, along with flocks and herds.
They had been in Egypt 430 years to the day.
God told them to remember this day forever, and to celebrate it every year as a festival to the Lord.
Why does this matter?
It is the center of the Old Testament.
Every year after, Israel kept the Passover to remember how God saved them.
And when Jesus came, he was called the Lamb of God.
John the Baptist said it when he saw him, look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.
Jesus was crucified at the time of the Passover.
He shared a Passover meal with his disciples on the night before he died, and he said the cup was his blood.
Paul wrote it plainly.
Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
The lamb without defect, the blood on the door, the people saved by a death in their place.
It was all pointing forward to Jesus.
What happened after?
The people walked out of Egypt, and at the Red Sea, God brought them through.
They became a free nation.
But they were not yet home.
A long journey in the desert lay ahead.
What does this mean for us today?
The Passover tells us that God saves by a substitute.
Nobody in Israel earned their way out.
They listened, trusted, and put the blood on the door.
The only thing they did was believe what God said and act on it.
It also means that when you feel judged or afraid, there is a way of safety.
The people inside the houses were not hiding in a perfect house.
They were safe because of the blood.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows what God does with people who cannot save themselves. He sends a lamb.
And for every one of us, he did.
red-sea: Israel had walked out of Egypt after the last plague.
God did not lead them by the short road to Canaan, which went through Philistine land.
He said they might change their minds if they faced war and want to go back to Egypt.
So he led them the long way, toward the Red Sea.
By day the Lord went ahead of them in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire.
He was literally leading them.
But then God told them to turn back and camp by the sea, with water in front of them.
It looked like a mistake.
Meanwhile, back in Egypt, Pharaoh changed his mind. What have we done?
We have let the Israelites go and have lost their services!
He got his chariots ready and took 600 of the best, along with all the other chariots of Egypt.
He chased after Israel, and caught up with them while they were camped by the sea.
The Israelites looked up and saw the Egyptians marching after them.
They were terrified and cried out to the Lord.
Then they turned on Moses.
Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us to the desert to die?
What have you done to us by bringing us out of Egypt?
Didn't we say to you in Egypt, leave us alone, let us serve the Egyptians?
It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the desert!
Moses gave one of the great answers in the Bible. Do not be afraid.
Stand firm and you will see the deliverance the Lord will bring you today.
The Egyptians you see today you will never see again.
The Lord will fight for you.
You need only to be still.
God said to Moses, why are you crying out to me?
Tell the Israelites to move on.
Raise your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea to divide the water, so that the Israelites can go through the sea on dry ground.
The angel of God, who had been traveling in front of Israel's army, moved behind them.
The pillar of cloud moved too, and stood between the Egyptians and Israel.
It brought darkness to one side and light to the other, so neither went near the other all night.
Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea.
All that night the Lord drove the sea back with a strong east wind and turned it into dry land.
The waters were divided, and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left.
The Egyptians pursued them, all Pharaoh's horses, chariots, and horsemen, into the sea.
During the last watch of the night, God threw the Egyptian army into confusion.
The wheels of their chariots came off, so that they had difficulty driving.
They said, let's flee from the Israelites!
The Lord is fighting for them against Egypt.
Then the Lord told Moses to stretch out his hand again.
At daybreak the sea went back to its place.
The Egyptians were fleeing toward it, and the Lord swept them into the sea.
Not one of them survived.
The Israelites saw the Egyptians lying dead on the shore.
The people feared the Lord and put their trust in him and in Moses.
Why does this matter?
It is the greatest rescue in the Old Testament, and the one that every later writer points back to.
The Psalms, the prophets, and the New Testament all say, remember the sea.
It tells us that God makes a way where there is none.
It also tells us that this wasn't a rescue where Israel did a lot.
They were told to stand still.
The Lord himself fought for them.
Later the New Testament uses the crossing as a picture of baptism, going through the water from slavery to freedom.
What happened after?
Moses and the people sang a song.
I will sing to the Lord, for he is highly exalted.
Miriam, Moses' sister, took a tambourine, and all the women followed her, dancing.
But three days later the people were already complaining about the lack of water.
Freedom was real, but learning to trust God took longer.
What does this mean for us today?
You may find yourself with the sea in front of you and the enemy behind you.
Everything says it's over.
God sometimes leads us right to the place where we're cornered, so that we know it is him who saves.
And the instruction is still the same. Be still.
That doesn't mean do nothing.
Israel did walk through the sea.
But it means that the outcome doesn't depend on us.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that God's way of rescue often goes through the very thing we fear.
The waters that looked like a dead end became the road to freedom.
sinai: Three months after leaving Egypt, the people of Israel reached the Desert of Sinai and camped in front of the mountain.
Moses went up to God, and God called to him from the mountain.
Tell the people what I did to Egypt.
You yourselves have seen how I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself.
Now if you obey me fully and keep my covenant, then out of all nations you will be my treasured possession.
Although the whole earth is mine, you will be for me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.
Notice the order.
God didn't say, obey me and I will rescue you.
He had already rescued them.
He said, I carried you to myself.
The law was not the price of freedom.
It was how a free people would live with their God.
And the people answered together.
We will do everything the Lord has said.
God told Moses to get the people ready.
They were to wash their clothes and be ready on the third day.
Boundaries were set around the mountain.
No one was allowed to touch it.
On the morning of the third day there was thunder and lightning, with a thick cloud over the mountain, and a very loud trumpet blast.
Everyone in the camp trembled.
Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God, and they stood at the foot of the mountain.
Mount Sinai was covered with smoke, because the Lord descended on it in fire.
The smoke billowed up from it like smoke from a furnace, and the whole mountain trembled violently.
As the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke and the voice of God answered him.
Then God spoke all the words of the Ten Commandments.
I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt, out of the land of slavery.
You shall have no other gods before me. No idols. Don't misuse my name.
Remember the Sabbath day.
Honor your father and mother. Do not murder. Do not commit adultery. Do not steal.
Do not give false testimony. Do not covet.
The people were terrified.
When they saw the thunder and lightning and heard the trumpet and saw the mountain in smoke, they trembled with fear.
They stayed at a distance and said to Moses, speak to us yourself and we will listen.
But do not have God speak to us or we will die.
Moses said, do not be afraid.
God has come to test you, so that the fear of God will be with you to keep you from sinning.
Moses then went up the mountain for forty days and forty nights.
God gave him more laws and told him how to build a tent where he would live among them.
The Tabernacle was to be built exactly as God showed him on the mountain.
Why does this matter?
Sinai is where Israel became a nation under God.
The Ten Commandments are the center of all the laws that follow.
