They show how to love God and how to love other people.
Jesus summed them up in two.
Love the Lord your God with all your heart, and love your neighbor as yourself.
It is also the first time in history that a whole people heard God's voice directly.
The people of Israel were not told about God by a priest.
They stood at the foot of the mountain, in fear and wonder.
What happened after?
While Moses was up on the mountain, the people grew impatient and made a golden calf, and broke the covenant almost before it was made. That is the next scene.
Even so, God did not give up on them.
He gave the law a second time, and he came to live among them.
What does this mean for us today?
God's commands are not meant to take our freedom.
They came after freedom, from a God who had already rescued his people.
They are how a free person stays free.
Without them, we fall into slavery again.
It also reminds us that God is holy, and that he is not to be treated lightly.
But there is a promise too.
At Sinai the people stayed at a distance, afraid.
Through Jesus, we can come close.
Hebrews says we have not come to a mountain that burns with fire, but to Mount Zion, the city of the living God.
That is why this story is so important.
It tells us that God gave us a way to live, and that he did it out of love.
The law says, here is how to live with the God who saved you.
tablets: Moses had been on top of Mount Sinai for forty days.
The people at the bottom grew restless.
They said to Aaron, come, make us gods who will go before us.
As for this fellow Moses who brought us up out of Egypt, we don't know what has happened to him.
They wanted something they could see.
Aaron said, take off the gold earrings that your wives, sons, and daughters are wearing, and bring them to me.
He melted the gold, formed it with a tool, and made it into an idol cast in the shape of a calf.
Then they said, these are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt.
Aaron saw this and built an altar in front of it, and announced, tomorrow there will be a festival to the Lord.
So the next day the people got up early, sacrificed burnt offerings, and sat down to eat and drink.
Then they got up to indulge in revelry.
Up on the mountain, God told Moses, go down, because your people have become corrupt.
They have been quick to turn away from what I commanded.
He said he would destroy them and make a great nation from Moses.
But Moses did something remarkable.
He interceded for the people.
He reminded God of his promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And the Lord relented.
Moses went down the mountain with the two tablets of the covenant law in his hands.
They were written on both sides, the work of God himself.
When Joshua heard the noise of the people shouting, he thought it was the sound of war.
Moses said, it is not the sound of victory, it is not the sound of defeat.
It is the sound of singing that I hear.
When Moses approached the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, his anger burned.
He threw the tablets out of his hands, breaking them to pieces at the foot of the mountain.
Then he took the calf they had made and burned it in the fire.
He ground it to powder, scattered it on the water, and made the Israelites drink it.
He said to Aaron, what did these people do to you, that you led them into such great sin? Aaron's answer was weak.
They gave me the gold, and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf.
As if it had happened by itself.
Moses stood at the entrance to the camp and called, whoever is for the Lord, come to me.
The Levites gathered around him.
About three thousand people died that day.
Then the next day, Moses told the people, you have committed a great sin.
But now I will go up to the Lord, and perhaps I can make atonement for your sin.
He went back up the mountain and prayed.
Please forgive their sin, but if not, then blot me out of the book you have written.
God didn't blot him out.
He told Moses to cut two new stone tablets, and he wrote the words on them again.

Then the Lord passed in front of Moses and proclaimed, the Lord, the Lord, the compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness, maintaining love to thousands, and forgiving wickedness, rebellion and sin.
Why does this matter?
The tablets broke because the covenant was broken, and almost as soon as it was made.
It showed that the people could not keep the law by themselves.
But it also shows that God does not walk away.
The second set of tablets was written by the same hand.
This is what grace looks like in the Old Testament.
It also shows what an intercessor does.
Moses stood in the gap between a holy God and a sinful people.
The New Testament says that Jesus does this for us, and that he is always living to intercede for us.
What happened after?
The people repented, and God told them to build the Tabernacle.
His presence came down and filled it.
He lived among them even after they had failed him.
What does this mean for us today?
Most of us have our own golden calf, something we turn to when God seems silent.
We want something we can see.
Aaron's story shows how quickly we can talk ourselves into it, and how thin the excuses are.
But the good news of this chapter is God's self-description.
Compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love.
When we fail, his first move is not to destroy.
It is to forgive, and to give us the words again.
That is why this story is so important.
A broken covenant and a broken set of tablets was not the end. God made it new.
That is what Jesus did for everyone, with a new covenant in his blood.
serpent: Israel had been wandering in the desert for almost forty years.
They had left Egypt, crossed the sea, and received the law at Sinai.
But they had refused to enter the Promised Land because they were afraid of the people who lived there.
So God had said that the whole generation would die in the wilderness, and that their children would enter instead.
Now that time was almost up.
Aaron had died and been buried on Mount Hor, and the people were traveling around the land of Edom, the long way.
The people grew impatient on the road.
They began to speak against God and against Moses.
Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? There is no bread! There is no water!
And we detest this miserable food.
The miserable food was the manna, the bread God had given them every morning for almost forty years.
Think about what they were saying.
God had saved them from slavery, split the sea, and fed them every day with bread from heaven.
And they called it miserable.
They had forgotten who they were dealing with. It is easy to do.
Then the Lord sent venomous snakes among the people.
They bit the people, and many Israelites died.
The people came to Moses and said, we sinned when we spoke against the Lord and against you.
Pray that the Lord will take the snakes away from us.
So Moses prayed for the people.
The Lord said to Moses, make a snake and put it up on a pole.
Anyone who is bitten can look at it and live.
So Moses made a bronze snake and put it up on a pole.
Then when anyone was bitten by a snake and looked at the bronze snake, they lived.
Think about how strange that is.
God did not take the snakes away.
He didn't give them an antidote or a medicine.
He told them to look at a bronze snake on a pole.
They had to believe that something that looked like the problem could be the cure.
The only thing they could do was look and trust.
If they refused to look, they died.
Why does this matter?
Jesus talked about this story himself, in one of the most famous conversations in the Bible.
He was talking to a man named Nicodemus at night.
He said, just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes may have eternal life in him.
Then he said the verse that is known all over the world.
For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.
The bronze snake was a picture of Jesus on the cross.
Snakes meant sin and death.
Jesus took on our sin, and became the thing that kills us, so that we could live.
Everyone who looks at him in faith is healed.
What happened after?
The Israelites kept the bronze snake.
Hundreds of years later, they started to worship it.
King Hezekiah broke it into pieces, because it had become an idol.
The thing God had used to heal them was never meant to be worshiped.
What does this mean for us today?
When we are bitten by the poison of our own mistakes, God doesn't ask us to fix ourselves first. He asks us to look. That is what faith is.
It is not a complicated thing.
It is turning toward the one God has lifted up.
It also warns us about complaining.
The people were bitten right after they complained about God's gift.
A thankful heart is a safe place to live.
That is why this story is so important.
It is the clearest picture in the Old Testament of how a person is saved.
Not by doing, but by looking. Fix your eyes on Jesus.
balaam: Israel was almost at the end of its journey.
The people were camped on the plains of Moab, just east of the Jordan River.
Balak, the king of Moab, was terrified.
He had heard what Israel had done to the Amorites, and he thought they were too many for him.
So he sent for a man named Balaam, a well-known prophet who lived far away on the Euphrates.
Balak told him, come and put a curse on these people.
I know that whoever you bless is blessed, and whoever you curse is cursed.
Balaam asked God.
God said, do not go with them.
You must not put a curse on those people, because they are blessed.
Balaam told the messengers to go home.
But Balak sent more princes, more important and with more money.
Balaam answered, even if Balak gave me his palace filled with silver and gold, I could not do anything great or small to go beyond the command of the Lord my God.
But he asked them to stay the night, and again asked God.
This time God said, go with them, but do only what I tell you.
The next morning, Balaam saddled his donkey and went.
But God was very angry that he went, and the angel of the Lord stood in the road to oppose him.
Balaam was riding on his donkey, and two servants were with him.
The donkey saw the angel of the Lord standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand.
She turned off the road into a field.
Balaam beat her to get her back on the road.
Then the angel stood in a narrow path between two vineyards, with walls on both sides.
When the donkey saw the angel, she pressed close to the wall, crushing Balaam's foot against it. So he beat her again.
Then the angel moved ahead and stood in a narrow place where there was no room to turn.
This time the donkey lay down under Balaam.
He was furious and beat her with his staff.
Then the Lord opened the donkey's mouth, and she said to Balaam, what have I done to you to make you beat me these three times?
Balaam answered, you have made a fool of me!
If I had a sword in my hand, I would kill you right now.
The donkey said, am I not your own donkey, which you have always ridden, to this day?
Have I been in the habit of doing this to you? No, he said.
Then the Lord opened Balaam's eyes, and he saw the angel standing in the road with his sword drawn.
He bowed low and fell facedown.
The angel asked him why he had beaten his donkey.
The donkey saw me and turned away three times.
If she had not turned away, I would certainly have killed you by now, and I would have spared her.
Balaam admitted, I have sinned.
The angel told Balaam to go on, but to speak only what he was told.
Balak took Balaam up to high places to look down at Israel and curse them.
Three times, Balaam tried to speak, and three times God put blessings in his mouth instead.
How can I curse those whom God has not cursed? Balak was furious.
I summoned you to curse my enemies, but you have blessed them these three times!
One of the blessings looks far into the future. I see him, but not now.
I behold him, but not near.
A star will come out of Jacob.
A scepter will rise out of Israel.
Christians have long seen this as pointing to Jesus.
It may also be why wise men from the east followed a star to Bethlehem.
Why does this matter?
It shows that no one can curse the people God has blessed.
Balak had the money, the army, and a famous prophet, and it didn't matter.
It also shows that God can speak through anyone, even a donkey.
What happened after?
Sadly, Balaam later found another way to hurt Israel.
He advised Moab to lure the Israelites into idol worship.
The New Testament uses Balaam as a warning about people who love money more than they love God.
Jude and Peter both mention him.
Balaam in the end was killed in battle.
What does this mean for us today?
The donkey saw what the prophet could not.
Sometimes the people or things we overlook see God's hand before the experts do.
And sometimes God uses interruptions, like the donkey stopping in the road, to save us from something worse.
It also tells us that God's blessing on his people cannot be undone by anyone's words.
Whoever belongs to him is safe from curses.
You may feel that people have spoken against you, or that the odds are against you.
But what God has blessed, no one can curse.
That is why this story is so important.
It tells us that God protects his people, even from enemies they don't know about.
They were safe because of him, not because of anything they had done.
jordan: Moses was dead.
He had led Israel for forty years in the desert, and he died on Mount Nebo, within sight of the Promised Land, but without entering it.
God had chosen a new leader, Joshua, who had been Moses' helper since the Exodus.
God told him, Moses my servant is dead.
Now then, you and all these people, get ready to cross the Jordan River into the land I am about to give to them.
Be strong and courageous.
Do not be afraid, for the Lord your God will be with you wherever you go.
It was the time of the spring harvest, when the Jordan River is at flood stage and overflows its banks.
This was not a small stream.
It would have been very deep, fast, and dangerous. And there was no bridge.
The people of Israel stood on one side of the river, with the land God had promised them on the other.
Joshua sent two spies ahead to Jericho.
They stayed in the house of a woman named Rahab, who hid them and told them that the people of the land were terrified of Israel.
Then they came back with good news.
The Lord has surely given the whole land into our hands.
Everyone who lives in the country is melting in fear because of us.
Early in the morning, Joshua and all the Israelites moved out and camped by the Jordan.
After three days, the officers went through the camp and gave orders.
When you see the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God, and the Levitical priests carrying it, you are to move out from your positions and follow it.
Then you will know which way to go, since you have not been this way before.
But keep a distance of about a thousand yards between you and the ark. Do not go near it.
Joshua told the people to consecrate themselves, for tomorrow the Lord will do amazing things among you.
Then he told the priests, take up the ark of the covenant and pass on ahead of the people.
So they took it up and went ahead of them.
The Lord told Joshua, today I will begin to exalt you in the eyes of all Israel, so they may know that I am with you as I was with Moses.
Tell the priests who carry the ark to go and stand in the Jordan.
Here is the amazing part.
The water did not part until the priests stepped into it.
As soon as the priests who carried the ark reached the Jordan and their feet touched the water's edge, the water from upstream stopped flowing.
It piled up in a heap a great distance away, at a town called Adam.
The water flowing down to the Dead Sea was completely cut off.
So the people crossed over opposite Jericho.
The priests who carried the ark of the covenant stood on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan, while all Israel passed by until the whole nation had crossed on dry ground.
They did not cross with the river bottom still wet.
It was dry land, like it was at the Red Sea.
Then Joshua told twelve men, one from each tribe, to take twelve stones from the middle of the riverbed and carry them to the camp.
They set them up as a memorial at Gilgal.
In the future, when your children ask you, what do these stones mean?
Tell them that the flow of the Jordan was cut off before the ark of the covenant of the Lord.
These stones are to be a memorial to the people of Israel forever.
Why does this matter?
This was Israel's second great crossing.
Their parents crossed the Red Sea when they left.
Now the children crossed the Jordan when they came home.
It showed that the God who had been with Moses was with Joshua, and that the miracles hadn't ended.
It also shows how God often works.
The water didn't part until the priests' feet were wet.
They had to step out in faith first.
God does not usually show the path all at once.
He shows it one step at a time.
What happened after?
On the other side, the manna stopped.
The people ate the food of the land for the first time.
And Joshua met a man with a drawn sword who said he was the commander of the Lord's army.
The conquest of Canaan began with Jericho.
What does this mean for us today?
We often want to see the river part before we step in.
This story says to step in first.
Obedience comes before the miracle.
God asked the priests to walk into a flooded river, carrying something heavy, and the water stopped as soon as they got their feet wet.
It also reminds us to build memorials.
Joshua piled up stones so that the next generation would ask what they meant.
We need to remember what God has done, and tell it to our children.
That is why this story is so important.
Israel entered the Promised Land with a miracle, and they did it behind the ark, which stood for the presence of God.
We too go forward into the unknown not because we can see the way, but because the one we follow has already gone ahead.
jericho: Jericho was the first city Israel faced in the Promised Land.
It was a fortress, and one of the oldest cities in the world.
The Bible says its gates were tightly shut because of the Israelites.
No one went out and no one came in.
The walls were thick and strong, and Israel had no siege weapons, no ladders, and no army trained for this.
Joshua was thinking about how to attack when he saw a man standing in front of him with a drawn sword in his hand.
Joshua walked up to him and asked, are you for us or for our enemies? Neither, he replied.
But as commander of the army of the Lord I have now come.
Joshua fell facedown to the ground in reverence.
The commander said, take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy.
This was the same thing God said to Moses at the burning bush.
It reminded Joshua that this was not his battle. It was the Lord's.
God gave Joshua the strangest battle plan in history.
March around the city once with all the armed men. Do this for six days.
Have seven priests carry trumpets of rams' horns in front of the ark.
On the seventh day, march around the city seven times, with the priests blowing the trumpets.
When you hear them sound a long blast, have the whole army give a loud shout.
Then the wall of the city will collapse, and the army will go up, everyone straight in.
Joshua told the people to keep quiet.
Do not give a war cry, do not raise your voices, do not say a word until the day I tell you to shout. Then shout!
So for six days, the whole army walked around the city, and nobody said anything, just the trumpets and the footsteps.
Imagine being a soldier on those walls, watching a silent army circle the city every day.
Imagine being an Israelite, walking around a city without fighting.
On the seventh day, they got up at daybreak and marched around the city seven times.
The seventh time around, when the priests sounded the trumpet blast, Joshua commanded the army, shout!
For the Lord has given you the city.
The Bible says that when the trumpets sounded and the people shouted, the wall collapsed.
Everyone charged straight in, and they took the city.
Joshua had given a command about the city.
It was devoted to the Lord, and the Israelites were not to take anything from it.
But there was one exception.
Rahab the prostitute, and everyone with her in her house, were to be spared, because she hid the spies.
Joshua sent the two spies to bring her out.
She and her family were saved, and the Bible says she has lived among the Israelites to this day.
Rahab shows up again in a surprising place.
Matthew's gospel lists her in the family line of Jesus.
She married Salmon, and their son was Boaz, who married Ruth, and from them came King David.
A woman from Jericho became an ancestor of the Messiah.
Hebrews also lists her in its hall of faith.
By faith the walls of Jericho fell, after the army had marched around them for seven days.
By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies, was not killed with those who were disobedient.
Why does this matter?
Jericho shows that victory comes from God and not from human strength.
The Israelites didn't do anything that would make a wall fall.
All they did was obey, even when it made no sense.
The battle was won before a single sword was drawn.
It also shows that the story of Israel was never only for Israel.
Rahab was an outsider who believed what she heard about God and risked her life. God honored it.
What happened after?
Jericho was the first city, and more were to come.
But soon after, Israel was defeated at the small city of Ai, because a man named Achan had taken some of the forbidden treasure from Jericho.
Victory came from obedience, and so did defeat.
What does this mean for us today?
Sometimes God's plan doesn't seem to make sense.
Marching in circles will not win a war.
But the plan he gives us is often built to make sure we know who deserves the credit.
When we do what God says, even when it looks foolish, we find that the wall comes down.
It also means that no one is too far gone.
Rahab had a hard past, and God used her.
Whatever your past has been, it doesn't decide where your story goes.
That is why this story is so important.
It teaches that faith is not a feeling.
It is walking around a wall for seven days because God said to.
And it reminds us that God keeps his promises, and that the walls that look the strongest are not strong enough to stop him.
sun-stands: After Jericho and Ai, Israel kept moving into the land.
News of what was happening spread quickly.
One of the cities nearby, Gibeon, was afraid.
The people of Gibeon tricked Joshua into making a treaty with them.
They pretended to come from a far country, and wore worn-out clothes and carried moldy bread.
Joshua and the leaders didn't ask the Lord.
They made a peace treaty, and only found out three days later that Gibeon was a close neighbor.
Because they had sworn an oath, Israel kept it.
When the other kings in the area heard that Gibeon had made peace with Israel, they were furious.
Five Amorite kings joined their armies together and attacked Gibeon.
The Gibeonites sent a message to Joshua at Gilgal.
Do not abandon your servants.
Come up to us quickly and save us!
Help us, because all the Amorite kings from the hill country have joined forces against us.
Joshua could have said, you tricked us.
Instead he kept his promise.
He marched all night from Gilgal with his whole army, a steep climb of about twenty miles.
The Lord said to Joshua, do not be afraid of them.
I have given them into your hand.
Not one of them will be able to withstand you.
Joshua took them by surprise, and the Lord threw the enemy into confusion.
Israel defeated them at Gibeon, and chased them along the road up to Beth Horon.
As they fled, the Lord hurled large hailstones down on them from the sky.
More of them died from the hailstones than were killed by the swords of the Israelites.
God was fighting for Israel, and the weather was part of the battle.
Then Joshua did something that no one had ever done before.
On the day the Lord gave the Amorites over to Israel, Joshua said to the Lord in the presence of Israel, sun, stand still over Gibeon, and moon, over the Valley of Aijalon.
So the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, till the nation avenged itself on its enemies.
The sun stopped in the middle of the sky and delayed going down about a full day.
The Bible says, there has never been a day like it before or since, a day when the Lord listened to a human being.
Surely the Lord was fighting for Israel!
People have wondered for centuries exactly what happened.
Some believe the Earth's rotation actually slowed or stopped.
Others think the light was prolonged in a way we can't explain.
The Bible doesn't say how God did it.
It just says that he did, and that it was an answer to the prayer of a man who had faith.
The five kings had hidden in a cave at Makkedah.
Joshua had them brought out, and he told his commanders to put their feet on the necks of the kings.
Do not be afraid, do not be discouraged.
Be strong and courageous.
This is what the Lord will do to all the enemies you are going to fight.
Then Joshua went on to take the southern cities of Canaan.
Why does this matter?
It shows that God defends his people and keeps his promises, and that he listens to prayer.
It also shows that when you make a promise, you keep it.
Joshua had been tricked into the treaty, but he honored it, and God backed him.
It also shows what a difference a leader's trust makes.
Joshua had seen the Red Sea part as a young man, and he had seen the Jordan stop.
He believed that if God said to go, God would win the battle.
So he prayed boldly, and asked for something huge.
What happened after?
Joshua kept on defeating the kings of the land, and eventually Israel got its share.
Then Joshua gave the land to the tribes.
At the end of his life he gave a final speech.
As for me and my household, we will serve the Lord.
What does this mean for us today?
Maybe you don't pray for the sun to stand still.
But this story invites us to pray big prayers.
Joshua asked for something impossible, and God did it.
Do not be afraid to ask for large things, in line with what God has promised.
It also says to keep your word, even when keeping it is costly.
A promise made in the name of the Lord is a serious thing.
It's easy to want to get out of it when it costs us.
Joshua kept it, and God honored him.
That is why this story is so important.
It reminds us that the God who made the sun is in charge of it.
Nothing is too large for him to move, and nothing in our lives is too small for him to hear.
gideon: After Joshua died, Israel went through a cycle again and again in the book of Judges.
The people turned away from God and followed other gods.
God let their enemies conquer them.
The people cried out, and God sent a judge to rescue them. Then it began again.
This time it was the Midianites.
For seven years they raided Israel every harvest.
They came with camels and flocks like swarms of locusts and left nothing behind.
The Israelites hid in caves and mountain strongholds.
Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress, to hide it from the Midianites.
The angel of the Lord appeared to him and said, the Lord is with you, mighty warrior.
Gideon was not feeling mighty.
He said, pardon me, my lord, but if the Lord is with us, why has all this happened to us?
Where are all his wonders?
He told the angel that his clan was the weakest in Manasseh, and he was the least in his family.
The Lord answered, I will be with you, and you will strike down all the Midianites.
Gideon asked for a sign.
He put a wool fleece on the threshing floor and said, if there is dew only on the fleece and all the ground is dry, then I will know that you will save Israel by my hand.
In the morning the fleece was soaked, and Gideon wrung out a bowl full of water. Then he asked again.
This time, make the fleece dry and the ground wet.
And that is what happened.
God was patient with his doubts.
Gideon gathered an army of 32,000 men.
But the Lord said, you have too many men.
In order that Israel may not boast against me that her own strength has saved her, announce to the army, anyone who trembles with fear may turn back.
Twenty-two thousand left, leaving 10,000.
The Lord said, there are still too many.
Take them down to the water.
Those who lap the water with their tongues, like dogs, put to one side. Only 300 men did.
The Lord said, with the 300 men that lapped I will save you and give the Midianites into your hands.
The Midianite camp was as thick as a swarm of locusts, 135,000 men. Gideon had only 300.
In the night, God told him to go down to the camp and listen.
If you are afraid, take your servant.
He heard a Midianite telling a dream about a loaf of barley bread that tumbled into the camp and flattened the tent.
His friend answered, this can be nothing other than the sword of Gideon.
God has given the Midianites into his hands.
Gideon bowed down and worshiped.
He divided the 300 men into three companies.
He gave each man a trumpet and an empty jar with a torch inside. Watch me, he told them. Follow my lead.
When I and everyone with me blow our trumpets, then from all around the camp blow yours and shout, for the Lord and for Gideon!
They arrived at the edge of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch.
They blew their trumpets and smashed the jars.
All three companies blew the trumpets and broke the jars.
They held the torches in their left hands and the trumpets in their right, and shouted, a sword for the Lord and for Gideon!
While every man held his position, all the Midianites ran, crying out as they fled.
The Lord caused the men throughout the camp to turn on each other with their swords.
Why does this matter?
God picks the weak on purpose, so that no one can take the credit.
Gideon began as a frightened man in a winepress, and God called him a mighty warrior before he showed any sign of it.
God saw what Gideon would become and spoke to that.
It also shows how God deals with our doubts.
He didn't rebuke Gideon for asking for the fleece twice.
He gave him what he needed to believe.
But in the end he asked Gideon to trust him with a battle plan that made no sense.
What happened after?
Israel had peace for forty years.
They wanted to make Gideon king, but he refused.
The Lord will rule over you.
Sadly, he made a gold ephod from the plunder, and the people worshiped it.
Even a great man can fail after a great victory.
What does this mean for us today?
If you feel small, inadequate, or hidden, so did Gideon.
God doesn't wait for us to feel ready.
He meets us in the winepress and tells us who we are in his eyes.
It also tells us that numbers don't win battles.
Three hundred men with torches and jars, and the Lord in front.
God likes to work with fewer resources, so that it is obvious it was him.
That is why this story is so important.
It reminds us that the God who works through the weak, through jars of clay as Paul puts it, can use anyone.
The light is in us, and the jars have to break for it to show.
samson-lion: Israel had again turned away from God, and this time he let the Philistines rule them for forty years.
Before Samson was born, an angel appeared to his mother, who had been unable to have children.
The angel told her she would have a son who would begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines.
The boy was to be a Nazirite from birth. This meant three things.
He would never drink wine, he would never touch anything dead or unclean, and no razor would ever touch his head.
His long hair was the sign of his promise to God.
Samson grew up, and the Lord blessed him.
The Spirit of the Lord began to stir him.
He was given enormous physical strength.
But he was also headstrong, and he often let his desires lead him instead of God.
One day Samson went down to Timnah, a Philistine town, and saw a young Philistine woman.
He came back and told his parents, I have seen a Philistine woman in Timnah.
Get her for me as my wife. His parents were upset.
Isn't there an acceptable woman among your relatives?
Why do you have to go to the uncircumcised Philistines? But Samson insisted. Get her for me. She's right for me.
The Bible adds that his parents did not know that this was from the Lord, who was seeking an occasion to confront the Philistines.
As Samson went down to Timnah with his parents, a young lion came roaring toward him.
The Spirit of the Lord came powerfully upon him, and he tore the lion apart with his bare hands as he might have torn a young goat.
But he told neither his father nor his mother what he had done.
Some time later, when he went back to marry her, he turned aside to look at the lion's carcass.
In it was a swarm of bees and some honey.
He scooped out the honey with his hands and ate as he went along.
He gave some to his parents, but he did not tell them that he had taken the honey from the lion's carcass. Honey from a dead lion.
It was a secret thing, and a strange one, because a Nazirite was not supposed to touch anything dead.
At his wedding feast, Samson told the thirty young Philistine companions a riddle.
Out of the eater, something to eat.
Out of the strong, something sweet.
If you can give me the answer within the seven days of the feast, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes.
If you can't, you must give me the same.
They couldn't solve it, so they pressured Samson's wife.
She wept and badgered him until on the seventh day, he told her.
She told the Philistines.
They answered, what is sweeter than honey?
What is stronger than a lion?
Samson was furious.
He went to Ashkelon, killed thirty Philistines, took their belongings, and gave their clothes to the men who had explained the riddle.
Then in anger he went back to his father's house.
His wife was given to his companion.
Why does this matter?
It sets the scene for the rest of Samson's life, and shows both his strength and his weakness.
God gave him power for a purpose, to start freeing Israel.
But Samson used it again and again for personal revenge.
He was like Israel itself, called by God and gifted by God but often doing what was right in his own eyes.
The riddle also has a deeper meaning.
Out of death came sweetness.
A dead lion had honey in it.
God often brings life out of things that seem dead.
And the greatest example is the cross.
What happened after?
A cycle of revenge between Samson and the Philistines began.
It led to the great story of Delilah, which is next.
In the end, Samson did begin to deliver Israel, but at a terrible cost.
What does this mean for us today?
Gifts are not the same as character.
Samson had more strength than anyone in the Bible, and yet he could not control his temper or his desires.
We need more than talents.
We need to be led by the Spirit and not by our impulses.
It also says that God can use flawed people to do his work.
He worked through Samson, not because of his choices but in spite of them.
That should humble us, and encourage us.
Hebrews lists Samson among the heroes of faith.
That is why this story is so important.
It is a warning and a promise together.
A life set apart for God can be wasted by small compromises that seem harmless, but God does not give up on the person who was set apart.
The story of Samson is not over yet.
delilah: Samson was twenty years into his time as a judge of Israel, and the Philistines still ruled the land.
He had killed many of them in revenge, but he had not freed his people. His weakness was women.
He fell in love with a woman named Delilah, who lived in the Valley of Sorek.
The Philistine rulers went to her and said, see if you can lure him into showing you the secret of his great strength, and how we can overpower him.
Each of us will give you eleven hundred shekels of silver.
That was a huge amount of money.
So Delilah asked Samson, tell me the secret of your great strength. He lied.
If anyone ties me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, I'll become as weak as any other man.
She tied him with seven bowstrings while men were hiding in the room.
She cried out, Samson, the Philistines are upon you!
He snapped the bowstrings like a thread of tow that comes close to a flame.
She said, you have made a fool of me. You lied to me.
Please tell me how you can be tied.
He said, new ropes that have never been used. She tried it.
He snapped them off his arms like thread.
A third time he told her it was the seven braids of his hair woven into a loom. She wove them in.
He pulled up the loom and the pin.
Each time, Delilah would cry out that the Philistines were on him, and each time they were. Samson never learned.
The Bible says that with such nagging she prodded him day after day until he was sick to death of it.
So he told her everything.
No razor has ever been used on my head, because I have been a Nazirite dedicated to God since birth.
If my head were shaved, my strength would leave me, and I would become as weak as any other man.
Delilah saw that he had told her the truth.
She sent word to the rulers.
This time, come back once more.
He has told me everything.
The rulers came with the silver in their hands.
She let him go to sleep on her lap, and called a man to shave off the seven braids of his hair.
Then she began to subdue him, and his strength left him.
She called, Samson, the Philistines are upon you!
He awoke from his sleep and thought, I'll go out as before and shake myself free.
But he did not know that the Lord had left him.
Then comes one of the saddest lines in the Bible.
Then the Philistines seized him, gouged out his eyes and took him down to Gaza.
Binding him with bronze shackles, they set him to grinding grain in the prison.
He was a slave, and blind, and working a mill like an ox.
But the hair on his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.
Why does this matter?
Samson's strength was never really in his hair. It came from the Lord.
The hair was a sign of his promise to God, and when he let the promise be broken bit by bit, the Lord's Spirit left him.
The tragedy is that he didn't even notice.
He woke up and thought he would shake himself free as before.
It is a warning for anyone with a gift.
We can lose it so slowly that we don't notice until it is gone.
Samson played with temptation again and again.
He lied about the secret three times, which meant he was keeping it close to the edge.
It was only a matter of time until he gave in.
What happened after?
Samson was alone, blind, and in the dark. His hair grew back.
And that is where the Bible turns the story, as we will see in the next scene.
Even the lowest point of his life was not the end.
What does this mean for us today?
Be careful what you play with.
Samson thought he could flirt with disaster and always get away.
We do that too, with habits, relationships, and decisions that seem small.
Each time, we think we can walk back from the edge.
It also means that the people we trust the most can hurt us, and that we can hurt the people who love us.
Delilah was paid to betray him, but the real problem was that Samson let her get close to the one secret that mattered.
That is why this story is so important.
It is a warning about what happens to people who are given much and take it lightly.
And yet it is also the first half of a story of grace.
The man who lost everything in this chapter would turn to God in the next one.
samson-death: Samson was in prison in Gaza.
He was blind, his head was shaved, and he was chained to a grinding wheel.
The Philistines thought they had won.
The Bible says that Samson had been a judge of Israel for twenty years, and he was now a slave.
But the hair on his head began to grow again.
The Philistine rulers gathered to offer a great sacrifice to their god Dagon, and to celebrate.
They said, our god has delivered Samson, our enemy, into our hands.
When the people saw him, they praised their god, saying, our god has delivered our enemy into our hands, the one who laid waste our land and multiplied our slain.
While they were in high spirits, they shouted, bring out Samson to entertain us.
So they called Samson out of the prison, and he performed for them.
They stood him between the pillars.
The temple was crowded with men and women.
All the rulers of the Philistines were there, and on the roof were about three thousand men and women watching Samson perform.
It was a large building, a place built to hold the whole Philistine leadership and a great crowd.
Samson said to the servant who held his hand, put me where I can feel the pillars that support the temple, so that I may lean against them.
Then Samson prayed to the Lord.
Sovereign Lord, remember me.
Please, God, strengthen me just once more, and let me with one blow get revenge on the Philistines for my two eyes.
Look at that prayer.
For years Samson had acted as if his strength belonged to him.
Now he prayed, God, please.
It was the first time in his story that he asked God for something instead of taking it. He was humble.
He was blind, and he had nothing left, and he knew it.
He remembered that God was the source.
Then Samson reached toward the two central pillars on which the temple stood.
Bracing himself against them, his right hand on the one and his left hand on the other, Samson said, let me die with the Philistines!
Then he pushed with all his strength, and the temple fell on the rulers and all the people in it.
Those he killed at his death were more than those he had killed during his life.
His brothers and his father's whole family went down to get his body.
They brought him back and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol, in the tomb of his father Manoah.
He had led Israel for twenty years.
Why does this matter?
Samson's last act is a picture of a man whose strength came back when he turned back to God.
God answered the prayer of a man who had thrown away almost everything. That is grace.
It doesn't mean that the damage was undone.
Samson lost his eyes, his freedom, and his life.
But it does mean that God was still working, and he was not finished with Samson.
The book of Hebrews lists Samson among the heroes of faith.
That is a surprise, and an encouragement.
He is not on the list for his record.
He is there because at the end, he trusted God.
What happened after?
Samson began to deliver Israel from the Philistines, as the angel had said, but it was not completed.
The book of Judges ends in a dark mess, with the repeated line, in those days Israel had no king, and everyone did as they saw fit.
The people needed a better king.
Samuel and David would come, and ultimately Jesus.
Jesus has a similarity to Samson, but he is the better version.
Samson died with his arms stretched out between two pillars, and in his death he defeated more enemies than he did in life.
Jesus died with his arms stretched out, and in his death he broke the power of sin and death.
What does this mean for us today?
It is never too late to turn back to God.
Samson was blind, chained, and humiliated. He had no one left.
But even there, the Lord heard his prayer.
It also means that our failures do not cancel God's purposes.
Samson's life was messy, and the cost was high.
But God still used his last act to do what he'd said he would do.
If you feel that you have wasted your gifts, this story says that God can still hear you.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows the one who is strong enough to save and gracious enough to hear the prayer of a failure.
Samson's last prayer was short, and it began with the right word. Lord.
ruth-naomi: This story happened in the days when the judges ruled Israel, a time of violence and confusion.
But the book of Ruth is a quiet one.
It is about a family, a famine, and two women.
A man named Elimelech from Bethlehem, which means house of bread, took his wife Naomi and two sons to live in the country of Moab, because there was no food in Judah.
Moab was a neighbor that Israel had a hard history with.
Elimelech died.
The sons married Moabite women, one named Orpah and the other Ruth.
After about ten years, both sons died too.
Naomi was left alone in a foreign country, with no husband and no sons.
In that world, a widow without a family had no support at all.
Naomi heard that the Lord had come to the aid of his people by providing food for them back in Bethlehem. She decided to go home.
Her two daughters-in-law started with her.
But on the road, Naomi told them to go back.
May the Lord show you kindness, as you have shown to your dead and to me.
May the Lord grant that each of you will find rest in the home of another husband.
Then she kissed them, and they wept aloud.
They said, we will go back with you to your people. But Naomi insisted.
Why would you come with me?
Am I going to have any more sons, who could become your husbands? No, my daughters.
It is more bitter for me than for you, because the Lord's hand has turned against me. They wept again.
Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye and went back. This wasn't wrong.
It was a reasonable decision. But Ruth clung to Naomi.
Naomi said, look, your sister-in-law is going back to her people and her gods. Go back with her.
Ruth answered with some of the most beautiful words in the Bible.
Don't urge me to leave you or to turn back from you.
Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay.
Your people will be my people and your God my God.
Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried.
May the Lord deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.
Ruth was not an Israelite.
She was a foreigner, a woman, and a widow.
Yet she gave up her home, her family, and her own gods to follow Naomi and Naomi's God.
She had nothing to gain and everything to lose.
When Naomi saw that she was determined, she stopped urging her.
They went on until they came to Bethlehem.
The whole town was stirred, and the women asked, can this be Naomi?
She said, don't call me Naomi, which means pleasant.
Call me Mara, which means bitter, because the Almighty has made my life very bitter.
I went away full, but the Lord has brought me back empty.
They arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.
Why does this matter?
Ruth's loyalty is a picture of what the Bible calls hesed, the Hebrew word for faithful, covenant love that doesn't quit.
She chose to stay with someone who could give her nothing.
It is one of the clearest pictures of love in the Old Testament.
It is also the story of a woman from Moab, an outsider, who came to trust the God of Israel.
The Bible shows again that God's plan was always bigger than one nation.
Ruth is one of only two books in the Bible named for a woman, and she was a foreigner.
What happened after?
Ruth went out to glean in the fields, and she met a man named Boaz. That is the next scene.
In the end, she married him and had a son, Obed.
Obed became the grandfather of King David, and through David's line came Jesus.
Ruth is in the family tree of the Messiah.
What does this mean for us today?
Naomi is a picture of anyone who feels empty.
She was honest about her pain, and she was heard.
She said I am bitter, and the story doesn't say she was wrong.
God didn't leave her there.
Ruth is a picture of faithfulness.
She stayed when it would have been easier to leave.
She did it for someone who couldn't pay her back.
Real love is often just that, staying.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that God is working in the background of everyday sorrow.
The famine, the funerals, and the road home were all part of a plan that would reach to Bethlehem and a manger.
The house of bread was where the Bread of Life would one day be born.
ruth-boaz: Ruth and Naomi had arrived in Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest. They were poor.
They had no land and no income.
But the law God gave Israel had a provision for people like them.
When farmers harvested their fields, they were not to go over the field a second time or pick up what was dropped.
That was left for the poor, the foreigner, the widow, and the orphan. It was called gleaning.
Ruth said to Naomi, let me go to the fields and pick up the leftover grain behind anyone in whose eyes I find favor.
Naomi said, go ahead, my daughter.
As it turned out, she found herself working in a field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelech.
The Bible says, as it turned out.
It doesn't say that she planned it.
This is how the writer shows God working behind the scenes.
Just then Boaz arrived from Bethlehem and greeted the harvesters. The Lord be with you!
The Lord bless you! he said.
He asked his foreman, whose young woman is that?
The foreman said, she is the Moabite who came back with Naomi.
She said, please let me glean and gather among the sheaves behind the harvesters.
She came into the field and has kept working steadily from morning until now, except for a short rest in the shelter.
Boaz spoke to Ruth.
My daughter, listen to me.
Don't go and glean in another field and don't go away from here.
Stay here with the women who work for me.
I have told the men not to lay a hand on you.
And whenever you are thirsty, go and get a drink from the water jars the men have filled.
This was a real protection.
A foreign woman alone in the fields was vulnerable.
Ruth bowed down with her face to the ground.
Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you notice me, a foreigner?

Boaz replied, I've been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband, how you left your father and mother and your homeland and came to live with a people you did not know before.
May the Lord repay you for what you have done.
May you be richly rewarded by the Lord, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.
At mealtime, Boaz invited her to come eat with them.
He offered her bread and roasted grain, and she ate until she was full and had some left over.
When she got up to glean again, Boaz ordered his men to let her gather even among the sheaves, and to pull out some stalks for her from the bundles and leave them for her to pick up.
She gleaned until evening.
She threshed the barley, and it was about an ephah, which is around thirty pounds.
She carried it back to town and showed her mother-in-law.
Naomi asked, where did you glean today? Where did you work?
Blessed be the man who took notice of you!
When Ruth told her it was Boaz, Naomi said, the Lord bless him!
He has not stopped showing his kindness to the living and the dead.
That man is our close relative.
He is one of our guardian-redeemers.
A guardian-redeemer was a relative who had the right and the duty to rescue a family member in need, to buy back the land and to marry the widow.
For the rest of the barley and wheat harvest, Ruth stayed close to the women who worked for Boaz and kept gleaning.
In the next chapter, Ruth went to Boaz on the threshing floor and asked him to be her redeemer. He agreed.
He went to the town gate and arranged for the closer relative to give up his claim.
Then he bought Elimelech's land and married Ruth.
Why does this matter?
Boaz is a picture of Christ.
He is the redeemer, the one who sees a stranger in need, pays the price to rescue her, and brings her into his family.
Ruth could not save herself, and she had no claim on him. Everything was by grace.
The kindness began with him.
What happened after?
Ruth and Boaz had a son named Obed, and the women of Bethlehem said to Naomi, praise be to the Lord, who this day has not left you without a guardian-redeemer.
Naomi took the child in her arms, and he was like a son to her.
Obed was the father of Jesse, and Jesse was the father of David.
A story that started with death ended with a birth.
What does this mean for us today?
It says that God is at work in ordinary things.
A woman went out to pick up leftover grain.
It doesn't look like history.
But it was exactly where God's plan was moving.
It also says something about how we treat the poor.
Boaz made it easy for Ruth.
He left extra grain for her and protected her dignity.
That is how God's people are meant to treat anyone in need, with generosity, not just minimum compliance.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that the Redeemer was already at work in the Old Testament, in a small field, with a foreign widow, and a kind man.
And it assures us that a God who cares about the gleaners cares about us.
goliath: For forty days, the Philistine army and the army of Israel faced each other across the Valley of Elah.
The Philistines were on one hill and the Israelites on another.
And every morning and evening a giant named Goliath stepped out and challenged Israel.
He was from Gath, and he stood over nine feet tall.
He wore bronze armor that weighed about 125 pounds, and carried a spear with an iron tip weighing fifteen pounds.
His shield bearer walked ahead of him.
Goliath shouted, why do you come out and line up for battle?
Am I not a Philistine, and are you not the servants of Saul?
Choose a man and have him come down to me.
If he is able to fight and kill me, we will become your subjects.
But if I overcome him and kill him, you will become our subjects.
This day I defy the armies of Israel!
Give me a man and let us fight each other.
When Saul and the Israelites heard this, they were dismayed and terrified.
King Saul was the tallest man in Israel.
If anyone should have gone out, it was him. But he was afraid too.
For forty days, no one in the army of Israel did anything.
Meanwhile, back in Bethlehem, a young shepherd named David was caring for his father's sheep.
His three oldest brothers were in Saul's army.
One day his father Jesse sent him to the camp with bread and cheese for his brothers.
David arrived just as the army was going out to the battle line, shouting the war cry.
He heard Goliath's challenge, and he saw the men of Israel run in fear.
David asked, what will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and removes this disgrace from Israel?
Who is this uncircumcised Philistine that he should defy the armies of the living God?
His oldest brother, Eliab, was angry.
Why have you come down here?
And with whom did you leave those few sheep?
I know how conceited you are and how wicked your heart is.
David said, now what have I done? Can't I even speak?
Word got to Saul, and he sent for David.
David told him, let no one lose heart on account of this Philistine.
Your servant will go and fight him.
Saul said, you are only a young man, and he has been a warrior from his youth.
David said, your servant has been keeping his father's sheep.
When a lion or a bear came and carried off a sheep from the flock, I went after it, struck it and rescued the sheep from its mouth.
The Lord who rescued me from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear will rescue me from the hand of this Philistine.
Saul put his own armor on David, but David couldn't walk in it. He took it off.
Instead he took his staff in his hand, chose five smooth stones from the stream, and put them in his shepherd's bag.
With his sling in his hand, he approached Goliath.
Goliath looked David over and saw that he was little more than a boy, and he despised him.
Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?
David said, you come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the Lord Almighty, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.
This day the Lord will deliver you into my hands.
The whole world will know that there is a God in Israel.
All those gathered here will know that it is not by sword or spear that the Lord saves.
For the battle is the Lord's.
David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet him.
He reached into his bag, took out a stone, and slung it.
It struck the Philistine on the forehead and sank in, and he fell facedown on the ground.
David had no sword in his hand.
He ran and stood over him, took Goliath's own sword, and cut off his head.
When the Philistines saw that their hero was dead, they turned and ran, and Israel chased them.
Why does this matter?
David wasn't chosen because he was strong.
God had already chosen him through the prophet Samuel, passing over his older and taller brothers.
God doesn't look at the outward appearance, but at the heart. David trusted God.
And he refused to see the situation the way everyone else did.
They saw a giant too big to fight.
David saw a giant too big to miss.
What happened after?
David became a hero, and Saul grew jealous.
This began years of running from Saul.
But David was also anointed to be the next king, and eventually he reigned for forty years.
Through his family, Jesus would come.
What does this mean for us today? Everybody faces a giant.
It might be a diagnosis, a debt, or a fear that has loomed over you for months.
This story says that the size of the problem is not the main thing. Whom you trust is.
David had a sling, but he had learned in private, with the lion and the bear, that God was faithful.
The little victories prepared him for the big one.
It also tells us not to use someone else's armor.
Saul's armor was fine, but it was not David's.
God uses us as we are, with the tools we know, and we don't need to be someone else.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that the battle belongs to the Lord.
It teaches courage that does not come from being strong, but from knowing who is on our side.
It points to Jesus, a shepherd from Bethlehem who went out alone to face the enemy, and won the victory for everyone else.
jonathan: After David defeated Goliath, King Saul brought him to the palace.
David was still a teenager, a shepherd boy from Bethlehem.
As soon as he finished speaking with Saul, something happened that would change his life.
The Bible says that the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as himself.
Jonathan was Saul's oldest son.
He was a prince, the heir to the throne.
He was also a brave soldier.

Earlier in the book of First Samuel, he and his armor bearer had climbed a cliff and attacked a whole Philistine outpost, because he trusted that nothing could keep the Lord from saving, whether by many or by few.
He had every reason to see David as a rival.
A shepherd boy had just done what no one in Saul's army, including Jonathan, had been willing to do.
But Jonathan didn't see a rival. He saw a friend.
He made a covenant with David because he loved him as himself.
Jonathan took off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his tunic, his sword, his bow, and his belt. This was no small gift.
A prince's robe and weapons were a sign of his position.
In giving them away, Jonathan was in a sense handing over his future as king.
David was successful in everything Saul sent him to do, and Saul gave him a high rank in the army.
But as the army came home, the women came out from all the towns of Israel to meet King Saul with singing and dancing, with joyful songs and with timbrels and lutes.
And they sang, Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands. Saul was very angry.
This refrain displeased him greatly.
What more can he get but the kingdom?
And from that time on, Saul kept a jealous eye on David.
The next day, an evil spirit came on Saul, and David was playing the lyre as he usually did.
Saul had a spear in his hand and he hurled it, saying to himself, I'll pin David to the wall.
But David eluded him twice.
Saul was afraid of David, because the Lord was with David but had departed from Saul.
Jonathan became David's protector.
When Saul told his servants and Jonathan to kill David, Jonathan warned David.
Jonathan spoke up for David to his father.
He said, let not the king do wrong to his servant David.
He has not wronged you, and what he has done has benefited you greatly.
He took his life in his hands when he killed the Philistine.
Saul listened and swore, as surely as the Lord lives, David will not be put to death.
But the jealousy came back. David ran away.
In secret, Jonathan and David met at a field.
Jonathan promised to find out what his father really planned.
They agreed on a signal with arrows.
Jonathan shot three arrows and told his servant boy, isn't the arrow beyond you? Hurry!
That was the sign that David had to flee.
Then the two friends kissed each other and wept together, though David wept the most.

Jonathan said to David, go in peace, for we have sworn friendship with each other in the name of the Lord, saying, the Lord is witness between you and me, and between your descendants and my descendants forever.
Why does this matter?
Jonathan chose to love David, even when it cost him the throne.
He knew that God had chosen David to be king.
He knew the crown that should have been his would go to David.
He gave up his claim willingly.
In a world where people fight for power, Jonathan is a picture of someone who put God's plan, and a friend, ahead of his own ambition.
It also shows what friendship can be.
Jonathan didn't just say nice words.
He risked his life to save David.
He was loyal when it cost him.
Proverbs says a friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for a time of adversity.
What happened after?
Jonathan died with his father in a battle on Mount Gilboa.
David wept for him and wrote a song.
I grieve for you, Jonathan my brother.
You were very dear to me.
Your love for me was wonderful, more wonderful than that of women.
Later, David kept his promise.
He found Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, who had been injured as a child, and invited him to eat at the king's table for the rest of his life.
What does this mean for us today?
Think about who the Jonathans in your life are.
Who has given you an encouragement, or a warning, or a place to belong?
And who needs you to be that for them?
It also asks us a hard question.
Can we cheer for someone who is getting what we wanted? Jonathan did that.
His joy in David's success was greater than his own desire for the throne.
That kind of generosity is rare, and it is how Jesus asks us to love.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows a friendship built on shared trust in God.
Jonathan and David swore their love in the name of the Lord, and that is what made it last.
Jesus said, greater love has no one than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends.
spares-saul: David was running for his life.
King Saul was jealous, and he had taken three thousand of his best soldiers to hunt David down in the wilderness near En Gedi, a desert oasis with cliffs and caves along the Dead Sea.
David and his six hundred men were hiding.
Saul came to a sheep pen along the way.
There was a cave there, and he went in to relieve himself.
It happened that David and his men were far back in that very cave.
They whispered to David, this is the day the Lord spoke of when he said to you, I will give your enemy into your hands for you to deal with as you wish.
David crept up unnoticed and cut off a corner of Saul's robe.
Afterward, David was conscience-stricken for having cut off a corner of his robe.
He said to his men, the Lord forbid that I should do such a thing to my master, the Lord's anointed, or lay my hand on him.
He is the anointed of the Lord.
With these words David sharply rebuked his men and did not allow them to attack Saul.
And Saul left the cave and went on his way.
Think about what David had every reason to do.
Saul had tried to kill him with a spear, had hunted him for years, and had even murdered the priests of Nob for helping him.
David had already been anointed by the prophet Samuel as the next king.
His men were telling him that God had handed Saul over. But David said no.
He would not take the throne by force.
He would wait for God to give it to him.
After Saul had left the cave and gone on his way, David went out and called out to him, my lord the king!
When Saul looked behind him, David bowed down and prostrated himself with his face to the ground.
He said, why do you listen when people say, David is bent on harming you?
This day you have seen with your own eyes how the Lord delivered you into my hands in the cave.
Some urged me to kill you, but I spared you.
I said, I will not lay my hand on my lord, because he is the Lord's anointed.
Then David held up the piece of Saul's robe.
See, my father, look at this piece of your robe in my hand!
I cut off the corner of your robe but did not kill you.
See that there is nothing in my hands to indicate that I am guilty of wrongdoing or rebellion.
I have not wronged you, but you are hunting me down to take my life.
May the Lord judge between you and me.
And may the Lord avenge the wrongs you have done to me, but my hand will not touch you.
Saul wept aloud.
He said, you are more righteous than I.
You have treated me well, but I have treated you badly.
You have just now told me about the good you did to me.
The Lord delivered me into your hands, but you did not kill me.
When a man finds his enemy, does he let him get away unharmed?
May the Lord reward you well for the way you treated me today.
Saul even admitted that David would be king.
Swear to me that you will not kill off my descendants. David gave his oath.
Then Saul returned home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.
Sadly, this was not the end of Saul's pursuit.
He would turn on David again.
But David had shown who he was.
Why does this matter?
David had the power to end his troubles in one stroke. He chose not to.
He understood that being right does not give us the right to take revenge. He left justice to God.
Later, David had the chance a second time, when Saul was asleep in his camp, and again he spared him.
Paul would later write, do not take revenge, my dear friends, but leave room for God's wrath.
It also shows how a leader should treat authority.
Saul was not a good king, and he had been rejected by God.
But David respected the office.
He waited for God to put him on the throne, not his own hand.
What happened after?
Saul died in battle on Mount Gilboa, and David became king.
He didn't gain the throne through violence against his master, and the people knew it.
That helped him unite the nation.
What does this mean for us today?
We will all have people who wrong us, and sometimes we will have the chance to get even.
This story teaches us to pause and ask, what would honor God here? Mercy is not weakness.
It takes more strength to spare an enemy than to hurt him.
It also tells us to wait.
David was promised a throne, and he could have taken it. He waited years.
Often, God gives us things in his time, and the waiting is part of what shapes us.
That is why this story is so important.
It is a preview of the way of Jesus.
He said, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.
David, in a dark cave, did it first.
And one day, a descendant of David, hanging on a cross, would say, Father, forgive them.
absalom: David was a great king, but his family was a mess.
His troubles started with his own sin.
He committed adultery with Bathsheba and had her husband Uriah killed.
The prophet Nathan told him that because of this, the sword would never depart from his house. And it didn't.
His oldest son Amnon assaulted his half-sister Tamar.
Her brother Absalom hated Amnon for it and, after two years, had him killed.
Absalom fled and stayed away for three years.
David longed for him, and eventually brought him home.
But he refused to see Absalom for two more years.
Absalom was handsome, the Bible says.
There was no one in all Israel so highly praised for his good looks.
When he cut his hair, it weighed about five pounds.
He began to stand at the city gate every morning and greet people who came with a complaint.
If only I were appointed judge in the land, he would say.
Then everyone who has a complaint could come to me and I would see that they receive justice.
And whenever anyone approached him to bow down, he would reach out, take hold of him, and kiss him.
In this way, the Bible says, Absalom stole the hearts of the people of Israel.
After four years, he went to Hebron and had himself declared king.
The conspiracy gained strength, and the number of people who supported him kept growing.
A messenger came to David and said, the hearts of the people of Israel are with Absalom.
David left Jerusalem on foot, weeping, with his head covered and his feet bare.
He had to flee from his own son.
The two armies met in the forest of Ephraim. David stayed behind.
As the army marched out, the king gave an order to Joab and the other commanders.
Be gentle with the young man Absalom for my sake.
Everyone heard the king giving orders about Absalom.
It is a startling sentence.
His son was trying to take his throne, and David's thought was for him.
The battle was fought, and the rebels were defeated.
Absalom happened to meet some of David's men.
He was riding his mule, and as it went under the thick branches of a large oak, his hair got caught in the tree.
He was left hanging in midair, while the mule he was riding kept on going.
When one of the men reported it to Joab, Joab, who was not so gentle, took three javelins and plunged them into Absalom's heart.
Ten of his armor bearers then surrounded Absalom and struck him and killed him.
Joab then sounded the trumpet, and the troops stopped.
They took Absalom's body, threw it into a big pit in the forest, and piled a large heap of rocks over it.
Meanwhile, David was sitting between the inner and outer gates of the city. A messenger arrived.
Good news for my lord the king!
The Lord has delivered you today from all who rose up against you.
David asked only one thing.
Is the young man Absalom safe?
The man said, may the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up to harm you be like that young man. The king was shaken.
He went up to the room over the gateway and wept.
As he went, he said, O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom!
If only I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!
Why does this matter?
It shows that even great people suffer from their mistakes, and that sin has long consequences.
David was forgiven by God, but the effects of what he'd done kept playing out in his family.
It also shows the heart of a father.
David was a king who had won a victory, and yet he grieved for a son who tried to kill him.
It points us to the heart of God.
The way David loved a rebellious son is the way God loves us.
And the words, if only I had died instead of you, were later made real.
Jesus did die in the place of those who rebelled against him.
What happened after?
Joab came to David and told him bluntly to pull himself together, since the army was ashamed.
David went back to the gate and sat down.
He returned to Jerusalem as king.
But the cost was heavy, and he spent the rest of his reign dealing with the aftermath.
What does this mean for us today?
If you are a parent grieving a child who has gone the wrong way, you are not alone.
David's cry is in the Bible so that people who feel this pain know that God understands.
He saw it in his own Son's case.
It also warns us about quiet ambition.
Absalom didn't begin with a sword.
He began at the gate, with a smile and a kiss and a promise.
Be careful about people who steal hearts, and about stealing them yourself.
That is why this story is so important.
It tells the truth about love and failure in the same family.
It shows a father who could not save his son, and it points to the Father who could.
When we were rebels, he did not say, be gentle, and then look away.
He gave his own Son so we could live.
solomon-judgment: David was dead.
His son Solomon became king of Israel, but he was young, probably in his twenties, and he knew it.
Early in his reign, he went to Gibeon to offer sacrifices.
That night, the Lord appeared to him in a dream.
God said, ask for whatever you want me to give you.
Think about that. Anything.
Solomon could have asked for riches, a long life, or the death of his enemies.
Instead, he answered with a humble prayer.
You have shown great kindness to your servant, my father David.
Now, Lord my God, you have made your servant king in place of my father David.
But I am only a little child and do not know how to carry out my duties.
Your servant is here among the people you have chosen, a great people, too numerous to count.
So give your servant a discerning heart to govern your people and to distinguish between right and wrong.
For who is able to govern this great people of yours?
The Lord was pleased that Solomon had asked for this.
God said, since you have asked for this and not for long life or wealth for yourself, nor have asked for the death of your enemies, I will do what you have asked.
I will give you a wise and discerning heart, so that there will never have been anyone like you, nor will there ever be.
Moreover, I will give you what you have not asked for, both wealth and honor.
Solomon woke up and realized it had been a dream.
He returned to Jerusalem and offered sacrifices.
Not long after, two women came to the king.
They lived in the same house, and each had given birth to a baby, three days apart.
One night, one of the babies died.
The woman whose child had died got up in the night and took the living child from the other woman's side, and put her dead child there.
In the morning, the second woman saw the dead baby and realized it wasn't hers.
They were both claiming the living child. One said, no! The dead one is yours. The living one is mine. The other said, no! The living one is mine. The dead one is yours.
They argued in front of the king.
There were no witnesses, no records, and no tests.
It was one woman's word against another's.
The king said, bring me a sword.
Then he said, cut the living child in two and give half to one and half to the other.
The woman whose son was alive was deeply moved out of love for her son.
She said, please, my lord, give her the living baby! Don't kill him!
But the other said, neither I nor you shall have him. Cut him in two!
Then the king gave his ruling.
Give the living baby to the first woman. Do not kill him. She is his mother.
When all Israel heard the verdict the king had given, they held the king in awe, because they saw that he had wisdom from God to administer justice.
Why does this matter?
Solomon's wisdom didn't come from his intelligence.
It was a gift that he asked for.
He knew what he lacked, and he asked God.
James says, if any of you lacks wisdom, you should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to you.
It also shows what true love looks like.
The real mother was willing to lose her child, so he could live.
She cared more about the baby's life than about winning.
This is the same kind of love God shows.
In a sense, it pictures the love of a Father who gives up his Son.
What happened after?
Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem and ruled in peace and wealth.
His fame went far and wide, as we see in the story of the Queen of Sheba.
But in his old age, he married many foreign women and allowed their gods into his heart.
He started well and ended poorly, and his kingdom was split after his death.
What does this mean for us today?
When we are asked what we want most, what do we say?
Solomon asked for wisdom, and he got that plus everything else.
Jesus said something similar.
Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.
It also encourages us.
You may feel too young, too new, or too unprepared for what you are facing.
Solomon said he was a little child.
God didn't tell him to be more confident.
He gave him what he needed.
And God gives wisdom to those who ask.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that real wisdom is a gift from God, and it begins with admitting we don't know.
Solomon's wisdom was great, but the Bible says one greater than Solomon has come. That is Jesus.
sheba: Solomon was now the most famous king in the world.
God had given him wisdom, wealth, and peace.
He had built the temple in Jerusalem, a magnificent house for the Lord, and a palace for himself.
His fame went far beyond Israel.
Visitors from many nations came to hear his wisdom.
One of them traveled from a distant land called Sheba, probably in southern Arabia, in what is today Yemen, though some think it may have been Ethiopia.
The Bible says the queen of Sheba heard about the fame of Solomon and his relation to the name of the Lord, and she came to test him with hard questions.
It was a long trip, over a thousand miles, across the desert by camel.
She came to Jerusalem with a very great caravan, with camels carrying spices, large quantities of gold, and precious stones.
This was more than a courtesy call.
She was a queen, and a smart one.
She wanted to see for herself.
She did not believe what she had been told.
When she came to Solomon, she talked with him about all that she had on her mind.
Solomon answered all her questions.
Nothing was too hard for the king to explain to her.

When the queen of Sheba saw all the wisdom of Solomon and the palace he had built, the food on his table, the seating of his officials, the attending servants in their robes, his cupbearers, and the burnt offerings he made at the temple of the Lord, she was overwhelmed.
She said to the king, the report I heard in my own country about your achievements and your wisdom is true.
But I did not believe these things until I came and saw with my own eyes.
Indeed, not even half was told me.
In wisdom and wealth you have far exceeded the report I heard.
How happy your people must be!
How happy your officials, who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom!
Praise be to the Lord your God, who has delighted in you and placed you on the throne of Israel.
Because of the Lord's eternal love for Israel, he has made you king to maintain justice and righteousness.
Notice what she said at the end.
She didn't just praise Solomon.
She praised the Lord his God.
A foreign queen, from a land with its own gods, was led by Solomon's wisdom to the God behind it.
That was what Israel was meant to do, to show the world what it looks like to follow the true God.
She gave the king 120 talents of gold, large quantities of spices, and precious stones.
Never again were so many spices brought in as the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.
And King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba all she desired and asked for, in addition to what he had given her out of his royal bounty.
Then she left and returned with her retinue to her own country.
Why does this matter?
It shows what God intended for Israel.
They were meant to be a light to the nations, so that when outsiders saw how God blessed his people, they would want to know him.
The queen of Sheba's visit is an early picture of what Isaiah promised, that nations would come to Zion's light.
It is also remembered by Jesus.

He said, the Queen of the South will rise at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to listen to Solomon's wisdom, and now something greater than Solomon is here.
Jesus was telling the people around him that they had greater evidence, and still didn't come to him.
She traveled a thousand miles for the wisdom of a king.
They had the wisdom of God standing in front of them.
What happened after?
Solomon's reign continued for forty years.
Tradition in Ethiopia says that the queen had a son by Solomon, who founded the royal line there.
The Bible doesn't say this, but tradition has said so for centuries.
What the Bible does tell us is that Solomon's heart later drifted, and his kingdom divided after his death.
What does this mean for us today?
She was willing to go the distance to find the truth.
She asked hard questions and didn't just accept what she'd heard.
God welcomes honest questions.
If you are searching for answers about God, don't be afraid to bring your hardest ones.
And once she saw, she gave.
