She didn't leave empty-handed or unchanged.
When we really meet the wisdom of God, it tends to move us to respond with generosity and praise.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that the God of Israel is for everyone, from every nation, and that those who seek him will find him.
And it points to Jesus, who is greater than Solomon, and who invites everyone who is thirsty to come and see.
widows-son: Israel had a wicked king named Ahab, and his wife Jezebel led the whole nation to worship a false god named Baal.
Baal was supposed to be the god of storms and rain.
So God sent a prophet named Elijah to say something bold to the king.
As surely as the Lord lives, there will be no dew or rain in the next few years except at my word.
The rain stopped. Rivers dried up. Crops failed.
For a while God hid Elijah by a stream, and ravens brought him bread and meat every morning and evening.
Then the stream dried up too.
God told Elijah to go to the town of Zarephath, which was in the homeland of Jezebel, not in Israel.
There, God said, a widow will feed you.
Elijah found a woman at the town gate gathering sticks.
He asked her for a drink of water and a piece of bread.
She answered that she had only a handful of flour and a little oil left.
She was gathering sticks to make one last meal for herself and her son.
After that, they expected to starve.
Elijah told her not to be afraid.
Make me a small loaf first, he said, then make something for yourself and your son.
For this is what the Lord says.
The jar of flour will not be used up and the jug of oil will not run dry until the day the Lord sends rain.
She went and did as Elijah said.
She gave away what looked like her last meal.
And the flour and the oil did not run out.
Day after day, there was enough.
Some time later, the woman's son became sick, and he grew worse until he stopped breathing.
The woman was heartbroken.
She said to Elijah, what do you have against me, man of God?
Did you come to remind me of my sin and kill my son?
Elijah didn't argue with her.
He said, give me your son.
He carried the boy up to the room where he was staying and laid him on his bed.
Then Elijah prayed out loud, and it was a raw prayer.
Lord my God, have you brought tragedy even on this widow I am staying with, by causing her son to die?
He stretched himself out over the boy three times and cried out, Lord my God, let this boy's life return to him.
The Lord heard Elijah's prayer.
The boy's life returned, and he lived.
Elijah picked him up, carried him downstairs, and gave him to his mother.
See, he said, your son is alive.
The woman said, now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the Lord from your mouth is the truth.
Why does this matter?
This is the first time in the Bible that someone is raised from the dead.
And it happened for a foreign woman, a widow, someone with no power and no standing, in the very land where Baal was worshiped.
Jesus later pointed to this story.
He said that there were many widows in Israel in Elijah's time, but Elijah was sent to none of them, only to a widow in Zarephath.
God's care reaches past borders and past the people who expect it.
What happened after?
The drought lasted three and a half years.
And in the third year, God told Elijah to go and face King Ahab, and that led to the showdown on Mount Carmel. The widow's son grew up.
Her jar of flour was a small daily miracle that kept a family alive through the worst famine in the land.
What does this mean for us today?
It shows that God sees people who think they are forgotten.
The widow had one meal left and no one to help her.
God sent a prophet to her door.
It also shows what faith looks like when you have almost nothing.
She gave first and trusted second.
And it shows that you can pray honestly.
Elijah didn't give God a polite speech.
He asked a hard question and then asked for a miracle, and God listened.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God cares for the poor and the grieving, and that no one is too small for him to notice.
And it points to Jesus, who met a widow at the town gate of Nain, touched her son's coffin, and gave him back to her alive.
carmel: Three years had passed without rain.
The land was dry and people were hungry.
King Ahab blamed Elijah for it, but Elijah said the trouble came from the king himself, because Ahab and his family had abandoned the Lord and followed Baal.
Then Elijah told Ahab to gather all Israel on Mount Carmel, along with 450 prophets of Baal.
When everyone was assembled, Elijah stood in front of the crowd and asked a question.
How long will you waver between two opinions?
If the Lord is God, follow him.
But if Baal is God, follow him. The people said nothing.
Elijah had come to make them choose.
He laid out a simple test.
Let the prophets of Baal build an altar and put a bull on it, but light no fire. He would do the same.
Then each side would call on their god.
The god who answers by fire is God.
The people said, that is a good idea.
The prophets of Baal went first.
They prepared their bull and called on Baal from morning until noon. O Baal, answer us!
But there was no sound, and no one answered.
They danced around the altar they had made.
At noon, Elijah began to tease them. Shout louder! Surely he is a god!
Perhaps he is deep in thought, or busy, or traveling.
Maybe he is sleeping and needs to be awakened.
They shouted louder, and in their desperation they hurt themselves, as their religion taught.
Midday passed, then the afternoon.
Still there was no response, no one answered, no one paid attention.
Then Elijah said to the people, come here to me.
He rebuilt the altar of the Lord that had been torn down.
He used twelve stones, one for each tribe of Israel.
He dug a trench around it.
He arranged the wood and the bull.
Then he did something no one expected.
He had people pour four large jars of water on the offering and the wood.
Do it again, he said, and they did. A third time.
The water ran down around the altar and filled the trench.
There would be no doubt about where the fire came from.
At the time of the evening sacrifice, Elijah stepped forward and prayed a short prayer.
Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel, let it be known today that you are God in Israel and that I am your servant.
Answer me, Lord, answer me, so these people will know that you, Lord, are God, and that you are turning their hearts back again.
Then fire from the Lord fell.
It burned up the sacrifice, the wood, the stones and the soil, and it licked up the water in the trench.
When the people saw it, they fell face down and said, the Lord, he is God. The Lord, he is God.
Why does this matter?
The whole story is about a choice, and Elijah wouldn't let anyone stay on the fence.
The test was fair, and the answer was clear.
Baal, the supposed god of lightning and storms, couldn't produce one spark.
The Lord could do it with soaked wood.
What happened after?
The prophets of Baal were removed from the land that day.
Then Elijah told Ahab to go eat, because he heard the sound of a heavy rain.
Elijah climbed to the top of Carmel and bowed down.
He sent his servant to look toward the sea, and the servant came back saying there was nothing.
Seven times Elijah sent him.
On the seventh, the servant said he saw a cloud as small as a man's hand rising from the sea.
Soon the sky was black with clouds and wind, and a heavy rain came. The drought was over.
What does this mean for us today?
We might not bow to a statue of Baal, but we all face the same question.
Who or what do we trust to give us what we need?
Money, success, approval, comfort.
Elijah's question is still fair. How long will you waver?
It also shows that God doesn't need our help to prove himself.
Elijah prayed one short prayer, and that was enough.
And the small cloud shows how God often works.
Elijah prayed and kept watching, and the rain started with something the size of a hand.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that the Lord alone is God, and that he answers prayer.
And it prepares us for what comes next, because right after this great victory, Elijah would run for his life.
elijah-angel: Elijah had just seen the greatest day of his life. Fire fell from heaven.
The people turned back to God. The rain came.
He even ran ahead of Ahab's chariot all the way to the city gates.
He must have thought the worst was over.
But when Ahab told his wife Jezebel everything, she sent a message to Elijah.
By this time tomorrow, I will make your life like that of one of those prophets.
Elijah had faced 450 prophets of Baal without blinking.
But this threat broke him.
He was afraid, and he ran for his life.
He went a day's journey into the desert, sat down under a broom bush, and prayed that he might die.
I have had enough, Lord, he said. Take my life.
Then he lay down and fell asleep.
Think about what Elijah was carrying.
He was exhausted from the contest, the long run, and years of being hunted.
He was also disappointed.
He had expected the whole nation to change, and they hadn't.
He felt like a failure and he felt completely alone.
God didn't scold him.
An angel touched him and said, get up and eat.
Elijah looked around and there, by his head, was a cake of bread baked over hot coals and a jar of water.
He ate and drank and lay down again.
The angel came a second time and touched him.
Get up and eat, for the journey is too much for you.
So Elijah ate and drank, and strengthened by that food, he traveled forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God.
This is the same mountain where Moses had received the law.
There, he went into a cave and spent the night.
The Lord asked him, what are you doing here, Elijah?
And Elijah poured out his heart.
I have been very zealous for the Lord.
The Israelites have rejected your covenant, and I am the only one left, and now they are trying to kill me.
God told him to go and stand on the mountain, because the Lord was about to pass by.
First a great and powerful wind tore the mountains apart, but the Lord was not in the wind.
After the wind came an earthquake, but the Lord was not in the earthquake.
After the earthquake came a fire, but the Lord was not in the fire.
And after the fire came a gentle whisper.
When Elijah heard it, he pulled his cloak over his face and went out and stood at the mouth of the cave.
God asked the same question again, and Elijah gave the same answer.
Then God gave him something to do. Go back. Anoint new kings.
Appoint Elisha as your successor.
And then God told him something Elijah didn't know.
I reserve seven thousand in Israel, all whose knees have not bowed down to Baal.
He wasn't alone after all.
Why does this matter?
It shows that even the greatest prophets get tired and afraid and discouraged.
The Bible doesn't hide it.
And it shows how God responds.
He didn't send a lecture first.
He sent sleep, food, water and a gentle voice.
He met Elijah's body before he met his questions.
What happened after?
Elijah went back and found a farmer named Elisha plowing a field with twelve pairs of oxen.
He threw his cloak over him, and Elisha left everything to follow him.
For the rest of Elijah's life, Elisha was his helper and friend.
Elijah no longer had to carry the work alone.
What does this mean for us today?
If you have ever hit a wall after a big win, you are not alone.
Sometimes the best next step isn't a bigger effort.
It's rest, a meal, and a friend.
Sometimes God speaks in a whisper, not in a storm, and we have to be quiet to hear him.
And when we feel like we are the only one, we may be wrong, because God often has more people than we can see.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God is gentle with people who are worn out.
And it points to Jesus, who invites everyone who is tired and carrying heavy burdens to come to him and find rest.
chariot: Elijah's work on earth was almost finished.
God had told him that he would be taken up to heaven.
Elijah and Elisha, his helper, were at a place called Gilgal.
Elijah said to Elisha, stay here.
The Lord has sent me to Bethel.
But Elisha said, as surely as the Lord lives and as you live, I will not leave you.
So they went down to Bethel together.
There, a group of prophets came out and asked Elisha, do you know that the Lord is going to take your master from you today?
Elisha said, yes, I know, so be quiet.
The same thing happened at Jericho.
Elijah said, stay here, and Elisha said, I will not leave you.
Fifty prophets stood at a distance and watched as the two of them walked to the Jordan River.
Elijah took his cloak, rolled it up, and struck the water with it.
The water divided to the right and to the left, and the two of them crossed over on dry ground.
It was the same river that Joshua had crossed with the whole nation, and the same kind of miracle.
When they had crossed, Elijah said to Elisha, tell me, what can I do for you before I am taken from you?
Elisha could have asked for anything.
He asked for something bold.
Let me inherit a double portion of your spirit.
In those days, the oldest son received a double share of his father's inheritance.
Elisha was asking to be Elijah's true heir, the one who carries on the work.
Elijah said, you have asked a difficult thing.
Yet if you see me when I am taken from you, it will be yours. If not, it will not.
They kept walking and talking.
Then suddenly a chariot of fire and horses of fire appeared and separated the two of them, and Elijah went up to heaven in a whirlwind.
Elisha saw it and cried out, my father! My father!
The chariots and horsemen of Israel!
And Elisha saw him no more.
He took hold of his own clothes and tore them in two, which was how people showed deep grief.
Then he picked up the cloak that had fallen from Elijah.
He went back to the bank of the Jordan, and he struck the water with the cloak.
Where now is the Lord, the God of Elijah? he asked.
When he struck the water, it divided to the right and to the left, and he crossed over.
The prophets at Jericho saw it and said, the spirit of Elijah is resting on Elisha.
They bowed to the ground in front of him.
Why does this matter?
Only two people in the Bible are said to have gone to heaven without dying.
One is Enoch, who walked with God. The other is Elijah.
His departure showed that death doesn't have the last word over God's faithful servants.
Centuries later, when Jesus was transfigured on a mountain, Moses and Elijah appeared and talked with him. Elijah was alive.
What happened after?
Elisha went on to do twice as many recorded miracles as Elijah.
He healed a general of leprosy, multiplied a widow's oil, and raised a boy from the dead.
The work didn't end when Elijah left.
It passed to the next person.
And the last prophet of the Old Testament, Malachi, promised that God would send Elijah again before the great day of the Lord.
When John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness, Jesus said that he was the Elijah who was to come.
What does this mean for us today?
Elisha shows us how to follow someone.
He refused to be sent away three times.
He stayed close, and he asked for the best thing, not for riches but for the spirit to do God's work.
It also shows that every generation hands the work to the next one.
No one is meant to do it forever.
And it reminds us that the people we depend on won't be here forever, but God will be.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that God honors those who serve him faithfully, and that his work goes on from one generation to the next.
It also points ahead to Jesus, who also went up into heaven and promised to send his Spirit on all who follow him.
sennacherib: Hezekiah was the king of Judah, and he was one of the best kings the nation ever had.
He trusted the Lord and he tore down the idols.
But in his time, the Assyrian empire was the most feared power in the world.
Its king, Sennacherib, had already conquered the northern kingdom of Israel and many of the walled cities of Judah.
Now he surrounded Jerusalem with a huge army.
Sennacherib sent his commander to stand outside the city walls and shout in the language of the people, so that everyone on the wall could hear. He mocked Hezekiah.
Do not let Hezekiah persuade you to trust in the Lord.
Has the god of any nation ever delivered his land from the king of Assyria?
Where are the gods of the other cities we have taken?
How then can the Lord deliver Jerusalem from my hand?
The people on the wall were silent, because Hezekiah had told them not to answer.
Hezekiah tore his clothes and put on rough cloth and went into the temple of the Lord.
He sent word to the prophet Isaiah, asking him to pray.
Isaiah sent a message back.
Do not be afraid of what you have heard.
Sennacherib will hear a rumor and return to his own land.
Then Sennacherib sent a letter to Hezekiah that said the same thing, only in writing.
Hezekiah took the letter, went up to the temple, and spread it out before the Lord.
It is something you can picture.
A king with a threat in his hands, laying it in front of God. Then he prayed.
Lord, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth.
Give ear, Lord, and hear.
Open your eyes, Lord, and see.
Listen to the words Sennacherib has sent to ridicule the living God.
Now, Lord our God, deliver us from his hand, so that all kingdoms on earth may know that you alone, Lord, are God.
Isaiah sent a message to Hezekiah that the Lord had heard his prayer.
The Lord said that the king of Assyria would not enter the city, shoot an arrow into it, or build a siege ramp against it.
He would go back the way he came.
God said, I will defend this city and save it, for my sake and for the sake of David my servant.
That night, the angel of the Lord went out and put to death a huge number of soldiers in the Assyrian camp.
When the people of Jerusalem got up the next morning, they looked, and there were dead bodies everywhere.
Sennacherib broke camp and withdrew.
He went back to Nineveh and stayed there.
Years later, he was killed by his own sons while he was worshiping in the temple of his god.
Why does this matter?
The Assyrians had beaten every army that stood in their way.
Their own records brag about trapping Hezekiah in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage.
But they never claim to have taken the city. The Bible tells us why.
The Lord, who has power over every king and army, protected it.
Sennacherib's mistake was thinking that the Lord was just another local god.
What happened after?
Hezekiah got seriously ill around that time, and he prayed again, and God added fifteen years to his life.
Jerusalem stood for more than a hundred years after this, until Babylon came.
But the lesson of the night the Assyrians were turned back lasted for generations.
God can rescue his people without a single sword drawn.
What does this mean for us today?
We may not face an army, but we all get threatening letters of one kind or another. A bad medical report. A pile of bills.
A message from someone who wants to hurt us.
Hezekiah's response is a good pattern.
He didn't pretend the letter wasn't real, and he didn't panic.
He took it to God and spread it out and prayed honestly.
He asked for help, and he asked for God's name to be honored in how it turned out.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that no power on earth is greater than the Lord, and that he hears the prayers of people who are afraid.
And it points to the God who says in the New Testament that nothing, no threat, no power, can separate us from his love.
ezra: For about seventy years, the people of Judah had lived in exile in Babylon.
Their city was in ruins and the temple was gone.
Then the Persian empire took over, and King Cyrus let the Jews go home and rebuild.
A first group returned and rebuilt the temple.
Decades later, a priest and scribe named Ezra led a second group back to Jerusalem.
The Bible says Ezra had set his heart to study the law of the Lord, to practice it, and to teach it to Israel.
The king of Persia gave Ezra letters, silver and gold, and the freedom to go.
The trip was long and dangerous.
Ezra was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers to protect them, because he had told the king that the hand of God was on everyone who looked to him.
So instead they fasted and prayed for a safe journey, and God answered.
They arrived in Jerusalem after about four months, with every piece of silver and gold accounted for.
A few days after he got there, Ezra's leaders came to him with bad news.
Many of the people, including priests and Levites, had not kept themselves separate from the pagan peoples around them.
They had married women from those nations and taken on their religious practices.
The leaders themselves had been the worst in this.
They were repeating the same mistakes that had sent their ancestors into exile in the first place.
When Ezra heard it, he tore his clothes and pulled hair from his head and beard. He sat down appalled.
Everyone who trembled at the words of God gathered around him.
He sat there until the evening sacrifice.
Then, still in his torn clothes, he fell on his knees, spread out his hands to the Lord, and prayed.
My God, I am too ashamed and disgraced to lift up my face to you.
Our sins are higher than our heads, and our guilt has reached to the heavens. Notice what he did.
Ezra hadn't married a foreign woman.
Yet he said, our sins, our guilt, we.
He joined the people in confession instead of standing outside and pointing a finger.
He reminded God that he had been gracious.
You have left us a remnant.
You have given us a firm place in your holy place.
Even in our slavery, you have not forsaken us.
And then he said, Lord, God of Israel, you are righteous.
We are left, a remnant, as in this day.
Here we are before you in our guilt, though because of it, not one of us can stand in your presence.
While Ezra was praying and weeping and throwing himself down in front of the house of God, a very large crowd of men, women and children gathered around him. They wept bitterly too.
One man, Shecaniah, spoke up.
We have been unfaithful to our God, but in spite of this, there is still hope for Israel.
Let us make a covenant before our God. Take courage and do it.
Ezra got up and had the leaders swear to follow through.
The people assembled in the rain, trembling over the matter, and they began to make things right.
Why does this matter?
Ezra's prayer shows what real repentance looks like.
It isn't a quick apology to get out of trouble.
It is grief over sin, honesty about it, and trust in God's mercy.
The people didn't wait for a program.
One man's broken prayer started a turn around.
What happened after?
Ezra later stood in front of the people at the Water Gate and read the law aloud from morning until noon.
People who had been away for generations heard it, and they wept.
Then the leaders told them it was a holy day, not a day for sadness.
The joy of the Lord is your strength, they said.
Ezra helped a whole nation remember who they were.
What does this mean for us today?
When something is wrong in our family, church or community, we are tempted to blame others. Ezra shows another way.
He took the problem to God first, and he spoke as someone who shared the guilt.
It also shows that grief over sin is not the end.
Ezra's prayer ends with honesty, but it began with God's mercy.
And it shows that God's word has to be known to change people. Ezra didn't just pray.
He studied, practiced and taught.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that repentance is the way home.
And it points to Jesus, the one who truly stands in for sinners before God, and who makes it possible for us to lift up our faces again.
nehemiah: Nehemiah lived in the Persian capital, far from Jerusalem. He had an important job.
He was the king's cupbearer, the person who tasted the king's wine to make sure it wasn't poisoned.
It meant he was close to the king and trusted by him.
But his heart was far away in the city of his ancestors.
One day his brother Hanani arrived from Judah with a group of men.
Nehemiah asked how things were in Jerusalem.
They told him the people there were in great trouble and disgrace.
The wall of Jerusalem was broken down, and its gates had been burned with fire.
In those days, a city without walls was open to anyone.
It was an easy target, and it was a shame to everyone who lived there.
When Nehemiah heard this, he sat down and wept.
For days he mourned and fasted and prayed to God. His prayer was honest.
He confessed his own sins and his family's sins.
He reminded God of his promise to gather his scattered people back if they returned to him.
Then he asked for one thing.
Give your servant success today by granting him favor in the presence of this man.
Nehemiah was talking about the king.
Four months later, Nehemiah was serving wine to King Artaxerxes when the king noticed his face.
Why does your face look so sad when you are not ill?
This can be nothing but sadness of heart.
It was dangerous to look sad in front of the king, and Nehemiah was very afraid.
But he answered carefully.
May the king live forever.
Why should my face not look sad when the city where my ancestors are buried lies in ruins?
The king said, what is it you want?
Nehemiah prayed to the God of heaven.
It was a quick prayer, in the moment, with the king waiting.
Then he asked to be sent to Judah to rebuild the city. The king agreed.
He even gave Nehemiah letters for safe passage and timber for the gates.
When Nehemiah arrived in Jerusalem, he didn't announce his plan. He waited three days.
Then at night, he went out with a few men and rode around the city to inspect the damage.
It was so bad that the animal he was riding couldn't get through in places.
The next morning, he gathered the officials and said it plainly.
You see the trouble we are in.
Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned.
Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, and we will no longer be in disgrace.
He told them how God had been gracious to him and how the king had helped.
They answered, let us start rebuilding.
So they began this good work.
Why does this matter?
Nehemiah is a good example of how prayer and planning work together.
He prayed for months, and he thought carefully about what he would need.
When the moment came, he prayed again and acted.
He didn't wait for someone else to fix the problem.
He let it break his heart, and then he did something.
What happened after? The work had enemies.
Men named Sanballat and Tobiah laughed at the Jews and then threatened them.
Nehemiah put half of his workers on guard with spears while the other half built, and the builders carried tools in one hand and a weapon in the other.
In spite of all the opposition, the wall was finished in just fifty-two days.
Even their enemies had to admit that the work was done with the help of God.
What does this mean for us today?
Is there something broken that you can't stop thinking about?
A relationship, a neighborhood, a church, a part of your own life.
Nehemiah suggests that this kind of burden may be where God is calling us to act.
Start with prayer, be honest about the problem, and ask for what you need.
Then take the first step. And expect opposition.
Good work often draws critics. Keep going anyway.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God uses ordinary people in ordinary jobs to rebuild what is broken.
And it points to Jesus, who left a place of comfort and came to a broken world to rebuild it from the ground up.
esther: Esther was a young Jewish woman living in the Persian empire.
Her parents had died, and her cousin Mordecai raised her as his own daughter.
When King Xerxes got rid of his queen and held a search for a new one, Esther was taken to the palace.
She won the king's favor, and he made her queen.
Mordecai had told her not to tell anyone that she was Jewish, and she kept it secret.
The king's highest official was a man named Haman.
He was proud and demanded that everyone bow to him. Mordecai refused.
Haman was furious, and when he found out Mordecai was a Jew, he wasn't satisfied with punishing one man.
He wanted to destroy all the Jews in the empire.
He went to the king and told him that there was a certain people scattered through his kingdom whose customs were different and who didn't obey the king's laws.
He offered a huge sum of money for the job.
The king gave him his signet ring, and a decree went out to every province.
On a single day, all the Jews, young and old, women and children, were to be destroyed.
Mordecai put on rough cloth and ashes and wept in the street.
When Esther heard about it, she sent clothes to him, but he sent back a message.
Tell her to go to the king and beg for mercy for her people.
Esther answered that anyone who approached the king without being called could be put to death, unless the king held out his golden scepter.
She hadn't been called in thirty days.
Mordecai's reply is among the most famous lines in the Bible.
Do not think that because you are in the king's house you alone of all the Jews will escape.
If you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father's family will perish.
And who knows but that you have come to your royal position for such a time as this?
Esther made her decision.
Go, gather all the Jews in Susa, and fast for me.
Do not eat or drink for three days.
My attendants and I will fast as you do.
When this is done, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law.
And if I perish, I perish.
On the third day, Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the palace, in view of the king.
When the king saw Queen Esther standing there, he was pleased with her and held out the gold scepter.
She approached and touched the tip of it.
The king asked, what is it, Queen Esther? What is your request?
Even up to half the kingdom, it will be given to you.
Esther didn't tell him everything right then.
She invited the king and Haman to a banquet.
At the second banquet, she told the king.
If I have found favor with you, my king, grant me my life, and spare my people.
For I and my people have been sold to be destroyed.
The king asked, who is he?
Where is the man who has dared to do such a thing?
Esther said, the adversary and enemy is this vile Haman.
Why does this matter?
The book of Esther never mentions God by name, yet his hand is all over it.
A young orphan becomes queen, a sleepless night leads the king to remember what Mordecai had done for him, and a plot turns against its author.
God works through timing and through people who choose to be brave.
What happened after?
Haman was removed, and Mordecai was given his position.
The king couldn't cancel his own decree, but he allowed the Jews to defend themselves. The people were rescued.
To this day, the Jewish festival of Purim celebrates this deliverance.
What does this mean for us today?
We may not face a king's palace, but we all have moments when we could speak up and don't.
Esther's story asks whether we are where we are for such a time as this.
It also shows that courage doesn't mean not being afraid. Esther was terrified.
She prayed, fasted, got help from her community, and then went in anyway.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God protects his people, even when he seems hidden.
And it points to Jesus, who laid down his life to save his people, and who also said what Esther said, and meant it more than anyone.
job: There was a man named Job who lived in the land of Uz.
The Bible says he was blameless and upright, and that he feared God and turned away from evil.
He had seven sons and three daughters, thousands of animals, and many servants.
He was the greatest man among all the people of the East.
Job also took care of his family spiritually.
He would offer sacrifices for his children after their feasts, just in case they had sinned in their hearts.
The book opens with a scene in heaven.
The angels came to present themselves before the Lord, and Satan, the accuser, came with them.
God pointed to Job as an example.
Have you considered my servant Job?
There is no one like him.
Satan answered that Job only served God because God had blessed him.
Take away what he has, and he will curse you to your face.
God allowed Satan to test Job, but only up to a point.
Then one day, the worst news arrived in waves.
A messenger came running to Job and said that raiders had stolen his oxen and donkeys and killed his servants.
While he was still speaking, another messenger came.
Fire had fallen from the sky and burned up the sheep and shepherds.
While he was still speaking, a third came.
Raiders had taken the camels.
And while he was still speaking, a fourth messenger arrived with the worst news of all.
Your sons and daughters were having a feast at their oldest brother's house, and a mighty wind swept in from the desert and struck the house.
It collapsed on them, and they are dead.
I am the only one who escaped to tell you.
In one day, Job lost his wealth and all ten of his children.
He stood up and tore his robe. He shaved his head.
Then he fell to the ground in worship.
Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I will depart.
The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away.
May the name of the Lord be praised.
In all this, Job did not sin by charging God with wrongdoing.
Then Satan struck Job's health.
Painful sores covered his body from head to foot, and Job sat among the ashes and scraped his skin with a piece of broken pottery.
His wife said, are you still maintaining your integrity? Curse God and die.
Job answered, you are talking like a foolish woman.
Shall we accept good from God and not trouble?
Three of Job's friends came to comfort him.
At first they did it right.
They sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights without saying a word.
But then they started to talk.
They insisted that Job must have done something terrible to deserve this. Job knew he hadn't.
He argued, he cried out, and he demanded that God answer him.
Why does this matter?
The book of Job faces a hard question honestly.
Why do good people suffer?
It doesn't give a neat answer.
When God finally speaks, he doesn't explain the reason.
He shows Job the vastness of creation and asks, where were you when I laid the earth's foundation? Job is humbled.
He says, my ears had heard of you, but now my eyes have seen you.
What happened after?
God told the friends that they had not spoken what was right about him, and Job prayed for them.
God gave Job twice as much as he had before.
He had seven more sons and three more daughters.
He lived another 140 years.
But the point of the book isn't the reward at the end.
It's that Job held on to God in the dark.
What does this mean for us today?
Suffering isn't always a punishment, and a friend's best comfort is often just showing up and sitting quietly.
Job also shows that honest complaint is allowed.
He didn't hide his pain, and God didn't reject him for it.
And Job said something in the middle of his misery that has held up many people since.
I know that my Redeemer lives.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God is trustworthy even when we can't understand what's going on.
And it points to Jesus, the one innocent person who suffered the most, and who understands our pain from the inside.
isaiah: The year King Uzziah died was a time of fear in Judah.
Uzziah had been a strong king for fifty-two years, and now he was gone.
The nation had no certainty about what came next.
In that year, a young man named Isaiah went to the temple, and what he saw there changed his life.
Isaiah saw the Lord, high and exalted, seated on a throne.
The train of his robe filled the temple.
Above him were seraphim, angelic beings, each with six wings.
With two wings they covered their faces, with two they covered their feet, and with two they were flying.
And they were calling to one another, holy, holy, holy is the Lord Almighty.
The whole earth is full of his glory.
The doorposts and thresholds shook at the sound of their voices, and the temple was filled with smoke.
Isaiah's reaction wasn't excitement. It was dread. Woe to me, he cried. I am ruined.
For I am a man of unclean lips, and I live among a people of unclean lips, and my eyes have seen the King, the Lord Almighty.
When he stood in front of a perfectly holy God, he saw his own sin clearly.
He was in the presence of the one he had spoken about for years, and he knew he didn't measure up.
Then one of the seraphim flew to him with a burning coal in his hand.
He had taken it with tongs from the altar.
He touched Isaiah's mouth with it and said, see, this has touched your lips.
Your guilt is taken away and your sin atoned for. Isaiah hadn't earned it.
He hadn't even asked for it.
God dealt with his sin himself.
Then Isaiah heard the voice of the Lord. Whom shall I send? And who will go for us? Isaiah didn't hesitate. Here am I. Send me.
It's the response of a man who has been forgiven and can't help but say yes.
God's assignment was a hard one.
Go and tell this people, be ever hearing but never understanding.
Be ever seeing but never perceiving.
Many of the people wouldn't listen.
Isaiah asked, for how long, Lord?
God said, until the cities lie ruined and without inhabitant.
But God also gave him a promise.
As the terebinth and oak leave stumps when they are cut down, so the holy seed will be the stump in the land.
There would always be a remnant, a seed from which God would start over.
Why does this matter?
The vision shows what God is like.
He is holy, which means completely set apart, completely good, completely other.
Isaiah's story shows that meeting God makes us aware of our sin, but God doesn't leave us there.
He provides the cleansing himself.
And only then does he send.
What happened after?
Isaiah served as a prophet for about sixty years, under four kings.
He warned Judah and comforted them.
He wrote some of the most beautiful and hopeful words in the Bible, including promises about a child to be born.
For to us a child is born, to us a son is given, and the government will be on his shoulders.
And he will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
He also wrote about a servant who would be pierced for our transgressions and by whose wounds we are healed.
What does this mean for us today?
Many of us want to be used by God but feel too flawed.
Isaiah felt that too, and God's answer was to forgive him first.
We don't have to be perfect to be sent.
We have to be cleansed and willing.
It also shows that saying yes to God may not mean quick success.
Isaiah was told that many would not listen. He went anyway.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God is holy, and that he is also the one who cleanses us and calls us. And it points to Jesus.
The apostle John said that Isaiah saw Jesus' glory and spoke about him, and it's Jesus who takes away our guilt for good.
leviathan: Isaiah wrote a short and strange verse about a sea monster.
In that day, the Lord will punish with his sword, his fierce, great and powerful sword, Leviathan the gliding serpent, Leviathan the coiling serpent.
He will slay the monster of the sea.
Leviathan appears in several places in the Bible.
In the book of Job, God describes it in great detail.
It is a creature so powerful that no human can catch it with a hook or tame it like a pet.
Its back is covered with rows of shields, smoke pours from its nostrils, and no weapon can harm it.
Nothing on earth is its equal, God says.
It is a king over all that are proud.
In the Psalms, God is said to have crushed the heads of Leviathan.
And in Isaiah, Leviathan is a sign of everything in the world that opposes God.
In the ancient world, the sea was a symbol of chaos.
It was deep and dark, and no one could control it. Sailors feared it.
Many nations around Israel told stories about sea monsters that fought their gods.
The Bible takes that picture and uses it in a surprising way.
In the Bible, God isn't one of the combatants. He has no rival.
The sea and every monster in it belong to him.
In Psalm 104, God made the sea and the great creatures in it, and Leviathan is described as playing in the water.
Isaiah's verse comes in a section that looks to the end of history.
Chapter 26 describes the dead rising.
Chapter 27 says that on that day, God will deal with the powers that have terrorized his people.
The images are vivid, but the message is plain.
The forces that seem too big for anyone to defeat will not last.
The serpent that has coiled itself around the world will be put down by God himself.
Why does this matter?
Many people feel that evil is too large to be beaten.
Wars, abuse, corruption, disease.
These can seem like sea monsters, huge and permanent.
The prophet says that they are not.
The monster is real, but it is not in charge. God is.
What happened after?
The picture of the serpent returns throughout the Bible.
In the garden, a serpent deceives Eve.
In the book of Revelation, John sees a great dragon, that ancient serpent, called the devil or Satan, who leads the whole world astray. He is thrown down.
The last book of the Bible finishes what Isaiah began.
And in the new heaven and new earth, there is no longer any sea, which in the Bible's language means that the threat of chaos is gone for good.
Jesus also had a moment like this.
One night, on a boat in a storm, the disciples woke him up, terrified of the waves.
Jesus stood up, rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, quiet, be still. The sea went calm.
The disciples were amazed and said, who is this?
Even the wind and the waves obey him.
In the Old Testament, only God rules the sea.
The disciples were beginning to see who was in the boat with them.
What does this mean for us today?
Whatever you are afraid of, whether it's a diagnosis, a debt, an addiction or a world that seems to be going wrong, you can bring it to the one who made the ocean and everything in it.
We aren't called to pretend that evil isn't there.
We are called to trust that it has an end.
And we are called to wait and work for that day with hope.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that the worst powers in the universe are not equals of God.
And it points to the cross and the empty tomb, where Jesus defeated the serpent once and for all.
jeremiah: Jeremiah was born into a family of priests in a small town called Anathoth, not far from Jerusalem.
He lived in one of the darkest times in Judah's history.
The nation had turned away from God, and the Babylonian empire was getting stronger.
Jeremiah would spend his whole life warning his people about what was coming.
He is sometimes called the weeping prophet.
God's call came when Jeremiah was young.
The word of the Lord came to him.
Before I formed you in the womb I knew you.
Before you were born I set you apart.
I appointed you as a prophet to the nations.
Jeremiah answered the way many of us would.
Alas, Sovereign Lord, I do not know how to speak. I am too young.
But the Lord said, do not say I am too young.
You must go to everyone I send you to and say whatever I command you.
Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you and will rescue you.
Then the Lord reached out his hand and touched Jeremiah's mouth.
Now I have put my words in your mouth.
God showed him two pictures.
The first was a branch of an almond tree, which was the first tree to bloom in spring.
It was a sign that God was watching to see that his word was fulfilled.
The second was a boiling pot, tilting toward the south from the north, a picture of disaster coming from the Babylonians.
God promised Jeremiah that he would be like a fortified city, an iron pillar and a bronze wall.
The people would fight against him, but they wouldn't overcome him, for I am with you and will rescue you, declares the Lord.
And that is exactly how Jeremiah's life went.
For about forty years, he preached to kings and priests, and almost no one listened.
He was beaten, put in the stocks, thrown into a muddy cistern, and called a traitor.
At one point he complained to God that he had become a laughingstock.
If I say I will not mention his word or speak anymore in his name, his word is in my heart like a fire, a fire shut up in my bones.
I am weary of holding it in. Indeed, I cannot.
Why does this matter?
Jeremiah's call shows that God knows us before we are born.
Before anyone else had a say, God had a purpose for him.
It also shows that God doesn't call people because they feel ready.
Jeremiah felt too young and too weak, and God said, I will be with you.
What happened after?
Jerusalem fell to Babylon, just as Jeremiah had said.
The temple was burned and many of the people were taken into exile.
Yet in the middle of the bad news, Jeremiah also spoke some of the most hopeful words in the Bible.
He wrote to the exiles, I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future.
And he promised a new covenant.
I will put my law in their minds and write it on their hearts.
I will be their God, and they will be my people.
What does this mean for us today?
Maybe you feel too young, too old, too ordinary or too scared for what God has asked of you.
Jeremiah felt that way too.
God's answer was never, you are enough. It was, I am with you.
It also shows that faithfulness matters more than results.
Jeremiah was faithful for forty years and saw little response.
God didn't measure him by the crowd.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God knows each of us and sets us apart for a purpose.
And it points to Jesus, who brought the new covenant that Jeremiah promised, in which God's law is written on our hearts.
ezekiel: Ezekiel was a priest who was taken from Jerusalem to Babylon when he was about twenty-five.
He was part of the first group to be sent into exile.
He lived by a canal called the Kebar.
When he was about thirty, the age when a priest would begin his service in the temple, God called him to be a prophet, even though he was far away from the temple and could not serve there.
His call began with an amazing vision.
He saw a windstorm coming from the north, with a great cloud and flashing lightning.
In it were four living creatures and wheels within wheels, covered with eyes.
Above them was something like a throne, and on the throne, a figure like a man glowing like fire. Ezekiel fell facedown.
This was the glory of the Lord, and it was in Babylon, not in the temple.
God wasn't confined to Jerusalem.
He was with his people, even in exile.
Ezekiel's early messages were heavy.
He told the exiles that Jerusalem would be destroyed because of the nation's sin.
Many people wanted to hear that everything would be fine, but Ezekiel told them the truth.
God had him act out his messages in odd ways, like lying on his side for months or drawing a model of the city under siege.
When Jerusalem fell, as he had said, the nature of his message changed. Now he spoke about hope.
In chapter 36, God made a promise through Ezekiel.
I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean.
I will cleanse you from all your impurities and from all your idols.
I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you.
I will remove from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.
And I will put my Spirit in you and move you to follow my decrees and be careful to keep my laws.
This was a promise that God would do for his people what they could not do for themselves.
The problem with the nation was not just bad behavior but a hard heart.
No amount of trying harder would fix that.
Only God could replace it.
Then in chapter 37, Ezekiel is carried by the Spirit to a valley full of dry bones.
They are scattered everywhere.
God asks him, son of man, can these bones live?
Ezekiel answers, Sovereign Lord, you alone know.
God tells him to speak to the bones.
As he does, there is a rattling sound, and the bones come together.
Tendons and flesh appear on them, and skin covers them.
Then breath enters them, and they come to life and stand up, a vast army.
God says, these bones are the people of Israel.
They say, our bones are dried up and our hope is gone.
But I am going to open your graves and bring you up from them.
I will put my Spirit in you, and you will live.
Why does this matter?
Ezekiel taught the exiles that God was not defeated.
The nation had hit bottom, and God said that even this was not the end.
He is the God who gives life where there is none.
What happened after?
About fifty years later, the Persian king Cyrus let the exiles return home.
The dry bones began to live.
And the deeper promise of a new heart and new spirit came true in a greater way when the Holy Spirit was poured out on the followers of Jesus at Pentecost.
What does this mean for us today?
Everyone has a dry valley sometime, a time when hope is gone.
Ezekiel's story says God can speak life into it.
It also shows that change from the inside is what God offers.
We can't make ourselves new by willpower alone.
He gives a new heart as a gift.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God is able to bring the dead to life and make hard hearts soft.
And it points to Jesus, who told a man named Nicodemus that you must be born again, and who rose from the dead to give new life to everyone who trusts in him.
furnace: When Babylon conquered Jerusalem, King Nebuchadnezzar took some of the brightest young men from Judah back to his capital to be trained for royal service.
Four of them were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah.
The Babylonians gave them new names.
Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah became Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego.
They did well in their studies, and Nebuchadnezzar gave them important jobs in the province of Babylon.
Nebuchadnezzar then made a huge gold statue, about ninety feet high and nine feet wide, and set it up on a plain near Babylon.
He summoned all the officials of the empire to its dedication.
A herald announced that when they heard the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre and harp, everyone must fall down and worship the statue.
Whoever did not would be thrown into a blazing furnace.
When the music started, the whole crowd bowed.
Everyone, that is, except three men.
Some of the astrologers went to the king and reported that Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego were ignoring his order.
Nebuchadnezzar flew into a rage and called them in.
Is it true that you do not serve my gods or worship the image of gold I have set up?
He gave them a second chance.
If you do not worship it, you will be thrown into the furnace.
Then what god will be able to rescue you from my hands?
Their answer is one of the great statements of faith in the Bible.
King Nebuchadnezzar, we do not need to defend ourselves before you in this matter.
If we are thrown into the blazing furnace, the God we serve is able to deliver us from it, and he will deliver us from your hand, Your Majesty.
But even if he does not, we want you to know, Your Majesty, that we will not serve your gods or worship the image of gold you have set up.
Look at that last part.
They believed that God could save them.
But they said they would stay faithful even if he didn't.
Their loyalty did not depend on the outcome.
Nebuchadnezzar was so angry that his face changed.
He ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter than usual.
He had the strongest soldiers in his army tie the three men up and throw them in.
The fire was so hot that it killed the soldiers who carried them to the edge.
Then the king jumped to his feet in amazement.
Weren't there three men that we tied up and threw into the fire? Look!
I see four men walking around in the fire, unbound and unharmed, and the fourth looks like a son of the gods.
Nebuchadnezzar went up to the opening of the furnace and shouted, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out!
They came out, and everyone crowded around them.
The fire had not harmed their bodies, not a hair of their heads was singed, their robes were not scorched, and there was no smell of fire on them.
Why does this matter?
The three friends showed what it looks like to put God first when it costs something.
They didn't pick a fight, and they didn't compromise.
They were respectful and firm.
And the story shows that God was with them in the fire.
He didn't keep them out of the furnace, but he went in with them.
What happened after?
Nebuchadnezzar praised the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who sent his angel and rescued his servants.
He gave a decree that no one in the empire should speak against their God.
And he promoted the three men in Babylon.
What does this mean for us today?
Most of us won't face a literal furnace, but we all face pressure to bow.
To go along with the crowd, to keep quiet about what we believe, to cut a corner at work.
The friends remind us that faith isn't a bargain.
We trust God whether or not things go the way we want.
And the fourth man in the fire is a promise.
When we go through hard places, we are not alone.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God is present with his people in their worst trials.
And many Christians see the fourth figure as a glimpse of Jesus, who walks with his people through every fire.
writing-wall: Many years after Nebuchadnezzar, Babylon was ruled by a king named Belshazzar.
One night he threw an enormous banquet for a thousand of his nobles.
As the wine flowed, he got an idea.
He ordered his servants to bring in the gold and silver cups that his predecessor had taken from the temple in Jerusalem.
These cups had been set apart for the worship of the Lord.
Belshazzar and his guests used them to drink wine while they praised their gods of gold and silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone.
Suddenly the fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster of the wall near the lamp stand in the royal palace.
The king watched the hand as it wrote.
His face turned pale and he was so frightened that his legs became weak and his knees knocked together.
He shouted for the enchanters and astrologers to be brought in.
Whoever reads this writing and tells me what it means will be clothed in purple and have a gold chain placed around his neck, and he will be made the third highest ruler in the kingdom.
But none of the wise men could read the writing or tell the king what it meant.
The king was even more terrified, and his nobles were baffled.
The queen mother heard the noise and came into the banquet hall.
She told the king not to be alarmed.
There was a man in his kingdom who had the spirit of the holy gods in him.
In the time of Nebuchadnezzar, he had shown insight and wisdom. His name was Daniel. Daniel was brought in.
By now he was an old man.
The king offered him the same rewards.
Daniel answered, you can keep your gifts for yourself or give them to someone else.
Nevertheless, I will read the writing for the king and tell him what it means.
Then he reminded Belshazzar of what had happened to Nebuchadnezzar, who had become proud and was humbled until he acknowledged that the Most High God is sovereign over all kingdoms.
But you, Belshazzar, his son, have not humbled yourself, though you knew all this.
Instead, you have set yourself up against the Lord of heaven.
You had the goblets from his temple brought to you, and you drank wine from them.
You praised the gods of silver and gold, but you did not honor the God who holds in his hand your life and all your ways.
Then Daniel read the words.
Mene, mene, tekel, parsin.
Mene means that God has numbered the days of your reign and brought it to an end.
Tekel means that you have been weighed on the scales and found wanting.
Peres means that your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians.
Belshazzar kept his promise and had Daniel dressed in purple, with a gold chain around his neck, and proclaimed him the third highest ruler.
That very night, Belshazzar, king of the Babylonians, was killed, and Darius the Mede took over the kingdom.
Why does this matter?
Belshazzar had everything.
A great city, a huge army, and thick walls.
But he treated holy things as party favors and ignored a warning he already knew about, the story of what happened to Nebuchadnezzar.
The writing on the wall shows that no one is too powerful for God to hold accountable.
What happened after?
The Persian army took Babylon that very night, as Daniel had said.
Within a few years, the Persian king allowed the exiles to go home.
Daniel continued serving under the new rulers, and his faithfulness there led to the lions' den.
What does this mean for us today?
We may not drink from stolen temple cups, but we can all treat sacred things lightly.
We can also ignore warnings that we know are true.
The story invites us to ask whether we are being weighed and found wanting, and to turn back before it is too late.
It also shows the quiet courage of Daniel.
He told the truth to the most powerful man in the room, and he didn't ask for a reward.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God is the ruler over all kings and that human pride has an end.
And it points to Jesus, whose kingdom is the one that will never be destroyed.
lions-den: Daniel was now an old man, and he had served under several kings.
When Darius the Mede took over Babylon, he put Daniel in charge of the other high officials, because Daniel had an excellent spirit and the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom.
The other officials were jealous.
They looked for something to use against him, but they couldn't find any corruption or negligence. He was trustworthy.
So they said to one another, we will never find any basis for charges against Daniel unless it has something to do with the law of his God.
They went to the king and persuaded him to sign a decree.
For thirty days, anyone who prayed to any god or man except the king would be thrown into the den of lions.
Once the king signed it, the law of the Medes and Persians could not be changed.
Daniel heard that the decree had been signed.
He went home to his upstairs room, where the windows opened toward Jerusalem.
Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed and gave thanks to his God, just as he had always done.
He didn't hide it or close the windows.
The officials were waiting, and they found him praying and asking God for help.
They went to the king and reminded him of the decree.
Then they told him that Daniel was ignoring it.
The king was deeply distressed.
He liked Daniel and made every effort until sundown to find a way to rescue him.
But the men reminded him that no decree could be changed.
At last the king gave the order, and Daniel was brought and thrown into the lions' den.
The king said to him, may your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you.
A stone was placed over the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own ring.
Then the king went back to his palace and spent the night fasting.
He refused entertainment and couldn't sleep.
At the first light of dawn, he got up and hurried to the lions' den.
When he came near, he called out in an anguished voice, Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to rescue you from the lions?
Daniel answered, may the king live forever.
My God sent his angel, and he shut the mouths of the lions.
They have not hurt me, because I was found innocent in his sight.
Nor have I ever done any wrong before you, Your Majesty.
The king was overjoyed and gave orders to lift Daniel out of the den.
When he was lifted out, no wound was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.
Why does this matter?
Daniel's habit is the key.
He didn't start praying when the law was passed.
He had been praying three times a day for years, and when the pressure came, he simply kept going.
Faith that holds in a crisis is usually built in ordinary days.
What happened after?
The men who plotted against Daniel faced the consequences of their own plan.
King Darius then wrote to everyone in his kingdom that they should fear and reverence the God of Daniel, for he is the living God and he endures forever.
Daniel continued to prosper through the reigns of Darius and Cyrus.
What does this mean for us today?
Most of us won't face lions, but we all face pressure to hide our faith or to drop our habits of prayer.
Daniel's example is to keep praying, quietly and steadily.
It also shows that God can protect his people, and that even when he doesn't change the situation, he is present in it.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God is the living God who rescues those who trust him.
And it points to Jesus, who was also sealed behind a stone with a royal seal, and who came out alive.
jonah-whale: God spoke to a prophet named Jonah and gave him a job.
Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before me.
Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, Israel's feared enemy. Jonah didn't want to go.
He didn't want the Ninevites to repent and be forgiven, because he thought they deserved punishment. So he ran the other way.
He went down to the port of Joppa, found a ship headed to Tarshish, which was in the opposite direction, paid the fare, and went below deck to get away from the Lord.
Then the Lord sent a great wind on the sea, and such a violent storm arose that the ship threatened to break up.
The sailors were terrified, and each cried out to his own god.
They threw cargo overboard to lighten the ship.
Meanwhile, Jonah was below deck, sound asleep.
The captain found him and said, how can you sleep?
Get up and call on your god!
Perhaps he will take notice of us, and we will not perish.
The sailors cast lots to find out who was responsible for the storm, and the lot fell on Jonah.
They asked him who he was.
He said, I am a Hebrew and I worship the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.
The men were even more afraid.
What have you done? they asked.
The storm was getting worse.
Jonah told them, pick me up and throw me into the sea, and it will become calm.
I know that it is my fault that this great storm has come upon you.
The sailors didn't want to do it.
They tried to row back to land, but they couldn't.
Finally, they prayed to the Lord, asking him not to hold them accountable for taking an innocent life.
Then they picked up Jonah and threw him overboard, and the raging sea grew calm.
The men were filled with awe of the Lord, and they offered a sacrifice and made vows to him.
But the Lord had arranged for a huge fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
From inside the fish, Jonah prayed.
In my distress I called to the Lord, and he answered me.
From deep in the realm of the dead I called for help, and you listened to my cry.
You hurled me into the depths, into the very heart of the seas, and the currents swirled about me.
When my life was ebbing away, I remembered you, Lord.
What I have vowed I will make good.
Salvation comes from the Lord.
And the Lord commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land.
Why does this matter?
Jonah tried to run from God, and the more he ran, the lower he went.
Down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into the sea.
But God didn't give up on him.
Even the storm and the fish were part of God's mercy, because they brought Jonah back.
And the sailors, who were not Israelites, ended up worshiping the Lord.
God was already reaching out to outsiders, even through a runaway prophet.
What happened after?
God spoke to Jonah a second time.
Go to the great city of Nineveh. This time Jonah went.
Jesus later said that just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the huge fish, so the Son of Man would be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.
Jonah's story was a sign pointing to the resurrection.
What does this mean for us today?
We all know what it is like to run from something God is asking us to do.
The story says that God is persistent, and that he doesn't throw us away when we fail.
It also shows that the way back can start with a prayer, even from the bottom.
Jonah prayed from the belly of a fish, and God heard him.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that you can't outrun God's mercy.
And it points to Jesus, who went down into death for us and came back up on the third day.
nineveh: God gave Jonah a second chance.
The word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time.
Go to the great city of Nineveh and proclaim to it the message I give you. This time Jonah obeyed.
He went to Nineveh, which was so large that it took three days to go through it.
On the first day, Jonah began to walk into the city, and he gave a short and blunt message.
Forty more days and Nineveh will be overthrown. That was all.
He didn't say anything about God's mercy or how they could be saved.
It is possible that he hoped they wouldn't listen.
But the Ninevites believed God.
They declared a fast, and all of them, from the greatest to the least, put on rough cloth.
When the news reached the king of Nineveh, he got up from his throne, took off his royal robes, covered himself with rough cloth, and sat down in the dust. He issued a decree.
By the decree of the king and his nobles, no one, not even animals, may taste anything.
Everyone must call urgently on God.
Let them give up their evil ways and their violence. Who knows?
God may yet relent with compassion and turn from his fierce anger so that we will not perish.
When God saw what they did and how they turned from their evil ways, he relented and did not bring on them the destruction he had threatened.
You might expect Jonah to celebrate. But he was furious.
He prayed to the Lord, and his prayer reveals why he ran in the first place.
Isn't this what I said, Lord, when I was still at home?
That is why I was so quick to flee to Tarshish.
I knew that you are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger and abounding in love, a God who relents from sending calamity.
Jonah knew exactly who God was, and he resented it.
He asked God to take his life.
God asked him a question.
Is it right for you to be angry?
Jonah went out and sat down east of the city to see what would happen.
The Lord God provided a leafy plant and made it grow up over Jonah to give him shade.
Jonah was very happy about the plant.
But the next day, God sent a worm that chewed the plant so that it withered.
When the sun rose, God sent a scorching wind, and Jonah grew faint.
He said, it would be better for me to die than to live.
God asked, is it right for you to be angry about the plant? Jonah said, yes, it is.
I am so angry I wish I were dead.
Then the Lord said, you have been concerned about this plant, though you did not tend it or make it grow.
It sprang up overnight and died overnight.
And should I not have concern for the great city of Nineveh, in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and also many animals?
The book ends there, with a question.
It never says how Jonah answered.
Why does this matter?
Nineveh was not a friendly place.
The Assyrians were known for cruelty.
And yet God cared about them, and when they repented, he forgave them.
It was Jonah, the prophet, who had the hard heart.
The story challenges anyone who thinks God's love is only for people like us.
What happened after?
Nineveh's repentance lasted for a while, and later Assyria returned to its old ways.

Jesus said that the people of Nineveh will stand up at the judgment and condemn the people who rejected him, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and now something greater than Jonah is here.
What does this mean for us today?
Is there someone you think is too far gone to be forgiven?
Jonah's story says that God's mercy is bigger than our list of who deserves it.
It also asks whether we are glad when God forgives someone we don't like.
It is easy to love mercy when it is for us.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God is gracious and compassionate, and that his love reaches everyone who turns to him.
And it points to Jesus, who came to seek and save the lost, including our enemies.
annunciation: In the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy, God sent the angel Gabriel to Nazareth, a small town in Galilee.
He went to a young woman named Mary.
She was engaged to a man named Joseph, a descendant of King David.
Mary was probably a teenager, and she lived an ordinary life in a town most people overlooked.
The angel said, greetings, you who are highly favored. The Lord is with you.
Mary was deeply troubled by his words and wondered what kind of greeting this was.
The angel said, do not be afraid, Mary, you have found favor with God.
You will conceive and give birth to a son, and you are to call him Jesus.
He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High.
The Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over Jacob's descendants forever.
His kingdom will never end.
Mary asked an honest question.
How will this be, since I am a virgin? She wasn't doubting God.
She wanted to understand.
The angel answered, the Holy Spirit will come on you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.
So the holy one to be born will be called the Son of God. Then he gave her a sign.
Your relative Elizabeth, who was thought to be unable to conceive, is going to have a child in her old age.
For no word from God will ever fail.
Mary answered with one of the bravest sentences in the Bible. I am the Lord's servant.
May your word to me be fulfilled. Then the angel left her.
She knew what this would cost.
A young woman who was pregnant before marriage could be shamed by her whole town.
Joseph could have ended the engagement. Yet she said yes.
Soon after, Mary hurried to visit Elizabeth.
When she arrived, Elizabeth's baby leaped inside her, and Elizabeth said, blessed is she who has believed that the Lord would fulfill his promises to her.
Mary then sang a song of praise.
My soul glorifies the Lord and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior.
Why does this matter?
This is the moment God began to enter the world as a human being.
He didn't come with an army.
He came through a young woman in a small town who trusted him.
What happened after?
Joseph, a good and quiet man, planned to end the engagement privately.
But an angel appeared to him in a dream and told him not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife.
He obeyed, and he named the child Jesus, which means the Lord saves.
What does this mean for us today?
Mary didn't have the whole plan.
She had a promise and a next step.
She said yes before she knew how it would work out.
Many of us wait to understand everything before we trust, and she shows another way.
She also asked honest questions, and God didn't rebuke her for that.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that nothing is impossible with God, and that he chooses humble people for great work.
It is the beginning of the good news that God has come to save his people.
nativity: Caesar Augustus, the Roman emperor, ordered a census of the whole empire.
Everyone had to go to their own town to register.
Joseph was from the family line of David, so he left Nazareth and traveled about ninety miles south to Bethlehem, David's town. Mary went with him.
She was about to give birth.
When they arrived, the town was crowded.
While they were there, the time came for the baby to be born.
She gave birth to her firstborn, a son.
She wrapped him in cloths and placed him in a manger, a feeding trough for animals, because there was no guest room available for them.
That night, there were shepherds out in the fields nearby, keeping watch over their flocks.
Shepherds were poor, and many people looked down on them.
An angel of the Lord appeared to them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified.
The angel said, do not be afraid.
I bring you good news that will cause great joy for all the people.
Today in the town of David a Savior has been born to you.
He is the Messiah, the Lord.
This will be a sign to you.
You will find a baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger.
Suddenly a great company of the heavenly host appeared with the angel, praising God and saying, glory to God in the highest heaven, and on earth peace to those on whom his favor rests.
When the angels left, the shepherds said to one another, let's go to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened.
They hurried off and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby, who was lying in the manger.
After they had seen him, they spread the word about what had been told them.
All who heard it were amazed.
But Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart.
The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for everything they had seen.
Why does this matter?
The Creator of the universe was born as a baby in a borrowed place.
The first people told were not kings or priests but shepherds.
From the very beginning, the good news was for ordinary people.
What happened after?
Eight days later, Jesus was named, and then Mary and Joseph took him to the temple in Jerusalem.
An old man named Simeon held him and thanked God.
Later, wise men from the East followed a star to find him.
King Herod felt threatened, so Joseph took his family to Egypt until it was safe.
Then they went home to Nazareth, where Jesus grew up.
What does this mean for us today?
Christmas is not only for people who have everything in order.
The message came to people working night shifts in the cold.
If you feel overlooked or tired, this story says that heaven came looking for people like you.
It also invites us to do what the shepherds did.
They didn't just hear it.
They went and saw, and then they told others.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God became one of us, and that he came for everyone.
This child is the Savior, the Messiah, the Lord.
temple-boy: Every year, Mary and Joseph traveled to Jerusalem for the Passover festival.
When Jesus was twelve, they went up as usual.
When the festival was over, they started the trip home.
They traveled in a large group of relatives and neighbors, and the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem.
His parents didn't realize it.
Thinking he was somewhere in their group, they traveled for a day.
Then they began looking for him among their relatives and friends.
When they didn't find him, they went back to Jerusalem to look for him.
After three days, they found him in the temple courts.
He was sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions.
Everyone who heard him was amazed at his understanding and his answers.
When his parents saw him, they were astonished.
His mother said to him, son, why have you treated us like this?
Your father and I have been anxiously searching for you.
Anyone who has lost track of a child for even a few minutes can feel what she felt.
Jesus answered with a question of his own.
Why were you searching for me?
Didn't you know I had to be in my Father's house?
They did not understand what he was saying to them.
This is the first recorded time that Jesus spoke, and he called God his Father.
Then he went down to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them.
His mother treasured all these things in her heart.
And Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man.
Why does this matter?
It is the only story in the Gospels from Jesus' childhood.
It shows that even at twelve, Jesus knew who he was and where he belonged.
It also shows that he was a real child who grew up under human parents.
He listened, he asked questions, and then he went home and obeyed them.
What happened after?
Eighteen more years passed before Jesus began his public work.
The Bible tells us almost nothing about those years, except that he grew up in Nazareth and worked as a carpenter like Joseph.
When he was about thirty, he was baptized by John, and his ministry began.
What does this mean for us today?
Parents can find comfort that even Mary and Joseph lost track of Jesus and had to go back and find him.
It is also an invitation to ask questions about God.
Jesus sat with teachers and asked honest questions.
Faith doesn't require us to stop wondering.
And it shows what to look for first.
Jesus was in his Father's house, with his Father's word.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus is the Son of God, who humbled himself to grow up like us.
And it points to the day when he would again be in Jerusalem at Passover, doing his Father's work for the world.
baptist: About four hundred years had passed since the last prophet spoke in Israel.
Then, in the fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius, the word of God came to a man named John in the wilderness.
John was the son of Zechariah, a priest, and Elizabeth.
His birth had been a miracle, since his parents were old and had no children.
An angel had told Zechariah that his son would prepare the way for the Lord.
John lived out in the desert.
He wore clothes made of camel's hair with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey.
He looked like the prophet Elijah, and that was no accident.
He went into the area around the Jordan River, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.
His message was short.
Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near.
Matthew says John was the one Isaiah spoke of when he wrote, a voice of one calling in the wilderness, prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for him.
In the ancient world, a road was cleared before a king arrived.
John's job was to get people ready for the King.
People came from Jerusalem, from all of Judea and the whole region of the Jordan.
Confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the river.
John didn't tell them what they wanted to hear.
When he saw many Pharisees and Sadducees coming to be baptized, he said, you brood of vipers!
Who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?
Produce fruit in keeping with repentance.
Don't think you can say to yourselves, we have Abraham as our father.
Being born into the right family was not enough.
The crowds asked him, what should we do then?
John said, anyone who has two shirts should share with the one who has none, and anyone who has food should do the same.
Tax collectors came and asked what to do.
Don't collect any more than you are required to.
Soldiers asked, and he said, don't extort money and don't accuse people falsely.
Be content with your pay.
His advice was practical.
Repentance meant changing how you lived on Monday morning.
John was also humble.
People began to wonder if he might be the Messiah.
He said, I baptize you with water, but one who is more powerful than I will come, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.
He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.
He must become greater, and I must become less.
Why does this matter?
John was the last of the Old Testament prophets and the first voice of the New.
He didn't try to attract attention to himself.
He pointed beyond himself.
Jesus later said that among those born of women, there has not risen anyone greater than John the Baptist.
What happened after?
John baptized Jesus, and then he saw the Spirit come down on him.
The next day he said, look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.
Some of John's followers left to follow Jesus, and John was glad.
Later, he told King Herod that it was wrong for him to marry his brother's wife, and Herod put him in prison. John was killed there. Jesus grieved for him.
What does this mean for us today?
John's message is still the first step.
We make room for God by being honest about what is wrong and turning toward him.
It also looks like fairness and generosity in everyday life, not just religious talk.
And John shows what a good messenger is like.
He didn't say, look at me. He said, look at him.
