That is why this story is so important.
It says that God sent someone ahead to get his people ready, and that the way to meet the King is through repentance.
And it points straight to Jesus, the Lamb of God.
baptism: Jesus was about thirty years old.
He had grown up in Nazareth, worked as a carpenter, and lived a quiet life.
Now the time had come to begin his work.
He left Galilee and traveled about sixty miles to the Jordan River, where John was baptizing.
He came to be baptized by him.
John tried to stop him.
I need to be baptized by you, he said, and do you come to me? John knew who Jesus was.
He knew that Jesus had no sins to confess, and he felt that it should be the other way around.
But Jesus replied, let it be so now.
It is proper for us to do this to fulfill all righteousness. Then John agreed.
Jesus didn't need to repent.
He was choosing to stand with the people he came to save.
He went down into the water with sinners, and he took his place beside them.
It was a sign of what he would do on the cross.
As soon as Jesus was baptized, he went up out of the water.
At that moment heaven was opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and alighting on him.
And a voice from heaven said, this is my Son, whom I love.
With him I am well pleased.
All three persons of the Trinity are present in this scene.
The Son is in the water, the Spirit comes down like a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven.
And the Father's words were spoken before Jesus had preached a sermon, healed anyone, or worked a miracle.
God said he loved his Son and was pleased with him before any of that happened.
John later told people what he had seen.
I saw the Spirit come down from heaven as a dove and remain on him.
I would not have known him, except that the one who sent me to baptize with water told me, the man on whom you see the Spirit come down and remain is the one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.
I have seen and I testify that this is God's Chosen One.
Why does this matter?
The baptism marks the start of Jesus' public work.
It confirms who he is, the beloved Son, and it shows he was anointed with the Holy Spirit for his mission.
It also shows that Jesus is willing to go all the way down to where we are.
What happened after?
Right after his baptism, the Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness.
He fasted forty days and was tempted by the devil.
The first temptation began with the words, if you are the Son of God.
The enemy tried to make him doubt what the Father had just said.
Jesus answered each one with Scripture and didn't give in.
Then he began to preach, call disciples, heal the sick, and announce the kingdom of God.
What does this mean for us today?
Christian baptism echoes this scene.
When we are baptized into Christ, we are joined to him.
What the Father said about the Son is also what he says about those who are in him.
You are mine, I love you.
And that comes first, before we earn anything.
It also shows that following Jesus starts with grace, not with a performance.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus is the beloved Son of God, and that he came down into the water with us.
And it shows the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit working together to save the world.
cana: Three days after Jesus called his first disciples, there was a wedding in Cana, a village in Galilee.
Jesus' mother Mary was there, and Jesus and his disciples had also been invited.
In those days, a wedding was a community celebration that could last for days.
Running out of wine would have been a serious embarrassment for the host, and it could haunt a young couple for years.
Partway through the feast, the wine ran out.
Mary noticed and went to Jesus.
They have no more wine, she said.
Jesus answered, woman, why do you involve me?
My hour has not yet come.
His time to be revealed publicly had not yet arrived. But Mary didn't argue.
She turned to the servants and said, do whatever he tells you.
Nearby stood six stone water jars, the kind used for ceremonial washing.
Each held twenty to thirty gallons.
Jesus said to the servants, fill the jars with water.
They filled them to the brim.
Then he told them, now draw some out and take it to the master of the banquet. They did.
The master of the banquet tasted the water that had been turned into wine.
He didn't know where it had come from, though the servants who had drawn the water knew.
Then he called the bridegroom aside.
Everyone brings out the choice wine first and then the cheaper wine after the guests have had too much to drink.
But you have saved the best till now.
The amount was staggering, around a hundred and twenty to a hundred and eighty gallons of excellent wine.
Jesus didn't just solve the problem. He overflowed it.
John tells us that this, the first of his signs, was performed by Jesus in Cana of Galilee.
He thus revealed his glory, and his disciples believed in him.
Why does this matter?
John calls the miracles signs, because they point to something.
Water that was used for ritual washing became wine for a celebration.
Jesus was showing that he came to bring joy that the old rituals couldn't.
The prophets often pictured the coming kingdom as a feast with the best wine.
Jesus began his work at a party.
What happened after?
From Cana, Jesus went to Capernaum, and then to Jerusalem for Passover.
His mother appears again later in John's gospel, standing near the cross.
Her advice at the wedding was the last thing she is recorded as saying in this gospel.
Do whatever he tells you.
What does this mean for us today?
Jesus cares about ordinary needs, even a social embarrassment at a wedding.
Mary didn't give him instructions.
She just told him the problem and trusted him.
It also shows what obedience looks like.
The servants did something that seemed pointless, filling jars with water, and they were the ones who saw the miracle.
And Jesus often gives more than we ask for.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that Jesus has power over creation, and it reveals his glory at the very start.
It also points ahead to the greater feast, when Jesus gave his disciples a cup and spoke of the new covenant in his blood, and to the wedding supper of the Lamb at the end of time.
fishers: Jesus was standing on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, also called Lake Gennesaret, and the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God.
He saw two boats at the water's edge.
The fishermen had left them there and were washing their nets.
One of the boats belonged to Simon, who is also called Peter.
Jesus got into it and asked him to push out a little from shore.
Then he sat down in the boat and taught the people from there.
When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, put out into deep water, and let down the nets for a catch.
Simon was a professional fisherman, and Jesus was a carpenter and teacher.
Simon had good reasons to say no.
Master, he said, we've worked hard all night and haven't caught anything.
Fishing was done at night, when the fish came near the surface, and they had just finished a long night with nothing to show for it.
But then Simon said, because you say so, I will let down the nets.
When they had done so, they caught such a large number of fish that their nets began to break.
They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them.
They came and filled both boats so full that they began to sink.
When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus' knees and said, go away from me, Lord. I am a sinful man. He was overwhelmed.
He had been a fisherman his whole life and knew he could not have made this happen.
He was in the presence of someone holy, and he felt unworthy.
He and all his companions were astonished at the catch of fish they had taken, and so were James and John, the sons of Zebedee, Simon's partners.
Then Jesus said to Simon, don't be afraid.
From now on you will fish for people.
Jesus didn't send him away.
He gave him a new purpose.
So they pulled their boats up on shore, left everything and followed him.
Why does this matter?
This is the moment these men gave up their careers to follow Jesus. It was a big decision.
They left behind boats and nets, and in Peter's case a business, a home and a family.
They didn't know where it would lead.
What happened after?
Peter became one of the closest followers of Jesus.
He was part of the inner three with James and John. He also failed badly.
On the night Jesus was arrested, he denied knowing him three times.
But Jesus forgave him and restored him, and on the day of Pentecost Peter preached to a crowd, and about three thousand people believed.
He had become a fisher of people.
There is also a quiet echo at the end of John's gospel.
After the resurrection, some of the disciples had gone back to fishing and caught nothing all night.
A man on the shore told them to throw the net on the other side, and they caught a huge number of fish.
Peter jumped into the water to get to Jesus.
What does this mean for us today?
Sometimes God asks us to do something that doesn't make sense to us.
Peter was tired and an expert, yet he said, because you say so.
Obedience can open the door to more than we expected.
It also shows that Jesus doesn't call people because they are perfect.
Peter said he was a sinful man, and Jesus said, don't be afraid.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus calls ordinary people, with all their flaws, into a bigger purpose.
And it invites each of us to say, because you say so.
sermon: Large crowds were following Jesus.
They came from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea and the region across the Jordan.
Many were sick, and he had been healing them.
When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up on a mountainside and sat down.
His disciples came to him, and he began to teach them.
This became the most famous sermon ever preached.
It begins with the Beatitudes.
Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.
Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.
Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled.
Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy.
Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.
Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.
Blessed are those who are persecuted because of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
These were surprising.
The world says that the blessed are the rich, the strong and the powerful.
Jesus said that the blessed are the people who know they need God.
He told his followers that they were the salt of the earth and the light of the world.
A city on a hill cannot be hidden.
Let your light shine before others, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.
Then he raised the bar.
You have heard that it was said, do not murder.
But I tell you that anyone who is angry with a brother or sister will be subject to judgment.
You have heard that it was said, do not commit adultery.
But I tell you that anyone who looks at someone lustfully has already committed adultery in his heart.
Jesus was showing that God cares about the heart, not just outward behavior.
He taught, you have heard that it was said, love your neighbor and hate your enemy.
But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, that you may be children of your Father in heaven.
If someone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to them the other cheek also.
He taught them to pray.
Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread.
And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.
And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.
He warned against worry.
Do not worry about your life, what you will eat or drink.
Look at the birds of the air.
They do not sow or reap or store away in barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them.
Are you not much more valuable than they?
Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.
He ended with a short story.
Everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock.
The rain came down, the streams rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house, yet it did not fall.
But everyone who hears these words and does not put them into practice is like a foolish man who built his house on sand.
When the storm came, it fell with a great crash.
When Jesus had finished, the crowds were amazed at his teaching, because he taught as one who had authority.
Why does this matter?
The Sermon on the Mount describes what life in God's kingdom looks like.
It isn't a list of rules to earn God's favor.
It describes people who have been changed from the inside.
What happened after?
Jesus came down from the mountain and began healing, including a man with leprosy.
The crowds kept following.
Over the centuries, this sermon has shaped believers and others, from the early church to Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.
What does this mean for us today?
The sermon is both challenging and comforting.
It shows us that we can't live this way on our own strength, and it points us to God's grace.
It also reminds us that hearing isn't enough.
The question is whether we build our lives on it.
And it frees us from worry, because we have a Father who knows what we need.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that the kingdom of God belongs to the humble, and that Jesus teaches with the authority of God himself.
samaritan-woman: Jesus and his disciples were traveling from Judea back to Galilee, and the shortest route went through Samaria.
Many Jews avoided Samaria.
The two peoples had a long history of hostility, and a Jewish teacher would not normally speak to a Samaritan, let alone a woman.
But John says Jesus had to go through Samaria.
About noon, Jesus came to a town called Sychar and sat down by Jacob's well, tired from the journey.
His disciples had gone into town to buy food.
A Samaritan woman came to draw water.
Most women came in the cool of the morning, so coming at noon suggests she may have wanted to avoid the others.
Jesus asked her, will you give me a drink?
She was surprised.
You are a Jew and I am a Samaritan woman.
How can you ask me for a drink?
Jesus answered, if you knew the gift of God and who it is that asks you for a drink, you would have asked him and he would have given you living water.
She said, sir, you have nothing to draw with and the well is deep.
Where can you get this living water?
Jesus replied, everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks the water I give them will never thirst.
Indeed, the water I give them will become in them a spring of water welling up to eternal life.
She said, sir, give me this water so that I won't get thirsty and have to keep coming here to draw water.
Then Jesus said something unexpected.
Go, call your husband and come back.
I have no husband, she replied.
Jesus said, you are right.
The fact is, you have had five husbands, and the man you now have is not your husband.
He wasn't trying to shame her.
He was showing her that he knew her whole story and still sat and talked with her.
She changed the subject to an old argument.
Our ancestors worshiped on this mountain, but you Jews claim that the place where we must worship is in Jerusalem.
Jesus said, a time is coming and has now come when the true worshipers will worship the Father in the Spirit and in truth.
God is spirit, and his worshipers must worship in the Spirit and in truth.
The place wasn't the point.
The woman said, I know that Messiah is coming.
When he comes, he will explain everything to us.
Then Jesus said, I, the one speaking to you, am he.
It was the first time in John's gospel that Jesus plainly said he was the Messiah, and he said it to a Samaritan woman.
Just then his disciples returned and were surprised to find him talking with a woman. But no one asked why.
Then, leaving her water jar, the woman went back to the town and said to the people, come, see a man who told me everything I ever did.
Could this be the Messiah?
They came out of the town and made their way toward him.
Why does this matter?
Jesus crossed every barrier of race, gender and reputation to offer this woman new life.
She left her water jar behind, because she had found something better.
She became one of the first evangelists.
What happened after?
Many of the Samaritans from that town believed in him because of her testimony.
They asked him to stay with them, and he stayed two days.
Many more became believers because of his words.
They said to the woman, we no longer believe just because of what you said.
Now we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this man really is the Savior of the world.
What does this mean for us today?
Everyone has a thirst that nothing else can satisfy.
Jesus meets us in our ordinary routines, knows everything about us, and offers living water anyway.
It also shows that no one is too far outside to be welcomed.
And it shows how to share faith.
She simply told what had happened and invited people to come see for themselves.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus is the Savior of the whole world, and that the water he gives satisfies for good.
tempest: It had been a long day.
Jesus had been teaching crowds beside the Sea of Galilee, telling parables from a boat pushed out a little from the shore.
When evening came, he said to his disciples, let us go over to the other side.
Leaving the crowd behind, they took him along in the boat, just as he was.
Other boats were with them.
The Sea of Galilee sits low among hills, and cold air rushing down can whip up violent storms without warning.
Several of the disciples were experienced fishermen who knew this lake well.
A furious squall came up, and the waves broke over the boat, so that it was nearly swamped.
These were professionals, and they were afraid.
And where was Jesus?
He was in the stern, sleeping on a cushion.
He was exhausted from the day, and he slept through the storm.
The disciples woke him and said, teacher, don't you care if we drown?
He got up, rebuked the wind and said to the waves, quiet! Be still!
Then the wind died down and it was completely calm.
He said to his disciples, why are you so afraid?
Do you still have no faith?
They were terrified and asked each other, who is this?
Even the wind and the waves obey him!
Their first fear was of the storm.
Their second fear, once it was calm, was of the man who had stopped it.
Mark says they were filled with great fear.
They had just seen something that only God does.
Why does this matter?
The Psalms say it is the Lord who stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves.
The disciples knew those songs.
When Jesus spoke to the sea and it obeyed, they began to realize who was in their boat.
He was a real man who got tired and fell asleep, and he was also the Lord of creation.
What happened after?
They reached the other side of the lake, where Jesus healed a man who had been suffering terribly.
The disciples' question, who is this, kept getting answered through the rest of the Gospels.
Later, Peter would say, you are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.
What does this mean for us today?
The disciples were in the storm because Jesus had told them to cross.
Obedience doesn't guarantee smooth water.
Storms come to the faithful too.
It also shows that Jesus is with us in the boat. He isn't far away.
And though the disciples woke him with a blunt question, don't you care, he answered them anyway.
We can bring our fear to him, even when it comes out sharp.
Notice also what he asked.
He didn't ask why they were in danger.
He asked why they were afraid, and where their faith was.
The point was never only the storm.
It was trust in the one who was with them.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus has authority over everything that frightens us.
And it invites us to say, with the disciples, who is this?
The answer is the Son of God, who can speak peace to the wildest waves.
walks-on-water: John the Baptist was Jesus' cousin and the man who announced him to the world.
Now John was dead.
King Herod had him killed, and John's followers came and told Jesus.
Jesus wanted to be alone, so he took a boat across the Sea of Galilee to a quiet place.
But the crowds saw him leave.
They ran along the shore and got there first.
Jesus looked at thousands of people and felt sorry for them.
He healed their sick all day.
When evening came, the disciples said, send them away to buy food.
Jesus said, you give them something to eat.
All they had was five loaves of bread and two fish.
Jesus thanked God for it, broke it, and handed it out.
About five thousand men ate, plus women and children, and twelve baskets of leftovers were picked up.
The crowd was so amazed that they wanted to take Jesus and make him king by force.
John's gospel tells us this.
So Jesus did something unexpected.
He made his disciples get in the boat and go ahead of him to the other side.
He sent the crowd home.
Then he climbed a mountain alone to pray.
Out on the lake, the disciples were in trouble.
A strong wind was blowing against them, and the waves were pounding the boat.
They had been rowing for hours.
John's gospel says they were only three or four miles from shore, but they couldn't get there.
Sometime between three and six in the morning, they were exhausted and afraid.
Then they saw someone walking toward them on the water.
They screamed. They thought it was a ghost.
Jesus called out, take courage.
It is I. Don't be afraid.
Peter was the bold, loud one of the twelve, a fisherman who had left his nets to follow Jesus.
He called back, Lord, if it's really you, tell me to come to you on the water.
Jesus said one word.
Come.
Peter climbed over the side and walked on the water toward Jesus.
Then he noticed the wind.
He got scared and started to sink.
He shouted, Lord, save me.
Jesus reached out and caught him right away.
He said, you of little faith, why did you doubt?
They climbed into the boat, and the wind stopped.
The disciples fell down and worshiped him.
They said, truly you are the Son of God.
In Matthew's gospel, this is the first time the disciples say that out loud.
Why does this matter?
In the Old Testament, only God walks on the sea.
Job says God alone treads on the waves.
And when Jesus says, it is I, those words can also be translated, I am.
That is the name God gave Moses at the burning bush.
This scene shows that Jesus is more than a teacher, and that he saves people who are sinking.
Peter's story didn't end in the water.
Later he would say out loud that Jesus is the Messiah, and Jesus would make him a leader of his followers.
Peter would also fail badly the night Jesus was arrested, and Jesus would reach for him again.
The boat reached the shore at Gennesaret, and people brought all their sick.
Everyone who touched Jesus' cloak was healed.
The next day, Jesus told the crowd that he is the bread of life.
What does this mean for us today?
Everyone ends up in a storm sometime.
It might be a sickness, a lost job, a broken family, or a fear that won't leave.
This story shows where Jesus is while it happens.
He came to the disciples in the middle of the storm.
He didn't wait for it to be over.
It also shows what faith looks like.
Peter didn't walk on the water because he was strong.
He walked because Jesus said, come.
He sank when he looked at the wind instead of at Jesus.
And when he sank, he did the only thing he could do.
He asked for help.
Lord, save me. Jesus caught him right away, with his hand already stretched out.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that Jesus is God, with power over everything that scares us.
It shows that doubt doesn't disqualify anyone, because Peter doubted and was still caught, still called, and still became a leader.
And it shows that the right prayer in a storm can be three words.
Lord, save me.
multitude: Jesus had just heard that John the Baptist was dead.
He withdrew by boat to a quiet place to be alone.
But the crowds heard about it and followed him on foot from the towns.
When Jesus landed and saw a large crowd, he had compassion on them and healed their sick.
He spent the whole day with them.
As evening approached, the disciples came to him.
This is a remote place, and it's already getting late.
Send the crowds away, so they can go to the villages and buy themselves some food.
Jesus said, they do not need to go away.
You give them something to eat.
The disciples were stunned.
Philip said that it would take more than half a year's wages to buy enough bread for each person to have a bite.
Andrew found a boy who had five small barley loaves and two small fish.
It was the lunch of a child.
How far will they go among so many?
Jesus said, have the people sit down.
There was plenty of grass in that place, and they sat down in groups, about five thousand men, besides women and children.
Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, and distributed them to those who were seated.
He did the same with the fish, as much as they wanted.
He took what was there, thanked God for it, and started giving it away.
When they had all had enough to eat, he said to his disciples, gather the pieces that are left over. Let nothing be wasted.
So they gathered them and filled twelve baskets with the pieces of the five barley loaves left over by those who had eaten.
After the people saw the sign Jesus performed, they began to say, surely this is the Prophet who is to come into the world.
Jesus knew that they intended to come and make him king by force.
So he withdrew again to a mountain by himself.
Why does this matter?
This is the only miracle, other than the resurrection, that appears in all four Gospels.
It shows Jesus as the one who provides.
It also echoes the manna in the desert, when God fed Israel with bread from heaven.
The next day, Jesus told the crowd, I am the bread of life.
Whoever comes to me will never go hungry.
What happened after?
Many people who had been fed wanted more bread, but not the deeper truth Jesus offered.
When he said that he was the bread from heaven, many of his followers turned away.
Peter said, Lord, to whom shall we go?
You have the words of eternal life.
What does this mean for us today? Look at what Jesus used.
A boy offered what he had, a small and ordinary lunch, and Jesus multiplied it.
We may think what we have is too little to matter.
Jesus doesn't ask for what we don't have.
He asks for what we do have.
It also shows that Jesus cares about physical needs. He fed hungry people.
And the disciples got to be part of it.
They passed out the food and collected the baskets, and each of the twelve had a basket left over.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus is the one who satisfies, and that he can do a lot with a little.
And it points to the bread he gave at the Last Supper, his body given for us.
jairus: When Jesus came back across the lake, a large crowd gathered around him on the shore.
Then a man named Jairus came.
He was a leader of the synagogue, a respected man in his town.
But he forgot his dignity.
He fell at Jesus' feet and begged him again and again.
My little daughter is very sick.
Please come and put your hands on her so that she will be healed and live.
She was twelve years old.
Jesus went with him, and a large crowd followed, pressing around him.
In the crowd was a woman who had been sick for twelve years.
She had spent everything she had on doctors, and instead of getting better, she had grown worse.
Her condition also made her an outcast under the law.
She had heard about Jesus.
She thought, if I just touch his clothes, I will be healed.
She came up behind him and touched his cloak, and immediately her illness was gone. She felt it in her body.
Jesus stopped.
He realized that power had gone out from him. Who touched my clothes?
His disciples said, you see the people crowding against you, and yet you ask, who touched me?
But Jesus kept looking around.
The woman, trembling with fear, came and fell at his feet and told him the whole truth.
He said to her, daughter, your faith has healed you.
Go in peace and be freed from your suffering.
He called her daughter, the only time he is recorded addressing someone that way.
Meanwhile, Jairus was waiting. Every minute counted.
While Jesus was still speaking, some people came from the house of Jairus with sad news. Your daughter is gone.
Why bother the teacher anymore?
Overhearing what they said, Jesus told him, don't be afraid. Just believe.
He let no one follow him except Peter, James and John.
When they came to the home, Jesus saw a commotion, with people crying and wailing loudly.
He went in and said, why all this commotion and wailing?
The child is not dead but asleep. They laughed at him.
After he put them all out, he took the child's father and mother and the disciples who were with him and went in where the child was.
He took her by the hand and said to her, talitha koum, which means, little girl, I say to you, get up.
Immediately the girl stood up and began to walk around.
She was twelve years old.
At this they were completely astonished.
He gave strict orders not to let anyone know about this, and told them to give her something to eat.
Why does this matter?
The two stories are woven together on purpose.
A powerful man and a nameless outcast woman both needed Jesus.
He gave time and attention to each of them.
And the number twelve ties them together, a girl of twelve years and a woman who had suffered for twelve years.
Jesus has power over illness and over the worst thing we fear.
What happened after?
Jesus kept teaching and healing.
The woman's story would be told wherever the gospel was preached.
Later, Jesus would raise his friend Lazarus, and then rise himself.
What does this mean for us today?
Jairus had to keep trusting while he waited, even when the interruption seemed to cost him. Jesus is never late.
It also shows that Jesus notices the people no one else notices.
And look at his words, don't be afraid, just believe.
He says that to anyone facing the hardest news.
Notice too that he took her by the hand and told them to give her something to eat.
He is both powerful and tender.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus has authority over sickness and death, and that he treats the high and the low with the same love.
magdalene: A Pharisee named Simon invited Jesus to have dinner with him.
Jesus went to his house and reclined at the table, as people did in those days.
A woman in that town who lived a sinful life learned that Jesus was eating at the Pharisee's house.
She brought an alabaster jar of perfume and went in.
Everyone at the table knew who she was, and no one expected her to be there.
As she stood behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears.
Then she wiped them with her hair, kissed them and poured perfume on them. She said nothing.
Her actions said everything.
When the Pharisee saw this, he said to himself, if this man were a prophet, he would know who is touching him and what kind of woman she is. She is a sinner.
He was judging both of them.
He thought Jesus was either unaware or unholy.
Jesus answered his thoughts.
Simon, I have something to tell you.
He said, teacher, tell me.
Jesus told a short story.
Two people owed money to a certain moneylender.
One owed him five hundred denarii, and the other fifty.
Neither of them had the money to pay him back, so he forgave the debts of both.
Now which of them will love him more?
Simon replied, I suppose the one who had the bigger debt forgiven.
You have judged correctly, Jesus said.
Then he turned toward the woman and said to Simon, do you see this woman? I came into your house.
You did not give me any water for my feet, but she wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.
You did not give me a kiss, but this woman, from the time I entered, has not stopped kissing my feet.
You did not put oil on my head, but she has poured perfume on my feet.
Therefore, I tell you, her many sins have been forgiven, as her great love has shown.
But whoever has been forgiven little loves little.
Then Jesus said to her, your sins are forgiven.
The other guests began to say among themselves, who is this who even forgives sins?
Jesus said to the woman, your faith has saved you. Go in peace.
Why does this matter?
Simon was a good, religious man who didn't think he needed much forgiveness.
The woman knew she needed a lot.
Her love wasn't what earned the forgiveness.
It was what showed she had received it.
And Jesus claimed a right that only God has, to forgive sins.
What happened after?

Luke's next lines tell us that Jesus traveled through towns and villages, and that many women who had been helped by him supported his work, including Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had come out.
Women like these were among his faithful followers, and they stayed at the cross and went to the tomb.
What does this mean for us today?
We can be like Simon, looking down on others while forgetting our own need.
Or we can be like the woman, honest about our debt and overwhelmed by being forgiven.
Jesus welcomes the second.
It also shows that he looks at people differently than we do. Simon saw a category. Jesus saw a person.
And the end of the story is peace.
She went in peace, forgiven and free.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus forgives freely, and that the more we realize how much we have been forgiven, the more we love.
adulteress: Early in the morning, Jesus appeared again in the temple courts, where all the people gathered around him, and he sat down to teach them.
The teachers of the law and the Pharisees brought in a woman caught in adultery.
They made her stand before the group.
The scene was meant to humiliate her, but it was really a trap for Jesus.
Teacher, they said to Jesus, this woman was caught in the act of adultery.
In the Law Moses commanded us to stone such women. Now what do you say?
If Jesus said to let her go, they could accuse him of ignoring the law of Moses.
If he said to carry out the penalty, he would lose his reputation for mercy and could be in trouble with the Roman authorities, who did not allow the Jews to carry out executions.
But Jesus bent down and started to write on the ground with his finger.
John doesn't tell us what he wrote.
When they kept questioning him, he straightened up and said to them, let any one of you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.
Again he stooped down and wrote on the ground.
At this, those who heard began to go away one at a time, the older ones first, until only Jesus was left, with the woman still standing there.
Jesus straightened up and asked her, woman, where are they?
Has no one condemned you? No one, sir, she said.
Then neither do I condemn you, Jesus declared.
Go now and leave your life of sin.
Why does this matter?
The accusers cared more about the trap than about the woman. They used her as a tool.
Jesus saw her as a person.
He didn't deny that sin is sin, and he told her to leave her life of sin.
But he gave her mercy first, and then he gave her a way forward.
Grace came before the instruction.
What happened after?
The next thing Jesus said in John's gospel was, I am the light of the world.
Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.
The woman went away without condemnation, and we are not told what became of her.
But those who stood against her had a different problem.
They had to face their own hearts.
What does this mean for us today?
We are all quick to pick up stones, whether real ones or the stones of gossip, judgment and shame.
Jesus' challenge still works.
Before condemning someone else, we need to check our own record.
And it also offers hope to those who know they have failed.
The only one without sin, the only one who had the right to condemn her, chose to forgive.
He did not say that what she did was fine.
He said that she was free to start again.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus meets sinners with mercy and truth together, and that he gives people a real chance to begin again.
And it points to the cross, where Jesus took the condemnation that we deserve.
martha: As Jesus and his disciples were on their way, he came to a village where a woman named Martha opened her home to him.
She had a sister called Mary.
Luke doesn't say where the village was, but John tells us it was Bethany, about two miles from Jerusalem.
The family were close friends of Jesus, and their brother Lazarus is mentioned elsewhere.
Hosting Jesus and his many followers was a big job. Martha went to work.
Mary sat at the Lord's feet listening to what he said.
In that culture, sitting at the feet of a teacher was the place for a student, and women were not normally given that place.
Mary had stepped into it.
But Martha was distracted by all the preparations that had to be made.
She came to him and asked, Lord, don't you care that my sister has left me to do the work by myself? Tell her to help me.
Anyone who has been stuck in the kitchen while others are visiting knows how she felt.
She wasn't wrong to want help, and hospitality is a good thing.
Jesus answered her gently.
Martha, Martha, you are worried and upset about many things, but few things are needed, or indeed only one.
Mary has chosen what is better, and it will not be taken away from her. He said her name twice.
It was a tender correction, not a harsh one.
Jesus wasn't criticizing the work.
He was pointing out that Martha was so consumed by serving that she had lost sight of the person she was serving.
She was worried and upset, and that was the problem.
He invited her to stop and sit.
Why does this matter?
The story is about priorities.
There is a time for serving, and there is a time for sitting still and listening.
If we only do the first, we can end up resentful and empty.
The one thing needed is to be with Jesus.
What happened after?
We see both sisters again in John's gospel when their brother Lazarus dies.
Martha is the one who goes out to meet Jesus on the road, and she makes a clear statement of faith.
I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, who is to come into the world.
Mary falls at his feet and weeps.
Jesus raises Lazarus from the dead.
In a later scene, Martha is serving at a dinner again, and Mary anoints Jesus with expensive perfume.
Both women are loved, and both grow.
What does this mean for us today?
Most of us are more like Martha.
We are busy, anxious, and feel like we are doing more than our share. Jesus doesn't scold us.
He says our name, and he tells us what we need.
We also don't have to pick between serving and listening.
The best service comes from time spent at his feet.
And this story shows us that Jesus welcomed women as students and that he wants everyone to learn from him.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that being with Jesus matters more than doing things for him.
And it invites us to put down what we are carrying, sit down, and listen.
transfiguration: About a week after Peter said that Jesus was the Messiah, Jesus took three of his closest disciples, Peter, James and John, and led them up a high mountain by themselves.
Just before this, Jesus had told his disciples that he would suffer and be killed and then rise again.
They did not understand, and Peter had argued with him.
Now Jesus gave them a glimpse of who he really was.
There he was transfigured before them.
His face shone like the sun, and his clothes became as white as the light.
Mark says they were whiter than anyone in the world could bleach them.
Then Moses and Elijah appeared, talking with Jesus.
Moses stood for the law, and Elijah for the prophets.
Luke tells us they spoke about his departure, which he was about to bring to fulfillment at Jerusalem.
Peter, as usual, spoke first.
Lord, it is good for us to be here.
If you wish, I will put up three shelters, one for you, one for Moses and one for Elijah.
Mark says he did not know what to say, they were so frightened.
He wanted to stay on the mountain and hold on to the moment.
While he was still speaking, a bright cloud covered them, and a voice from the cloud said, this is my Son, whom I love.
With him I am well pleased. Listen to him!
When the disciples heard this, they fell facedown to the ground, terrified.
The cloud was the same sign of God's presence that Israel had seen at Sinai.
But Jesus came and touched them. Get up, he said. Don't be afraid.
When they looked up, they saw no one except Jesus.
Moses and Elijah were gone. Only Jesus remained.
As they were coming down the mountain, Jesus gave them orders.
Don't tell anyone what you have seen, until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead.
They kept it to themselves.
Why does this matter?
The voice from heaven had a particular message. Listen to him.
Moses and Elijah were great, but they were pointing to Jesus.
And the disciples needed this glimpse of glory before they faced the cross.
When Jesus was arrested and killed, they could remember what they had seen on the mountain.
What happened after?
At the bottom of the mountain, they met a crowd and a father with a boy that the other disciples had not been able to help. Jesus healed him.
Real life was waiting below.
And Peter never forgot it.
Years later he wrote, we did not follow cleverly devised stories when we told you about the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ in power, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
We ourselves heard this voice that came from heaven when we were with him on the sacred mountain.
What does this mean for us today?
Peter wanted to stay on the mountain, and many of us would too.
Mountaintop moments are wonderful, but they are not where we live.
Jesus led his disciples back down to the ordinary and the hard.
The glimpse of glory was meant to carry them through the valley.
And the Father's instruction is for us as well. Listen to him.
In the middle of a lot of voices, it is Jesus we should listen to most.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that Jesus is the Son of God in glory, greater than Moses and Elijah.
And it gives us a promise that the one who walks with us through the valley is the same one who shines on the mountain.
prodigal-decides: Tax collectors and sinners were gathering around to hear Jesus.
The Pharisees and the teachers of the law muttered, this man welcomes sinners and eats with them.
So Jesus told them three stories about lost things, a lost sheep, a lost coin, and a lost son.
The third is the best known.
There was a man who had two sons.
The younger one said to his father, father, give me my share of the estate.
In that culture, asking for an inheritance while your father was still alive was a deep insult.
It was like saying, I wish you were dead.
Yet the father divided his property between them.
Not long after that, the younger son got together all he had, set off for a distant country, and there squandered his wealth in wild living.
He had plenty of friends while the money lasted.
After he had spent everything, there was a severe famine in that whole country, and he began to be in need.
So he went and hired himself out to a citizen of that country, who sent him to his fields to feed pigs.
For a Jewish young man, this was as low as it could get.
He longed to fill his stomach with the pods that the pigs were eating, but no one gave him anything.
Then Jesus said, when he came to his senses.
The Bible's words are simple and powerful.
He was finally seeing the truth.
How many of my father's hired servants have food to spare, and here I am starving to death!
I will set out and go back to my father and say to him, father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.
I am no longer worthy to be called your son.
Make me like one of your hired servants.
So he got up and went to his father.
Why does this matter?
Jesus told this story to people who thought God only welcomed the respectable.
It describes a man who made a terrible choice and hit the bottom.
But it also shows the turning point, which is honest recognition.
He didn't blame the famine or his friends. He said, I have sinned.
He rehearsed his speech and he started walking.
What happened after?
The next part of the story describes the father who ran to meet him.
The son had prepared to ask for a servant's job, but the father had something else in mind.
That part is the heart of the parable.
What does this mean for us today?
Many people feel that they have gone too far to come back.
Jesus told this story to say that the way home is open.
It begins with coming to our senses, which means seeing where we really are and what we really need.
It doesn't require us to fix ourselves first.
The son was still dirty and hungry when he decided to go. And it takes a step. He got up.
The turn from far away begins with one decision to head home.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that no one is beyond coming home, and that repentance is as simple as turning around.
And it prepares the way for the best news in the story, the father who is already watching the road.
prodigal-return: The younger son had rehearsed his speech all the way home.
He was still a long way off when something happened that he didn't plan for. His father saw him.
The father had been watching the road.
Jesus says that the father was filled with compassion for his son.
He ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him.
In that culture, an older man did not run. It was undignified.
But this father didn't care what anyone thought.
He ran, and in that moment he took on the shame that his son deserved.
The son began his speech.
Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.
I am no longer worthy to be called your son.
But he didn't get to finish the last part, the part about being made like a hired servant. His father cut him off.
The father said to his servants, quick!
Bring the best robe and put it on him.
Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet.
Bring the fattened calf and kill it.
Let's have a feast and celebrate.
For this son of mine was dead and is alive again.
He was lost and is found.
So they began to celebrate.
The robe, the ring and the sandals were not small gifts.
The robe covered his rags, the ring carried the family authority, and sandals were worn by sons, not servants.
The father didn't restore him as an employee.
He restored him as a son.
Meanwhile, the older son was in the field.
When he came near the house, he heard music and dancing.
He called one of the servants and asked what was going on.
Your brother has come, he replied, and your father has killed the fattened calf because he has him back safe and sound.
The older brother became angry and refused to go in.
So his father went out and pleaded with him.
He answered his father, look!
All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders.
Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends.
But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!
Notice that he said, this son of yours.
He wouldn't call him brother.
My son, the father said, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours.
But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again.
He was lost and is found.
Jesus ended the story there, without telling us whether the older brother went in.
Why does this matter?
The two sons stand for two kinds of people.
One ran away with his sins on the surface.
The other stayed home and was just as far from the father's heart.
The Pharisees listening to Jesus were the older brother.
The father loved both and went out to meet both.
What happened after?
We don't know whether the older brother joined the party.
The story is left open on purpose.
Jesus was asking his listeners to decide.
What does this mean for us today?
If you have run, the father is watching the road for you.
If you have stayed and kept the rules, check whether your heart is still at home. Both sons needed grace. Both could be welcomed.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows the heart of God as a Father who runs to meet us.
And it points to Jesus, who told it to show who he came to welcome.
rich-man: Jesus told a story about two men whose lives could hardly have been more different.
There was a rich man who dressed in purple and fine linen and lived in luxury every day.
Purple dye was very expensive.
He feasted well, and he did not seem to be a bad man in the usual sense.
At his gate was laid a beggar named Lazarus, covered with sores and longing to eat what fell from the rich man's table.
Even the dogs came and licked his sores.
This is the only person in any of Jesus' parables who is given a name. Lazarus means God helps.
The rich man is never named.
The time came when the beggar died, and the angels carried him to be with Abraham.
The rich man also died and was buried.
In Hades, where he was in torment, he looked up and saw Abraham far away, with Lazarus by his side.
So he called to him, father Abraham, have pity on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am in agony in this fire.
Abraham replied, son, remember that in your lifetime you received your good things, while Lazarus received bad things, but now he is comforted here and you are in agony.
And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been set in place, so that those who want to go from here to you cannot, nor can anyone cross over from there to us.
He answered, then I beg you, father, send Lazarus to my family, for I have five brothers.
Let him warn them, so that they will not also come to this place of torment.
Abraham replied, they have Moses and the Prophets. Let them listen to them.
No, father Abraham, he said, but if someone from the dead goes to them, they will repent.
He said to him, if they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead.
Why does this matter?
The rich man's sin was not that he was wealthy.
It was that he didn't see the man at his gate.
He walked past Lazarus every day, and it never bothered him.
Jesus is warning that comfort can make us blind to the needs right in front of us.
And the story shows that this life matters and that our choices have lasting consequences.
What happened after?
The last line was a quiet prediction.
Not long after, Jesus would be raised from the dead, and many would still refuse to believe.
The point was that Scripture already tells us what God wants, which is justice, mercy and care for the poor.
What does this mean for us today? Who is at your gate?
It may be a neighbor, a coworker or someone you pass every day on the street.
The story isn't meant to make us feel guilty about having things.
It asks us to look up and notice people. Jesus always did.
It also tells us not to wait for a dramatic sign.
We already have what we need to know what to do.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God cares about the poor, and that how we treat the person at our door matters now and forever.
And it points to Jesus, who left his heavenly home and came to the gate of our world.
publican: Jesus told this parable to some who were confident of their own righteousness and looked down on everyone else.
Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.
A Pharisee was a respected religious leader who studied the law and tried hard to keep it.
A tax collector was a Jew who worked for the Roman occupiers and collected taxes from his own people, often taking more than required.
Everyone considered him a traitor and a thief.
In the minds of the people listening, the Pharisee was the good guy and the tax collector was the bad guy.
The Pharisee stood by himself and prayed about himself.
God, I thank you that I am not like other people, robbers, evildoers, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week and give a tenth of all I get.
Everything he said might have been true. He did fast and tithe.
But notice that his prayer is really a list of how good he is and how bad others are.
He wasn't asking for anything, because he didn't think he needed anything.
But the tax collector stood at a distance.
He would not even look up to heaven, but beat his breast and said, God, have mercy on me, a sinner.
His prayer was just one sentence. He didn't make excuses.
He didn't compare himself to anyone. He simply asked.
Then Jesus said, I tell you that this man, rather than the other, went home justified before God.
For all those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted. This was shocking.
The man everyone despised was the one God accepted.
Why does this matter?
The Pharisee did good things, but he trusted in himself.
The tax collector had nothing to offer but his need, and that was exactly what God was looking for.
The difference was not in their résumés. It was in their hearts.
Jesus makes it plain that we cannot earn God's favor by comparing ourselves with others. We receive it by asking.
What happened after?
Right after this parable, people brought little children to Jesus, and the disciples tried to send them away.
Jesus said, let the little children come to me.
The kingdom of God belongs to such as these.
Humility and childlike trust are what the kingdom is made of.
What does this mean for us today?
It's easy to read this parable and think, I'm glad I'm not like that Pharisee.
And that is the trap, because then we are praying the Pharisee's prayer.
The better question is whether we have been comparing ourselves to others to feel better.
The tax collector's prayer is available to anyone, at any time.
It is short, and it is honest.
God, have mercy on me, a sinner.
Some Christians pray it slowly, over and over, as a daily habit.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God welcomes the humble and not the proud.
And it points to Jesus, who made the mercy that this man prayed for possible.
palm-sunday: Jesus and his disciples were nearing Jerusalem.
It was the week of Passover, and the city was packed with pilgrims.
When they reached the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two disciples ahead.
Go to the village ahead of you, and at once you will find a donkey tied there, with her colt by her.
Untie them and bring them to me.
If anyone says anything to you, say that the Lord needs them, and he will send them right away.
This took place to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Zechariah.
Say to Daughter Zion, see, your king comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey, and on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
Kings of war rode horses.
A king who comes in peace rode a donkey.
Jesus was making a deliberate statement.
The disciples did as Jesus had instructed.
They brought the donkey and the colt and placed their cloaks on them for Jesus to sit on.
A very large crowd spread their cloaks on the road, while others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.
Laying down cloaks was how people honored a king.
The crowds that went ahead of him and those that followed shouted, hosanna to the Son of David!
Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!
Hosanna in the highest heaven! Hosanna means save us.
These words came from Psalm 118, a song about the coming of God's chosen one.
When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred and asked, who is this?
The crowds answered, this is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.
Some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to Jesus, teacher, rebuke your disciples.
He replied, I tell you, if they keep quiet, the stones will cry out.
Luke adds that as he approached the city, he saw it and wept over it.
If you, even you, had only known on this day what would bring you peace.
But now it is hidden from your eyes.
Why does this matter?
This is the only time in the Gospels that Jesus accepted public praise as the king.
He had spent his ministry telling people to keep quiet about who he was.
Now, as he moved toward the cross, he let the praise happen.
But he came as a humble king, riding a donkey, not as the warrior many people wanted.
What happened after?
Within days, the cheering crowd was gone.
Jesus cleared the temple, taught in the courts, and was challenged by the leaders.
By Friday, voices in a crowd were shouting a different word, crucify him.
Many who welcomed a king on Sunday wanted a different kind of king than the one they got.
What does this mean for us today?
We are tempted to want Jesus on our terms, as a king who solves our problems the way we want.
Palm Sunday invites us to welcome him as he is, humble and gentle, and to let him be Lord of our lives.
It also reminds us that he is willing to go to the cross for us.
The donkey was taking him there.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that the King has come, gentle and humble, bringing peace.
And that every Palm Sunday since has been a day to say, hosanna, save us.
tribute: After Jesus entered Jerusalem, the religious leaders were looking for a way to trap him.
The Pharisees went out and laid plans to trap him in his words.
They sent their disciples to him along with the Herodians.
These two groups usually disliked each other.
The Pharisees resented Roman rule, and the Herodians supported Herod and the Romans.
But they were willing to work together against Jesus.
Teacher, they said, we know that you are a man of integrity and that you teach the way of God in accordance with the truth.
You aren't swayed by others, because you pay no attention to who they are.
Tell us then, what is your opinion?
Is it right to pay the imperial tax to Caesar or not?
It began with flattery, and it hid a trap.
If Jesus said yes, he would lose the support of the crowds who hated the tax.
If he said no, he could be reported to Rome as a rebel.
But Jesus knew their evil intent.
Why are you trying to trap me, you hypocrites?
Show me the coin used for paying the tax.
They brought him a denarius, and he asked them, whose image is this? And whose inscription? Caesar's, they replied.
Then he said to them, give back to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's.
When they heard this, they were amazed.
So they left him and went away.
His answer avoided the trap and said something deeper.
The coin had Caesar's face on it, so it was fair to give it back to him.
But people bear another image.
Genesis says that God made human beings in his own image.
If the coin belongs to Caesar because it carries his image, then people belong to God because they carry his.
Why does this matter?
Jesus showed that he was not caught between politics and religion.
He accepted that we have duties to earthly governments, and he put those duties in their place.
The final claim on our lives belongs to God.
What happened after?
The questions kept coming that day.
The Sadducees asked about the resurrection, and a scribe asked which commandment was the greatest. Jesus answered them all.
Then he asked them a question that no one could answer.
After that, no one dared to ask him any more questions.
What does this mean for us today?
Many people feel torn between loyalty to their country and loyalty to their faith.
Jesus says that we can pay our taxes, obey the law and be good citizens, and that none of it replaces what we owe to God.
It also asks us a pointed question.
If the coin has Caesar's image, what bears God's image? We do.
Everything we are belongs to him.
And it is a reminder not to be taken in by flattery, which can be the first step of a trap.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God has the first claim on our lives, because we are made in his image.
And it shows Jesus' wisdom in the face of people who wanted to catch him.
last-supper: It was the first day of the Festival of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed.
Jesus sent Peter and John ahead to prepare the meal.
They found an upper room, large and furnished, just as he had told them.
That evening, Jesus reclined at the table with his twelve disciples.
He said to them, I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.
Passover was the meal that remembered how God rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt, when the blood of a lamb marked the doors and the people were spared.
Jesus was about to give that old meal a new meaning.
During the meal, Jesus got up from the table, took off his outer clothing, and wrapped a towel around his waist.
He poured water into a basin and began to wash his disciples' feet.
This was the job of the lowest servant. Peter objected at first.
Lord, are you going to wash my feet?
Jesus told him that unless he washed him, Peter had no part with him.
When he was done, he said, I have set you an example that you should do as I have done for you.
Then he took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, this is my body given for you.
Do this in remembrance of me.
In the same way, after the supper he took the cup, saying, this cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you.
He was telling them that his death was coming, and that it would be the new way for people to be forgiven and brought to God.
He also told them that one of them would betray him.
They were deeply distressed and each asked, surely you don't mean me, Lord?
He gave them a new command.
A new command I give you. Love one another.
As I have loved you, so you must love one another.
By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.
He told them not to let their hearts be troubled.
In my Father's house are many rooms.
I am going there to prepare a place for you.
And he promised to send the Holy Spirit to be with them.
He said, I am the way and the truth and the life.
No one comes to the Father except through me.
Before they went out, they sang a hymn.
Why does this matter?
This meal is the root of Communion, which Christians have shared ever since.
Jesus took the bread and cup of an old story and showed how he would fulfill it.
He is the Lamb who saves his people.
And it shows his heart in what he did first, which was to wash their feet.
What happened after?
After supper, he led them out to the Garden of Gethsemane, and the events of Good Friday began.
The disciples scattered, but they would gather again after the resurrection, and they continued to break bread together.
What does this mean for us today?
Each time we share Communion, we remember what he did.
It is also a call to serve.
The greatest person in the room knelt to wash feet, and he asks us to do the same.
And it gives us a new commandment that people will recognize his followers by, which is love.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus gave himself willingly for us, and that he left us a meal to remember him by until he returns.
gethsemane: After the Last Supper, Jesus went out with his disciples across the Kidron Valley to a garden on the Mount of Olives called Gethsemane, which means olive press.
It was a place he often went with them.
When he arrived, he said to his disciples, sit here while I go over there and pray.
He took Peter, James and John along with him, and he began to be deeply distressed and troubled.
My soul is overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death, he said to them.
Stay here and keep watch with me.
Notice that Jesus asked for company.
He didn't want to be alone.
Going a little farther, he fell with his face to the ground and prayed, my Father, if it is possible, may this cup be taken from me.
Yet not as I will, but as you will.
Jesus knew what was coming the next day.
The cup stood for the suffering and the judgment that he was about to take.
He was honest with his Father about how hard it was. And he surrendered.
Then he returned to his disciples and found them sleeping.
Could you men not keep watch with me for one hour? he asked Peter.
Watch and pray so that you will not fall into temptation.
The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.
He went away a second time and prayed the same thing.
Again he came back and found them sleeping, because their eyes were heavy.
So he left them and went away once more and prayed the third time, saying the same thing.
Luke, who was a doctor, adds that an angel from heaven appeared to him and strengthened him.
And being in anguish, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat was like drops of blood falling to the ground.
Then he returned to the disciples and said to them, are you still sleeping and resting? Look, the hour has come. Rise, let us go. Here comes my betrayer. He was calm.
The struggle was over, and he was ready.
Why does this matter?
Gethsemane shows the full humanity of Jesus. He wasn't pretending.
He felt sorrow and dread.
And it shows his obedience.
The first Adam, in a garden, chose his own will.
Jesus, in a garden, chose the Father's will.
The result was the road to the cross.
What happened after?
Within minutes, Judas arrived with soldiers, and Jesus was arrested. The disciples fled.
But the prayer in the garden had been answered in a way.
The cup was not taken away, but he was given strength to drink it.
What does this mean for us today?
Jesus teaches us how to pray when things are hard.
We can tell God exactly how we feel and ask for what we want, and then say, not my will but yours.
It also shows that he understands.
When we face something we dread, we pray to someone who has been in that garden.
And it reminds us that the people who love us can fail us when we are most in need. But Jesus never fails.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus willingly accepted the Father's will to save us.
And it gives us a pattern for praying through our own hardest nights.
judas-kiss: While Jesus was still speaking in the garden, a crowd arrived.
It was led by Judas, one of the twelve.
He had been a disciple for three years.
He had heard the teaching and seen the miracles, and he had been trusted with the group's money.
But he had agreed with the chief priests to hand Jesus over for thirty pieces of silver.
That was the price of a slave in the law of Moses.
Judas had given the crowd a signal.
The one I kiss is the man. Arrest him.
A kiss on the cheek was a normal greeting between a student and a teacher.
He had picked the sign of friendship to point out his friend.
Going at once to Jesus, Judas said, greetings, Rabbi! and kissed him.
Jesus replied, friend, do what you came for.
In Luke's account, Jesus asked him, Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?
Even then, Jesus called him friend.
He gave Judas a chance to turn back.
Then the men stepped forward, seized Jesus and arrested him.
One of Jesus' companions, whom John names as Peter, reached for his sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear.
Jesus said, no more of this!
And he touched the man's ear and healed him.
Put your sword back in its place, he said to him, for all who draw the sword will die by the sword.
Do you think I cannot call on my Father, and he will at once put at my disposal more than twelve legions of angels?
But how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that say it must happen in this way?
Then Jesus said to the crowd, am I leading a rebellion, that you have come out with swords and clubs to capture me?
Every day I sat in the temple courts teaching, and you did not arrest me.
But this has all taken place that the writings of the prophets might be fulfilled.
Then all the disciples deserted him and fled.
Why does this matter? Jesus was not captured. He gave himself up.
He had the power to stop it and chose not to.
He also showed love in the middle of betrayal, healing a wounded enemy and calling his betrayer friend.
And everything happened according to what the prophets had written.
What happened after?
Judas was filled with remorse when he saw that Jesus was condemned.
He tried to return the money, but the priests wouldn't take it.
He threw it down in the temple and left.
His story ended in despair.
The Bible doesn't hide how heavy that is.
Peter also failed that night, but his story went on to forgiveness.
What does this mean for us today?
Betrayal by someone close is among the deepest pains there is, and Jesus knows that pain.
He also shows us how to respond, without revenge, and still reaching out. And it is a warning.
Judas was close to Jesus and still betrayed him.
Being near religious things is not the same as trusting him.
We need to guard our hearts.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus went to the cross willingly, even when betrayed by a friend.
And it shows a love that does not stop at betrayal.
peter-denies: After Jesus was arrested, they led him to the house of the high priest Caiaphas.
Peter followed at a distance.
John, another disciple, got him into the courtyard.
It was a cold night, and the servants and officials stood around a fire they had made.
Peter joined them and sat down to warm himself.
Earlier that night, Peter had been very confident.
At the Last Supper, he had said, even if all fall away on account of you, I never will.
Jesus had told him, truly I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows, you will disown me three times.
Peter insisted, even if I have to die with you, I will never disown you.
All the other disciples said the same.
Now a servant girl saw him sitting there in the firelight.
She looked closely at him and said, this man was with him. But he denied it. Woman, I don't know him.
A little later someone else saw him and said, you also are one of them.
Man, I am not, Peter replied.
About an hour later, another one insisted, certainly this fellow was with him, for he is a Galilean.
Peter replied, man, I don't know what you're talking about.
Just as he was speaking, the rooster crowed.
The Lord turned and looked straight at Peter.
Luke tells us this detail.
Jesus was being led through the courtyard at that moment.
Then Peter remembered the word the Lord had spoken to him.
Before the rooster crows today, you will disown me three times.
And he went outside and wept bitterly.
Why does this matter?
Peter was not a coward by nature.
He had stepped out of a boat onto the water and drawn a sword against a crowd.
But in a moment of fear, he failed.
The story is honest about how even the closest followers of Jesus can fall.
Peter's confidence was the thing that failed him.
What happened after?
After the resurrection, Jesus appeared to his disciples by the Sea of Galilee.
By a charcoal fire, he asked Peter three times, do you love me?
Peter, hurt, answered each time, Lord, you know all things.
You know that I love you.
Each time, Jesus said, feed my sheep.
The three denials were matched by three affirmations, and Peter was restored.
Fifty days later, he stood up in Jerusalem and preached boldly to thousands.
What does this mean for us today?
We all have moments we are not proud of, times we said we would stand firm and didn't.
Peter's story says that failure is not the end.
Jesus had said in advance, I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith may not fail.
And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.
Jesus knew Peter would fail, and he planned for his return.
The tears of Peter were the start of a deeper faith.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus forgives and restores people who have failed him.
And it gives hope to every follower who has fallen short.
thorns: The night Jesus was arrested, he was brought before the Jewish council and then taken to the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate.
Pilate questioned him and said he found no basis for a charge.
But the crowd, stirred up by the religious leaders, kept demanding that Jesus be put to death.
Pilate was afraid of losing control.
Then Pilate took Jesus and had him flogged.
The soldiers of the governor then took Jesus into the Praetorium and gathered the whole company of soldiers around him.
They stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him.
Then they twisted together a crown of thorns and set it on his head.
They put a staff in his right hand.
Kneeling in front of him, they mocked him.
Hail, king of the Jews! they said.
They spit on him, and took the staff and struck him on the head again and again.
After they had mocked him, they took off the robe and put his own clothes on him.
This is hard to read.
The soldiers were treating Jesus as a joke, a pretend king.
They wanted to humiliate him.
But what they did was more true than they knew.
He was a king, and he was wearing a crown.
The thorns were a sign of the curse that came into the world through human sin.
In Genesis, God said that the ground would produce thorns and thistles.
Jesus took the curse on his own head.
John adds, once more Pilate came out and said to the Jews gathered there, look, I am bringing him out to you to let you know that I find no basis for a charge against him.
Jesus came out wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe.
Why does this matter?
The prophet Isaiah had written about a servant who would be despised and rejected, a man of suffering.
He was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities.
By his wounds we are healed.
Jesus did not endure this because he was weak.
He had the power to stop it, and he stayed.
He endured it for the sake of the people who mocked him.
What happened after?
Jesus was led out to be crucified, and it was a crown of thorns that he wore on the road.
The kingdom he came to establish was not like the kingdoms of this world.
He had told Pilate, my kingdom is not of this world.
If it were, my servants would fight to prevent my arrest.
A kingdom built on love, forgiveness and sacrifice looked like weakness, but it has changed the world.
What does this mean for us today?
When we feel mocked or humiliated, we can remember that Jesus has been there. He understands.
He wasn't angry at his tormentors.
Later he would pray, Father, forgive them.
And the crown of thorns invites us to look at what real kingship is. It isn't force or fame.
It is a willingness to give yourself for others.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus took our shame and our curse on himself, and that the King of kings was crowned with thorns for us.
ecce-homo: Pilate had tried several ways to avoid condemning Jesus.
He had questioned him, sent him to Herod, and offered to release him in place of a prisoner.
Now he brought Jesus out in front of the crowd, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe.
Pilate said to them, here is the man! In Latin, ecce homo. Behold the man.
He may have hoped the sight of Jesus would stir pity.
The man in front of them was bruised and bleeding and exhausted.
But when the chief priests and their officials saw him, they shouted, crucify! Crucify!
Pilate said, you take him and crucify him.
As for me, I find no basis for a charge against him.
The Jewish leaders insisted, we have a law, and according to that law he must die, because he claimed to be the Son of God.
When Pilate heard this, he was even more afraid.
He took Jesus back inside the palace and asked him, where do you come from?
But Jesus gave him no answer.
Do you refuse to speak to me? Pilate said.
Don't you realize I have power either to free you or to crucify you?
Jesus answered, you would have no power over me if it were not given to you from above.
From then on, Pilate tried to set Jesus free, but the crowd kept shouting, if you let this man go, you are no friend of Caesar.
Anyone who claims to be a king opposes Caesar.
When Pilate heard this, he brought Jesus out.
Here is your king, Pilate said. Take him away!
Crucify him! shouted the crowd.
Shall I crucify your king? Pilate asked.
We have no king but Caesar, the chief priests answered.
Finally Pilate handed Jesus over to them to be crucified.
Why does this matter?
Pilate said more than he knew when he said, behold the man.
Here was the true human being, the one who showed what humanity was made to be, and he was being rejected by the people he came to save.
Pilate also illustrates a danger.
He knew that Jesus was innocent, and he still gave in to pressure.
What happened after?
Jesus was led away, carrying his cross.
The words that Pilate spoke were remembered.
Later, he even had a sign written and placed on the cross that said, Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.
It was written in three languages, so that everyone could read it.
The chief priests protested, but Pilate said, what I have written, I have written.
What does this mean for us today?
We are all asked to look at Jesus and decide what to do with him.
Pilate tried to stay neutral, but there is no neutral.
We also learn how easy it is to know what is right and still choose what is convenient, out of fear of the crowd.
And the phrase, behold the man, still invites us to look at Jesus and see what love looks like when it costs everything.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus was innocent, and that he accepted rejection so that we could be accepted. Behold the man. Behold the Lamb of God.
calvary: Jesus was led out of Jerusalem, carrying his own cross.
A man named Simon from Cyrene, who was coming in from the countryside, was forced to carry it behind Jesus.
A large number of people followed him, including women who mourned and wailed for him.
Jesus turned to them and said, daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me.
Weep for yourselves and for your children.
Even on the way to the cross, he was thinking of others.
They came to a place called Golgotha, which means the place of the skull. Luke calls it the Skull.
It was outside the city walls, where the Romans carried out executions.
There they crucified him, along with two criminals, one on his right and one on his left.
Jesus was placed in the middle.
The Gospels are quiet about the details.
They tell it plainly and don't dwell on the pain.
They were more concerned with what it meant.
Pilate had a notice prepared and fastened to the cross.
It read, Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.
Many of the Jews read this sign, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city.
It was written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek.
The soldiers divided up his clothes by casting lots.
This was what Psalm 22 had said a thousand years earlier.
They divided my clothes among them and cast lots for my garment.
The people stood watching, and the rulers even sneered at him.
He saved others, they said, let him save himself if he is God's Messiah, the Chosen One.
The soldiers mocked him too.
If you are the king of the Jews, save yourself.
Why does this matter?
The cross is at the center of the Christian faith.
Everything before it leads to it, and everything after flows from it.
The Bible says that God demonstrates his own love for us in this.
While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
The one who made the world gave himself for it.
What happened after?
Jesus spoke from the cross several times.
He prayed for those who crucified him.
He promised paradise to a man next to him who asked to be remembered. He cared for his mother.
And he finished the work he came to do.
What does this mean for us today?
The cross shows how serious sin is and how great God's love is.
We don't have to carry our guilt anymore, because Jesus has carried it.
It also gives dignity to our own suffering.
God does not stand far away from pain. He entered it.
And it invites us to do what Simon of Cyrene did, who picked up the cross when Jesus needed help.
We follow Jesus by carrying our own cross, and by helping to carry the burdens of others.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus gave his life for us, out of love.
