And it is the place where the world's worst sin met God's greatest mercy.
nailed: As Jesus hung on the cross, he spoke.
The first words recorded are among the most remarkable ever spoken.
Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.
Think about who he was praying for.
The soldiers who carried out the crucifixion.
The religious leaders who had pushed for it.
The crowd who had shouted for it.
The people who mocked him as he hung there.
Jesus had told his followers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them.
Now he did it himself, at the moment of greatest pain.
The soldiers didn't understand what they were doing.
They were just doing their job.
The leaders did not see that this was the Messiah.
Peter later said, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders.
Jesus asked the Father to forgive them, and that prayer reached further than anyone could see.
The people stood watching, and the rulers sneered.
One of the criminals who hung there hurled insults at him. Aren't you the Messiah? Save yourself and us!
But the other criminal rebuked him.
Don't you fear God, since you are under the same sentence?
We are punished justly, for we are getting what our deeds deserve.
But this man has done nothing wrong.
Then he said, Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.
Jesus answered him, truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise.
The man had done nothing to earn it.
He had no time to be baptized, to change his life or to do good works.
He simply asked, and Jesus gave.
Why does this matter?
The cross shows forgiveness before anyone asks for it.
Jesus didn't wait for apologies.
And the thief shows that it is never too late to turn to Jesus.
A man who had spent his life on the wrong side was promised paradise in his last hours.
What happened after?
Many of the people who had joined in the mocking would later hear Peter preach on the day of Pentecost, and thousands of them believed.
The prayer, Father, forgive them, was answered.
What does this mean for us today?
Is there someone you find hard to forgive?
Jesus shows that forgiveness can come even in the middle of the wrong.
It doesn't mean pretending it didn't matter.
It means refusing to let hatred take over.
And is there something in your own life that you think is too big to be forgiven?
The thief on the cross says no.
All he said was, remember me. And it was enough.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus forgives even those who put him on the cross, and that salvation is a free gift for anyone who asks.
And it shows his heart in the worst hour of his life.
darkness-cross: It was about noon, and darkness came over the whole land until three in the afternoon, for the sun stopped shining.
In the middle of the day, in the middle of the crucifixion, the sky went dark.
The Old Testament prophet Amos had written about a day when God would make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight.
About three in the afternoon, Jesus cried out in a loud voice, Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani? which means, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
These are the opening words of Psalm 22, a psalm that begins in anguish and ends in praise.
He was feeling the full weight of what he had come to bear.
Some of the bystanders heard him and thought he was calling Elijah.
Later, knowing that everything had now been finished, and so that Scripture would be fulfilled, Jesus said, I am thirsty.
A jar of wine vinegar was there, so they soaked a sponge in it, put the sponge on a stalk of the hyssop plant, and lifted it to Jesus' lips.
When he had received the drink, Jesus said, it is finished.
Then he called out with a loud voice, Father, into your hands I commit my spirit.
With that, he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
It is finished.
In the Greek, it is a single word.
It was used in the ancient world when a debt was paid in full.
The work Jesus came to do was complete.
He had lived the life we could not live and borne the debt we could not pay.
At that moment the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.
This heavy curtain had separated the Most Holy Place, where God's presence dwelled, from the rest of the temple.
Only the high priest could enter, once a year.
Now it was torn from the top, as if by God's own hand.
The way into God's presence was open.
The earth shook, the rocks split, and the tombs broke open.
When the centurion, the Roman officer in charge of the crucifixion, and those with him saw what had happened, they were terrified and exclaimed, surely he was the Son of God!
The crowd that had gathered went away beating their breasts.
The women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance and watched.
Why does this matter?
These are the most important hours in history.
The darkness, the cry and the torn curtain all point to one thing.
Jesus bore the judgment for sin, and the barrier between God and people was removed.
And the first person to say who he was, was a Roman soldier.
What happened after?
Joseph of Arimathea took the body down, and Jesus was buried.
The disciples hid in fear.
But the story was not over.
What does this mean for us today?
When we feel abandoned by God, we are not the first.
Jesus prayed the same words, and he knows what it is like.
It also means that we don't need to earn our way to God. It is finished.
Nothing is left for us to add.
We can come with confidence, because the curtain has been torn.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus completed our salvation, and that the way to God is now open to all. It is finished.
dead-christ: Evening was approaching, and it was the day of Preparation, the day before the Sabbath.
The Jewish law required that bodies not remain on crosses overnight during the Sabbath.
A man named Joseph came from the Judean town of Arimathea.
He was a rich man and a respected member of the Jewish council.
Luke tells us he was a good and upright man, who had not consented to the council's decision and action.
He was a secret disciple of Jesus, because he feared the Jewish leaders.
Now, however, Joseph found courage.
He went boldly to Pilate and asked for Jesus' body.
Pilate was surprised to hear that Jesus was already dead.
He called the centurion and made sure.
When he learned it from the centurion, he gave the body to Joseph.
Joseph took the body down.
He was joined by Nicodemus, the man who had first visited Jesus at night.
Nicodemus brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds.
Taking Jesus' body, the two of them wrapped it, with the spices, in strips of linen, as was the Jewish burial custom.
It was a costly and loving act, the kind given to a king.
At the place where Jesus was crucified, there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb, in which no one had yet been laid.
It was Joseph's own tomb, cut out of rock.
Because it was the Jewish day of Preparation and since the tomb was nearby, they laid Jesus there.
Joseph rolled a big stone in front of the entrance to the tomb and went away.
Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were sitting there opposite the tomb.
The women who had come with Jesus from Galilee followed Joseph and saw the tomb and how his body was laid in it.
Then they went home and prepared spices and perfumes.
But they rested on the Sabbath in obedience to the commandment.
The next day, the chief priests and the Pharisees went to Pilate.
They remembered that Jesus had said that after three days he would rise again.
So they asked that the tomb be made secure.
Pilate said, take a guard.
Make the tomb as secure as you know how.
So they went and made the tomb secure by putting a seal on the stone and posting the guard.
Why does this matter?
Two respected men who had been afraid to speak up came forward in the darkest hour.
They stood up when the twelve had run away.
And the burial confirms that Jesus really died.
It was a real death and a real tomb, so the resurrection would be a real resurrection.
Isaiah had said that he would be assigned a grave with the wicked and with the rich in his death.
It was fulfilled in Joseph's tomb.
What happened after?
The disciples spent a quiet and heartbroken Sabbath.
They thought it was over.
But on the third day, early in the morning, the women came to the tomb and found the stone rolled away.
What does this mean for us today?
Sometimes God's silence is not his absence.
The Saturday between the cross and the empty tomb was the longest day for his followers, and God was still at work.
It also shows that it is never too late to step out of the shadows and act on your faith.
Joseph and Nicodemus found their courage when it mattered.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus truly died for us, and that even the grave could not hold him.
And it sets the stage for the greatest morning in history.
ascension: After his suffering, Jesus presented himself to his disciples and gave many convincing proofs that he was alive.
He appeared to them over a period of forty days and spoke about the kingdom of God.
He ate with them, let them touch him, and opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.
Those weeks changed frightened, scattered men into witnesses.
On one occasion, while he was eating with them, he gave them this command.
Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait for the gift my Father promised, which you have heard me speak about.
For John baptized with water, but in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.
So when they met together, they asked him, Lord, are you at this time going to restore the kingdom to Israel?
They were still thinking about politics.
Jesus answered, it is not for you to know the times or dates the Father has set by his own authority.
But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.
After he said this, he was taken up before their very eyes, and a cloud hid him from their sight.
They were looking intently up into the sky as he was going, when suddenly two men dressed in white stood beside them.
Men of Galilee, they said, why do you stand here looking into the sky?
This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen him go into heaven.
Luke ends his gospel with the same event.
While he was blessing them, he left them and was taken up into heaven.
Then they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy.
And they stayed continually at the temple, praising God.
There was joy, not sadness.
They knew he was alive and reigning.
Why does this matter?
The Ascension means that Jesus is now seated at the right hand of the Father.
He reigns over everything.
It also means that a human being is now in heaven, which is a promise for all who belong to him.
And it was needed so that the Holy Spirit could come.
Jesus had told them that it was for their good that he was going away.
What happened after?
Ten days later, on the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit came on the believers with wind and fire.
Peter preached, and three thousand people were added to the church that day.
The disciples began to carry the message from Jerusalem outward, just as Jesus had said.
What does this mean for us today?
Jesus' last words were not about heaven.
They were about the work.
We are called to be witnesses where we live, in our own Jerusalem, and as far as we can reach.
We are not left alone, since he gave us the Spirit.
And the angels' words are a promise. He will return.
We live between the Ascension and his return, trusting, working and waiting.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that Jesus is the risen and ruling Lord, and that he sends his followers to carry his message to the whole world.
stephen: In the early church in Jerusalem, a man named Stephen stood out.
The apostles chose him as one of seven men to oversee the care of widows who were being overlooked in the daily distribution of food.
He was full of faith and of the Holy Spirit.
Acts says that he was full of God's grace and power, and he performed great wonders and signs among the people.
Some men from a synagogue began to argue with Stephen, but they could not stand up against the wisdom the Spirit gave him as he spoke.
So they secretly persuaded some men to say they had heard Stephen speak words of blasphemy.
They stirred up the people, the elders and the teachers of the law.
They seized Stephen and brought him before the Sanhedrin.
At that, all who were sitting in the Sanhedrin looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
The high priest asked him if the charges were true.
Stephen gave a long speech, going through Israel's history from Abraham, to Joseph, to Moses, to the temple.
His point was that the people had always resisted God's messengers.
You stiff-necked people! he said.
You are just like your ancestors.
Was there ever a prophet your ancestors did not persecute?
They even killed those who predicted the coming of the Righteous One.
And now you have betrayed and murdered him.
When the members of the Sanhedrin heard this, they were furious.
But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
Look, he said, I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.
Usually Jesus is described as seated at God's right hand.
Here he stands, as if rising to welcome his servant.
At this they covered their ears and, yelling at the top of their voices, they all rushed at him.
They dragged him out of the city and began to stone him.
Meanwhile, the witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul.
While they were stoning him, Stephen prayed, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.
Then he fell on his knees and cried out, Lord, do not hold this sin against them.
When he had said this, he fell asleep.
Why does this matter?
Stephen was the first Christian martyr.
His death echoed the death of Jesus.
He prayed for his killers as Jesus had, and he committed his spirit to the Lord.
And the word the Bible uses for his death is that he fell asleep.
For believers, death is not the end.
What happened after?
A great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and the believers scattered throughout Judea and Samaria.
But as they went, they preached the gospel wherever they were.
The young man named Saul, who held the coats, was there.
He would soon be knocked to the ground on the road to Damascus, meet the risen Jesus, and become the apostle Paul.
Some have wondered whether Stephen's prayer was part of the reason.
What does this mean for us today?
Few of us will be asked to give our lives, but we may be asked to speak up for the truth, and Stephen's calm and courage give us a model. He was not bitter. He forgave.
And his story shows that God can bring good out of the worst events.
The church was scattered, and the gospel spread further.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that faithfulness may cost everything, and that the Lord is near to those who suffer for him.
And it shows the power of forgiveness in the face of hatred.
cornelius: In the city of Caesarea lived a Roman army officer named Cornelius.
He was a centurion, in charge of about a hundred soldiers.
He was not Jewish, but he was devout.
He and all his family feared God.
He gave generously to those in need and prayed to God regularly.
One afternoon, Cornelius had a vision.
He saw an angel of God, who said to him, Cornelius!
Your prayers and gifts to the poor have come up as a memorial offering before God.
Now send men to Joppa to bring back a man named Simon who is called Peter.
He is staying with Simon the tanner, whose house is by the sea.
Cornelius sent two servants and a soldier to find him.
The next day, as they approached Joppa, Peter went up on the roof to pray.
He was hungry, and while the meal was being prepared, he fell into a trance.
He saw heaven opened and something like a large sheet being let down to earth by its four corners.
It contained all kinds of animals, including some that the Jewish law said were unclean.
Then a voice told him, get up, Peter. Kill and eat. Surely not, Lord! Peter replied.
I have never eaten anything impure or unclean.
The voice spoke to him a second time.
Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.
This happened three times, and immediately the sheet was taken back to heaven.
While Peter was wondering what the vision meant, the men sent by Cornelius arrived.
The Spirit told him, simon, three men are looking for you.
Go with them, for I have sent them.
Peter went with them to Caesarea.
Cornelius had gathered his relatives and close friends.
When Peter entered the house, Cornelius fell at his feet in reverence. Peter made him get up.
Stand up, I am only a man myself.
Then Peter said, you are well aware that it is against our law for a Jew to associate with or visit a Gentile.
But God has shown me that I should not call anyone impure or unclean.
So when I was sent for, I came without raising any objection.
May I ask why you sent for me? Cornelius explained.
Then Peter began to speak.
I now realize how true it is that God does not show favoritism, but accepts from every nation the one who fears him and does what is right.
He told them about Jesus, who had gone about doing good and healing, whom God raised from the dead.
While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit came on all who heard the message.
The Jewish believers who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on Gentiles.
So Peter ordered that they be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.
Why does this matter?
This is the moment the gospel crossed the line from the Jewish world to the whole world. It was a huge change.
God was making it clear that his love was for everyone.
What happened after?
Peter went back to Jerusalem, and some believers criticized him for eating with Gentiles. He explained everything.
When they heard it, they praised God and said, so then, even to Gentiles God has granted repentance that leads to life.
What does this mean for us today?
We all have people we think are outside.
God invites us to see them differently.
It also shows how God arranges meetings.
He spoke to Cornelius and to Peter at the same time, so each was ready for the other.
And it reminds us that most of us are descendants of this moment.
The gospel reached us because Peter said yes.
That is why this story is so important.
It says that God shows no favoritism, and that the good news of Jesus is for every nation.
peter-escape: By this time, the church in Jerusalem was growing, and trouble was growing with it.
King Herod Agrippa, a grandson of the Herod who tried to kill baby Jesus, wanted to win favor with the Jewish leaders.
He arrested some members of the church and had James, the brother of John, killed with a sword.
James was one of the first three disciples, and one of Jesus' closest friends.
When Herod saw that this pleased the people, he arrested Peter too.
This happened during the Festival of Unleavened Bread, around Passover.
Herod planned to put Peter on trial after the festival.
Peter was put in prison and guarded by four squads of four soldiers each.
That means sixteen men, watching him in shifts.
The night before the trial, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and there were guards at the door. There was no way out. Herod made sure of it.
But the Bible says, the church was earnestly praying to God for him.
That is the most important sentence in the story.
The believers did not have a plan, an army, or any power. They had prayer.
Suddenly an angel of the Lord appeared, and a light shone in the cell.
He struck Peter on the side and woke him up.
Quick, get up! he said, and the chains fell off Peter's wrists.
The angel told him, put on your clothes and sandals. Peter did.
Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.
Peter followed him out of the prison, but he had no idea that what the angel was doing was really happening.
He thought he was seeing a vision.
They passed the first and second guards and came to the iron gate leading to the city.
It opened for them by itself, and they went through it.
When they had walked the length of one street, suddenly the angel left him.
Then Peter came to himself and said, now I know without a doubt that the Lord sent his angel and rescued me from Herod's clutches and from everything the Jewish people were anticipating.
Peter went to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where many people had gathered and were praying.
He knocked at the outer entrance, and a servant named Rhoda came to answer the door.
When she recognized Peter's voice, she was so overjoyed she forgot to open it.
Instead she ran back and exclaimed, Peter is at the door!
You're out of your mind, they told her.
When she kept insisting, they said, it must be his angel.
But Peter kept on knocking, and when they opened the door and saw him, they were astonished.
It is a funny moment, and an honest one.
These people had been praying all night for Peter's release, and when God answered, they could hardly believe it.
Peter motioned for them to be quiet and described how the Lord had brought him out of prison.
Tell James and the other brothers and sisters about this, he said.
Then he left for another place.
In the morning, there was no small commotion among the soldiers about what had become of Peter.
Herod had a thorough search made, and when he did not find him, he cross-examined the guards and ordered that they be executed.
Soon after, Herod gave a speech, and the people shouted, this is the voice of a god, not of a man.
Immediately, because Herod did not give praise to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down, and he was eaten by worms and died.
But the word of God continued to spread and flourish.
Why does this matter?
Two apostles were arrested by the same king.
One, James, was put to death.
The other, Peter, was set free.
The Bible does not explain why.
It shows us that God's ways are not always the same, and that both stories are part of his plan.
We don't get to know why one is rescued and another is not.
But both are in his hands.
It also shows the power of the church praying together.
They didn't have influence or weapons.
They had one another and God.
The same Peter who denied Jesus and ran away now slept peacefully in chains, the night before a trial that could have ended in his death.
What happened after?
Peter left Jerusalem, and we see less of him in the book of Acts.
Tradition says that he eventually went to Rome.
The Bible doesn't say exactly, but tradition has said that he was put to death there, as Jesus had said he would be. The church kept growing.
What does this mean for us today?
When something looks hopeless, pray.
Not as a last resort, but as a first response.
The believers in this story didn't know the outcome.
They prayed anyway, through the night, while the chains were still on.
And when God answers, don't be surprised if you find it hard to believe, like Rhoda's friends.
That is a very human thing.
God is gracious to people who ask, and a little slow to believe.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that the power of earthly kings is limited.
Herod had soldiers, chains, and iron gates, and none of it held.
The church's greatest strength was a prayer meeting in a house.
paul-prison: Paul and his friend Silas had come to Philippi, a Roman city in Macedonia, in what is now Greece.
They had come because of a vision.
Paul saw a man from Macedonia begging him, come over to Macedonia and help us.
On the Sabbath, they went to a place of prayer by the river, and spoke to some women who had gathered there.
One of them, a businesswoman named Lydia, who sold purple cloth, listened.
The Lord opened her heart, and she and her household were baptized.
Philippi had its first church.
Soon after, they met a slave girl who had a spirit by which she predicted the future.
She earned a great deal of money for her owners by fortune-telling.
She followed Paul and the rest of them, shouting, these men are servants of the Most High God, who are telling you the way to be saved.
She did this for many days.
Finally Paul became so troubled that he turned around and said to the spirit, in the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her!
At that moment it left her.
When her owners realized that their hope of making money was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace to face the authorities.
These men are Jews, and are throwing our city into an uproar by advocating customs unlawful for us Romans to adopt.
A crowd joined in the attack.
The magistrates ordered them to be stripped and beaten with rods.
After they had been severely flogged, they were thrown into prison, and the jailer was commanded to guard them carefully.
Receiving such orders, he put them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in the stocks.
Think about the picture.
Paul and Silas had done nothing wrong.
They had brought healing to a girl, and they had been beaten, bleeding, and chained in the darkest cell in the city. And what did they do?
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was such a violent earthquake that the foundations of the prison were shaken.
At once all the prison doors flew open, and everyone's chains came loose.
The jailer woke up, and when he saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself because he thought the prisoners had escaped.
In the Roman world, a jailer who lost his prisoners could be executed.
But Paul shouted, don't harm yourself! We are all here!
The jailer called for lights, rushed in, and fell trembling before Paul and Silas.
He then brought them out and asked, sirs, what must I do to be saved?
They replied, believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.
Then they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all the others in his house.
At that hour of the night, the jailer took them and washed their wounds.
Then immediately he and all his household were baptized.
The jailer brought them into his house and set a meal before them.
He was filled with joy because he had come to believe in God, he and his whole household.
In the morning the magistrates sent word to release them.
But Paul said, they beat us publicly without a trial, even though we are Roman citizens, and threw us into prison.
And now do they want to get rid of us quietly? No!
Let them come themselves and escort us out.
When the officials heard that Paul and Silas were Roman citizens, they were alarmed.
They came to appease them and escorted them out of the prison, requesting them to leave the city.
Why does this matter?
Paul and Silas chose to sing in the dark.
They didn't know there would be an earthquake.
They sang before the answer came.
Their joy didn't depend on the circumstances.
It is one of the best pictures of faith in the New Testament.
Later Paul would write to the church at Philippi, from another prison, rejoice in the Lord always.
I will say it again, rejoice!
It also shows how God uses hard places.
The jailer and his family would never have heard the gospel if Paul had not been put in that cell.
A beating, chains, and a night in the stocks led to a whole family coming to Jesus.
What happened after?
The church in Philippi grew and stayed close to Paul.
They were the one church that sent him money again and again.
Paul's letter to the Philippians is a letter of thanks and joy, written to the church that began with a businesswoman, a freed slave girl, and a jailer.
What does this mean for us today?
When life puts you in the inner cell, with no way out, you still have a choice about what to do at midnight.
Praise doesn't change the walls.
But it changes you, and the people listening.
The other prisoners heard them.
It also gives the simplest answer to the most important question in the Bible.
What must I do to be saved?
Believe in the Lord Jesus.
It is no more complicated than that, and the jailer was baptized that very night.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows that God is at work in our worst nights, and that the gospel is for anyone, from a rich businesswoman to a rough jailer.
And it shows that the song of a believer can make a prison tremble.
thessalonica: After Philippi, Paul and Silas traveled about a hundred miles west along a great Roman road, the Via Egnatia, and came to Thessalonica.
It was the capital of Macedonia, a busy port city.
There was a Jewish synagogue there, and as was his custom, Paul went in.
On three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, explaining and proving that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead.
This Jesus I am proclaiming to you is the Messiah, he said.
Some of the Jews were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a large number of God-fearing Greeks and not a few prominent women.
These were people who were interested in the God of Israel but were not Jewish themselves.
For them, this message of grace was good news.
But other Jews were jealous.
They rounded up some bad characters from the marketplace, formed a mob, and started a riot in the city.
They rushed to Jason's house, where Paul and Silas had been staying, in search of them.
When they didn't find them, they dragged Jason and some other believers before the city officials, shouting, these men who have caused trouble all over the world have now come here!
Jason has welcomed them into his house.
They are all defying Caesar's decrees, saying that there is another king, one called Jesus.
The charge was partly true.
The Christians did say that Jesus was king.
But they were not rebelling against Rome.
Their loyalty to Jesus was just deeper than any other loyalty.
Jason had to post bond, and the city officials let them go.
That night, the believers sent Paul and Silas away to Berea.
Notice the line, men who have caused trouble all over the world.
Other translations say, these men who have turned the world upside down.
A few men, with no weapons and no army, had so changed the lives of the people they met that their opponents said the world was being turned upside down.

In Berea, the Jews were of more noble character than those in Thessalonica, for they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if what Paul said was true. Many of them believed.
But when some Jews from Thessalonica heard that Paul was preaching in Berea, they went there to stir up the crowds.
So Paul had to move on to Athens.
Paul was worried about the new believers he had left behind.
He wrote to them from Corinth, and the letter, First Thessalonians, is probably the oldest book in the New Testament.
In it he said, we always thank God for all of you.
We remember before our God and Father your work produced by faith, your labor prompted by love, and your endurance inspired by hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.
You became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you welcomed the message in the midst of severe suffering with the joy given by the Holy Spirit.
He also gave them hope about the ones who had died.
Brothers and sisters, we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you do not grieve like the rest of mankind, who have no hope.
For we believe that Jesus died and rose again, and so we believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in him.
Why does this matter?
Thessalonica shows what the first church was like.
These were new believers, in a hostile city, with a few weeks of teaching.
And they became a model church.
The faith they had was real, and they were willing to suffer for it.
It also shows that the gospel goes forward in the face of opposition, and often because of it.
The Bereans are a model too.
They did not just accept what Paul said.
They checked it against the Bible every day.
That is exactly how we should hear any teacher, with eagerness, and with the Scriptures open.
What happened after?
Paul went on to Athens and Corinth, and the church at Thessalonica kept growing.
Paul wrote them a second letter.
They remained one of the churches he was most proud of.
Today, the city is still there, called Thessaloniki, one of the largest cities in Greece.
What does this mean for us today?
Do you want to turn the world upside down?
Most of the people who did it in the first century were ordinary.
They worked at jobs, opened their homes, and told people about Jesus.
A few of them, like Jason, took risks to host a meeting.
It also means we have hope in grief.
Paul told them not to grieve like people who have no hope.
When someone we love who belonged to Jesus dies, we will see them again.
That promise is not a small thing.
That is why this story is so important.
It shows the gospel arriving in a new city, and how the first believers lived.
They were joyful, brave, and clear about their hope.
And it reminds us that when the Word is believed, the world is never quite the same.
patmos: John was the last of the twelve apostles still alive.
He had been the young disciple Jesus loved, who leaned against him at the Last Supper and stood at the foot of the cross.
Jesus had trusted him to look after his mother.
Now he was an old man, probably in his nineties, and he had spent decades leading the churches around Ephesus, in what is now Turkey.
Peter, James, and Paul were all long gone.
Nearly all of the other apostles had been put to death for their faith.
Now there was a new wave of persecution.
The Roman emperor Domitian demanded that people call him lord and god, and Christians refused.
They would not say anyone but Jesus was Lord.
Because of this, John was arrested and sent into exile on Patmos, a small, rocky island in the Aegean Sea, about forty miles off the coast.
It was a place the Romans sent prisoners.
He was there because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.
Think about what this must have been like.
John was old, alone, and cut off from the churches he had cared for.
He had lost his friends and his freedom.
It could have been the worst time of his life.
But it was on this island that John received one of the most amazing experiences in the Bible.
On the Lord's Day, which was Sunday, John was in the Spirit.
He heard behind him a loud voice like a trumpet, which said, write on a scroll what you see and send it to the seven churches.
He turned around to see the voice that was speaking to him.
And when he turned, he saw seven golden lampstands, and among the lampstands was someone like a son of man, dressed in a robe reaching down to his feet.
His head and hair were white like wool, as white as snow, and his eyes were like blazing fire.
His feet were like bronze glowing in a furnace, and his voice was like the sound of rushing waters.
In his right hand he held seven stars, and out of his mouth came a sharp, double-edged sword.
His face was like the sun shining in all its brilliance.
It was Jesus, but not the Jesus John remembered from Galilee.
This was the risen and glorified Lord.
John had known him as a friend, and had rested his head on his chest.
Now when he saw him, he fell at his feet as though dead.
Then Jesus placed his right hand on John and said, do not be afraid.
I am the First and the Last. I am the Living One.
I was dead, and now look, I am alive forever and ever!
And I hold the keys of death and Hades.
These are the words that John needed most in exile.
Whoever holds the keys of death is not afraid of Rome.
Jesus then told John to write down what he saw.
First were letters to seven churches in Asia, with praise for what they were doing well and warnings about what they needed to fix.
To the church at Ephesus, you have forsaken the love you had at first.
To Smyrna, be faithful, even to the point of death, and I will give you life as your victor's crown. To Laodicea, here I am!
I stand at the door and knock.
If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in and eat with that person, and they with me.
Why does this matter?
This is the beginning of the book of Revelation, the last book in the Bible.
It was written to encourage persecuted Christians.
They were being told that the emperor was lord, and Jesus told them, no, I am.
The seven churches were small and weak, but they were in his hand, and he walked among them.
It also shows that God does not abandon his people in the worst places.
John was banished to the end of the earth, and that was where Jesus appeared to him.
What happened after?
John wrote down everything he saw, the visions of heaven, the final battle, and the new heaven and new earth.
He sent it to the churches.
Tradition says that after Domitian died, John was released and went back to Ephesus, where he died of old age.
He was the only apostle who did not die as a martyr.
The Bible doesn't say this exactly, but tradition has said it.
What does this mean for us today?
If you are in your own Patmos, a place of exile, loneliness, or loss, you are not out of reach.
Jesus found John on a rocky island, and he finds people in hospital rooms, empty houses, and hard seasons.
It also means that the one who holds the keys to death is not just a memory. He is alive.
And his first words to a frightened old man are the words he says to us. Do not be afraid.
That is why this story is so important.
It opens the last book of the Bible with a picture of Jesus as he is now, living, ruling, and walking among his people.
No emperor is above him, and no island is beyond him.
new-jerusalem: The Bible ends with a vision of the future.
John, exiled on Patmos, was shown the end of the story, and he wrote it down for all of us.
After many visions of judgment and the defeat of evil, he saw something new.
Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and there was no longer any sea.
The old world is gone.
The world that was broken by sin, filled with pain, war, and death, has given way to something new.
And then John saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband.
This is the opposite of Babel.
The people tried to build a tower up to heaven, and failed.
Here, God brings the city down to us.
John heard a loud voice from the throne saying, look!
God's dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them.
They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God.
He will wipe every tear from their eyes.
There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away.
Read that slowly.
He will wipe every tear from their eyes.
Not a general feeling of comfort, but a personal act.
God himself, close enough to wipe away tears.
He who was seated on the throne said, I am making everything new!
Then he said, write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true. He said, it is done.
I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End.
To the thirsty I will give water without cost from the spring of the water of life.
Those who are victorious will inherit all this, and I will be their God and they will be my children.
An angel then showed John the city.
It shone with the glory of God, and its brilliance was like that of a very precious jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal.
It had a great, high wall with twelve gates, with twelve angels at the gates, and on the gates were written the names of the twelve tribes of Israel.
The wall had twelve foundations, and on them were the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
The city was laid out like a square, as long as it was wide, and the streets were pure gold, like transparent glass.
The gates of the city were never shut, because there is no night there.
I did not see a temple in the city, John wrote, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.
The city does not need the sun or the moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and the Lamb is its lamp.
The nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their splendor into it.
Then the angel showed him the river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb down the middle of the great street of the city.
On each side of the river stood the tree of life, bearing twelve crops of fruit, yielding its fruit every month.
The leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.
No longer will there be any curse.
Do you see what happened?
The garden of Eden is back.
The tree of life that was guarded by angels at the beginning is now open to everyone.
The curse that began in Genesis is gone.
The story that began in a garden ends in a city that has a garden in it.
The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in the city, and his servants will serve him.
They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.
There will be no more night.
They will not need the light of a lamp or the light of the sun, for the Lord God will give them light.
And they will reign for ever and ever.
Why does this matter?
It is the end of the Bible, and it is the promise that the end is good.
Everything God started in Genesis, he finishes. Evil does not win.
Death does not have the last word.
The relationship broken in Eden is fully restored, with God living among his people, face to face.
The book closes with an invitation.
The Spirit and the bride say, come!
And let the one who hears say, come!
Let the one who is thirsty come, and let the one who wishes take the free gift of the water of life.
And the last prayer in the Bible is, come, Lord Jesus.
What does this mean for us today?
It means that what we're living now is not all there is.
If you have lost someone, are in pain, or are weary of a broken world, this is your hope.
One day God will wipe every tear.
That is not wishful thinking.
It is a promise from the one who sits on the throne, who says these words are trustworthy and true.
It also means that what we do now matters.
The city is coming, and we are called to live as its citizens.
We are to love, forgive, and serve now in a way that shows what's coming.
That is why this story is so important.
It is the last page of the Bible, and it answers the question of how the story ends.
It ends with God and his people together, forever, in a world made new.
Whoever is thirsty can come.
